full_text: Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images Anytime the Dallas Cowboys and the Green Bay Packers play one another it’s almost guaranteed to be a slobber-knocker type of game. These two teams genuinely dislike one another and this Week 6 matchup in primetime Sunday night will be no exception. This could be described as a must-win game for the Cowboys and that’s exactly how it should be approached. The Cowboys desperately need to get things back on track and start stringing some wins together and it starts this week against the Packers. To come away with the “W” in hostile territory at Lambeau Field, they’ll need to play much better than they have recently. Below we’ve listed an offensive and defensive player we believe will make a big impact this week. Offense – RB Javonte Williams Javonte Williams rushed for 85 yards and a touchdown on 20 carries the last time these two teams squared off against one another last year that resulted in a 40-40 tie in overtime. He could not only replicate that production Sunday night against the Green Bay Packers, but hit the 100+ rushing yard mark for the first time this season. With his offensive line fully healthy for only the second time this year, they should be clear lanes against a banged up defense. The Packers have been hit pretty hard by the injury bug in back-to-back weeks. First they lost LB Edgerrin Cooper to a season-ending Achilles injury in Week 4 and DT Javon Hargrave to a season-ending Achilles injury as well last week. Those are two big losses Dallas should exploit in the running game by pounding the rock with Williams early and often. By doing this they not only can win time of possession, but kept their defense from getting exposed as well. Defense – DT Quinnen Williams Quinnen Williams is off to a disappointing start in his first full season with the Dallas Cowboys, but there’s still plenty of time for them to turn things around and it could start this week against the Green Bay Packers. Although Travis Glover has played well in the last two games at right guard, Sunday could be the season debut of Kevin Zeitler. Whether It’s Glover or Zeitler, neither should stop Williams if he’s playing up to his standards. If this comes to fruition like we predict, William should be able to be a disruptive force against both the run and the pass this week. Considering QB Jordan Love prefers to operate within the pocket, continuously making him uncomfortable could negatively impact his production in the passing game, possibly forcing him to make a mistake or two. With all that in mind, we believe Dallas’ All-Pro DT could be a difference maker this week in this Week 6 matchup.

full_text: Photo by David Buono/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Someone has to take the blame. Inevitably in sports, when something goes wrong, blame is assigned. This week, we decided to assign blame for the slow start to the Dallas Cowboys season. A season that began so optimistically with many pundits calling the team a possible contender. Those were the good ol’ days. Today, on the precipice of Week 6 for the team, they have a 2-3 record and the infamous loss at home to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. The team is sputtering and if they get further into a hole, they may not be able to get themselves out. So who is to blame? We put that question to Cowboys fans, and the biggest winner loser in the blame game was none other than Jerry Jones with 43% of the vote. It all starts at the top. The players (21%) and Brian Schottenheimer (19%) came in second and third, well behind Jones. This kind of vote says that fans believe the issue in Dallas is more systemic, it’s baked in as long as Jones is the GM and final word on everything. We also did a confidence poll, and only 13% were confident the team was headed in the right direction. If the Cowboys drop another game in Week 6, things are going to get spicy. They head to Green Bay on Sunday night, now as 1.5-point underdogs. They need the upset in the worst way. For your NFL odds, head over to FanDuel.

full_text: Photo by Stephen Dunn/Getty Images | Getty Images Where is this team headed? Can’t fire the head coach, can’t fire the defensive coordinator, could fire the special teams guy, but won’t. They could bring in some consultants like a defensive consultant (which they kind of did), a special teams consultant, or a game-planning consultant, but probably won’t be doing that either. That pretty much leaves scheme and personnel. If your players can’t communicate, understand, and execute your scheme, you need a new scheme or you need to simplify, simplify, simplify. If your player personnel isn’t good enough, then you’ve got to think about redistributing snaps away from the underperformers towards other players. Five games in, that last point is going to be our focus today, as we look at positional rankings (or percentile rankings) to identify which players elevated their performance more than others and players whose play has deteriorated. We’ve covered positional rankings extensively this offseason, go here if you need a quick primer . The idea is that instead of using a player’s raw PFF Grade, we look at where a given player is ranked relative to the other players in the league at his position, just as we did last week. The results shouldn’t change too much after a full Week 5, so we’re sticking with that original data set.) For individual players, we’ll use their positional ranking. Offensive Line – Finally Trending Up What a great start it’s been for Tyler Guyton. Mike Pettine is the new senior defensive assistant for the Dallas Cowboys, and the hope is that his experience brings some hope to a struggling unit. Cowboys could have new plan for rookie Caleb Downs ahead of Sunday’s showdown vs. Packers – Joseph Hoyt, Dallas Morning News The Cowboys have adjusted how they’ve used Caleb Downs over the last few games due to players being banged up. However, a change back to his original usage could be coming. FRISCO — The Cowboys have used rookie first-round pick Caleb Downs mostly at safety over the last two games due to injuries in the team’s secondary. “That’s not the design for Caleb,” Cowboys coach Brian Schottenheimer said this week. “We want Caleb down near the line of scrimmage.” That could be the design against the Packers on Sunday Pettine ready to lend support, experience to Cowboys’ defense – Todd Archer, ESPN Mike Pettine is now in Dallas after he planned on being away from the league for a while. His mission is to give everything he’s got for his close friend Christian Parker as a senior defensive assistant. The subject of joining the staff was first broached in the winter, but Pettine had recently announced his retirement. Pettine visited the Cowboys in the spring and was with the coaches for a few days. Pettine will be in the coaches booth during games while Parker will remain on the sideline. “I’m just obviously trying to hit the ground running here,” Pettine said. “I feel like I’m trying to sip water from a firehose but trying to get caught up on all the film and make observations here and there. full_text: (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images After a 10-day mini bye week, the Dallas Cowboys return to action on Sunday night, facing off against the Green Bay Packers. While it’s still very early in the season, this feels like a game the Cowboys need to win if they want any shot at winning the NFC East. Before the two teams square off, here are three causes for concern in this matchup. 1) Matthew Golden and Christian Watson’s big-play ability Last week against the division rival Chicago Bears, the Green Bay Packers offense came alive. For the first time since Week 1, the Packers recorded 400+ yards of total offense, reaching 428 total yards to go with 31 points in their victory over the Bears. The biggest reason for Green Bay’s success on offense was their ability to lean on their explosive offensive weapons to record chunk plays. In the game, the Packers recorded three separate receptions of 45 or more yards, including two of 50 or more yards from Matthew Golden and Christian Watson. While Golden and Watson may not have the stats of some of the NFL’s elite receiving duos, both have excellent speed and are two of the most explosive deep threats in the entire league. Last week, for the first time all year, the Packers got both of them going in the same game, leading to the duo wreaking havoc on Chicago’s defense. Golden and Watson combined for 12 catches for 266 yards and two touchdowns in the matchup, each averaging over 20 Y/R. If the Cowboys want any chance of walking out of Green Bay with a win, they’ll absolutely need to limit the big plays by Golden and Watson. That will be easier said than done for this struggling Cowboys’ defense. 2) Packers’ defense forcing turnovers Another big factor in their blowout victory last week was the ability of Green Bay’s defense to register takeaways. The Packers totaled a season-high five takeaways against the Bears, recording three interceptions to go with two fumble recoveries. Since their Week 3 matchup against the Atlanta Falcons, the Packers’ defense has excelled at taking the ball away. They have recorded at least one takeaway in each of their last three games, taking them up to nine on the year, the fourth-most of any team in the league. Talented safety Xavier McKinney has been the catalyst for the Packers’ defense in this department, recording three interceptions in Green Bay’s last three matchups. With all the problems Dallas is having on the defensive side of the ball, the last thing they need in this game is for their offense to turn the ball over. If McKinney and the rest of the Packers’ defense are able to continue and take the ball away, it could be a long night for the Cowboys. 3) Cowboys’ recent history against Green Bay This may sound hard to believe, but Friday, October 16th marks exactly 10 years since the last Cowboys victory over the Packers. Since that 2016 win in Lambeau, Dallas has lost five of their last six matchups against Green Bay, with the only non-loss being the tie last season. If you look back a little further, Dallas is 1-10-1 in the two teams’ last 12 matchups, including a 1-5 record in games at Lambeau Field. While year-over-year trends don’t amount to much in the NFL, it’s hard to look at Dallas’ recent track record against the Packers and not be a bit concerned. Let’s hope the Cowboys flip the script on Sunday.

title: Denver Broncos are 4-2 and in excellent position for a stretch run

In fact, my snap analysis was exactly this: “Frankly, if Denver can get through this stretch of games at or above .500 then we have to chalk that up as a major win.” Here they are at 4-2 and it feels like around Broncos County that we’re reacting to an 0-6 team right now. But here’s the thing, they are 4-2 and nowhere near playing good offensive football. And 4-2 against mostly playoff contenders (ChargersLOL). Denver has gotten through the worst part of their schedule with a winning record and have a chance to reset the whole season. Road games against the Arizona Cardinals and Carolina Panthers with a home game against the Kansas City Chiefs in between. Punch the Chiefs in the mouth and make them doubt Week 1 happened and go into the Bye Week at 7-2. title: Detroit Lions to wear alternate uniforms in each of next 2 games
summary: On Friday night, the Detroit Lions’ social media dropped a not-so-subtle hint about their next uniform combination. On Twitter, the Lions not only tweeted out a photo of a black Lions logo with a bright blue outline, but they also changed their Twitter logo to the same image. Detroit has done this several times in […]
full_text: Jan 5, 2025; Detroit, Michigan, USA; Detroit Lions running back Jahmyr Gibbs (26) and teammates pose for the cameras after his touchdown against the Minnesota Vikings during the second half at Ford Field. Mandatory Credit: David Reginek-Imagn Images | USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con On Friday night, the Detroit Lions’ social media dropped a not-so-subtle hint about their next uniform combination. On Twitter, the Lions not only tweeted out a photo of a black Lions logo with a bright blue outline, but they also changed their Twitter logo to the same image. Detroit has done this several times in the past, and it means only one thing: the black uniforms are coming out this upcoming week. If you’re unfamiliar, the black Lions uniforms—dropped in 2024 and officially called Motor City Muscle—feature a black jersey, black pants, and a popping blue helmet with the black Lions logo. You can see it used in action below. Assuming all the hint dropping is true, the Lions will wear these for their home Week 7 game against the Green Bay Packers next week. The following week, the Lions host the Minnesota Vikings, and they’ve already announced that they will be wearing their new Rivalry Uniforms for that Week 8 divisional matchup . This offseason, the NFL announced and debuted the Rivalry design for all of the NFC North and AFC South teams. The Lions’ uniforms feature an all-grey look with black and blue stripes on the shoulder pads designed to mimic the eyes of a Lion. In Detroit’s debut photoshoot of the Rivalry uniforms , the jerseys and pants were paired with the same blue helmet from the Motor City Muscle uniforms. So we’ve got a couple of weeks of non-traditional Lions uniforms for what will be a pivotal two-game stretch of divisional games out of Detroit’s Week 6 bye.

full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - DECEMBER 4: Brian Branch #32 of the Detroit Lions stretches prior to an NFL football game against the Dallas Cowboys at Ford Field on December 04, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. Now, after their third victory of the season, this time over the Cardinals, fans’ confidence in the team has rebounded again, though not quite to where it was before. But before we get to that, let’s take a look at the results from this survey: Let’s take a closer look at the comment section of our original article and The Feed post to see fans’ explanations for why they voted the way they did (lightly edited for clarity). Most approved/interacted with “right direction” comments: No Username : “Since a “yes” answer implies full confidence, I’ll stay with “no” until I see some consistency in the defense, and steady performance against better teams.“ Matt48912 : “I answered “no” because I am not confident right now, but I still think they might be. summary: The Dallas Cowboys (2-3) bring a top-10 offense and the NFL’s worst defense to Lambeau for Sunday Night Football. The Green Bay Packers (3-2) are coming off a 31-7 win over Chicago that included five takeaways by the defense. This sets up as a shootout, and the Packers face the best quarterback and receiver group […]
full_text: (Photo by Sam Hodde/Getty Images) The Dallas Cowboys (2-3) bring a top-10 offense and the NFL’s worst defense to Lambeau for Sunday Night Football . The Green Bay Packers (3-2) are coming off a 31-7 win over Chicago that included five takeaways by the defense. This sets up as a shootout, and the Packers face the best quarterback and receiver group they have seen this season. All three Dallas losses were by fewer than 10 points, and the Cowboys lost at home to winless Tampa Bay as a 9.5-point favorite last week. 2025 recap Dallas went 7-9-1 in Brian Schottenheimer’s first season and missed the playoffs after losing four of its final five games. The offense carried the team: Dak Prescott threw for 4,552 yards (3rd), George Pickens had 1,429 receiving yards (3rd), and Javonte Williams ran for 1,201. The defense was historically bad, allowing 30.1 points per game (last), 251.5 passing yards per game (last), a 47.3% third-down conversion rate (last) and a 109.6 passer rating (31st). Defensive coordinator Matt Eberflus was fired after one season. Key Losses DC Matt Eberflus was fired. DL coach Aaron Whitecotton left for Tennessee. DE Jadeveon Clowney signed with Houston. DE Dante Fowler signed with Seattle. DT Osa Odighizuwa was traded to San Francisco. DT Solomon Thomas was traded to Tennessee. DE Sam Williams signed with Cleveland. DE Payton Turner signed with Detroit. LB Kenneth Murray and S Donovan Wilson left in free agency. LB Logan Wilson and CB C.J. Goodwin retired. WR Jalen Tolbert signed with Miami. C Brock Hoffman signed with Pittsburgh. Key Additions DC Christian Parker came over from the Eagles. Pass game coordinator Derrick Ansley came over from the Packers. DL coach Marcus Dixon came over from the Vikings. Edge Rashan Gary was acquired from Green Bay for a 2027 fourth-round pick. LB/edge Von Miller signed for 1 year, $7.5M. S Jalen Thompson signed for 3 years, $36M. S P.J. Locke signed for 1 year, $5M. CB Cobie Durant signed a one-year deal. LB Dee Winters, DT Otito Ogbonnia and DL Jonathan Bullard were also added. RB Javonte Williams re-signed for 3 years, $24M. WR George Pickens is playing on the franchise tag. K Brandon Aubrey signed an extension that makes him the league’s highest-paid kicker. S Caleb Downs was a 1st-round pick (No. 11). Edge Malachi Lawrence was a 1st-round pick (No. 23). LB Jaishawn Barham was a 3rd-round pick. OT Drew Shelton, CB Devin Moore and DT LT Overton were 4th-round picks. Schottenheimer still calls the offense. Efficiency, 2026 through Week 5 (SumerSports) Cowboys offense EPA/play: 0.09 (7th) EPA/dropback: 0.16 (~8th) EPA/rush: -0.03 (~10th) Success rate: 47.5% (6th) Points per game: 27.6 Rushing yards per game: 81.6 (29th) Cowboys defense EPA/play allowed: 0.16 (32nd) EPA/dropback allowed: 0.36 (32nd) EPA/rush allowed: -0.02 (~23rd) Success rate allowed: 50.7% (32nd) Rushing yards allowed per game: 168.4 (32nd) Sacks: 5 (29th) Interceptions: 0 Packers offense EPA/play: -0.07 (20th) EPA/dropback: 0.07 (~11th) EPA/rush: -0.33 (32nd) Success rate: 40.1% Rushing yards per game: 60 (32nd) Packers defense EPA/play allowed: -0.10 (8th) EPA/dropback allowed: -0.15 (tied 3rd) EPA/rush allowed: -0.04 (~20th) Success rate allowed: 43.3% Rushing yards allowed per game: 127.6 (24th) Cowboys’ first five games L 20-28 at NYG: lost the opener on the road. W 37-20 vs. WAS: the offense’s best game of the season. L 31-34 vs. BAL (in Rio): lost a shootout; Prescott threw for 276 yards and a TD. W 34-30 at HOU: Dallas rallied from down 16-6 at halftime. Prescott threw for 335 yards, CeeDee Lamb caught 17 passes for 189 yards and the game-winning TD, and Williams ran for three TDs. The defense allowed 347 passing yards to C.J. Stroud. L 16-24 vs. TB: three turnovers (two Prescott interceptions and a special teams fumble), and Lamb left with a quad injury. Keys for Green Bay Find a run game this week. Dallas has allowed a league-high 842 rushing yards, and Green Bay has the league’s worst run game. If the Packers can’t run on this defense, they won’t run on anyone. Let Love cook. The Cowboys allow the most EPA per dropback in the league, have 5 sacks and have no interceptions. Love threw for 367 yards against Chicago, and Christian Watson and Matthew Golden should have room downfield. Limit Lamb and Pickens without Parsons. Micah Parsons is still out, and the cornerback depth is thin. Lamb is questionable with a quad injury, but Prescott plus Pickens is still the best passing attack Green Bay has faced. Keep winning the turnover battle. Green Bay forced five takeaways last week, and Dallas gave the ball away three times against Tampa Bay. Expect familiarity. Rashan Gary returns to Lambeau, and former Packers assistant Derrick Ansley now runs Dallas’ pass game. Kick it straight. Trey Smack missed an extra point and two field goals against Chicago, while Dallas has Brandon Aubrey. In a game projected for 52.5 points, missed kicks can decide it.

full_text: (Photo by Mike Carlson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers announced a flurry of moves on Saturday as the team tries to get their roster in order for their Sunday Night Football matchup against the Dallas Cowboys. The Packers are dealing with several injuries, which led to four players being ruled out on Friday , forcing Green Bay to push up some reinforcements. The Packers placed defensive lineman Jonathan Ford, defensive lineman Javon Hargrave and wide receiver Skyy Moore on the injured reserve today. Those were three of the four players who were already ruled out against the Cowboys, with the non-IR’d player being cornerback Benjamin St-Juste. Backfilling on the game-day roster are receiver Savion Williams, who was activated from the injured reserve on Saturday, and elevated practice squadders Arron Mosby (edge) and Coleman Owen (receiver). Below is a full breakdown of the Packers’ position groups heading into the game, including their injury statuses. Quarterback Jordan Love Tyrod Taylor Running Back MarShawn Lloyd Pierre Strong Jr. Kaleb Johnson Receiver Christian Watson Matthew Golden Bo Melton Savion Williams (questionable) J. title: Majority of Packers fans expect Green Bay to be a playoff team
summary: What a difference a week makes. Heading into last Sunday’s game against the Chicago Bears, Green Bay Packers fans were still pretty down about their team. Despite a win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers the week before, Cheeseheads still overwhelmingly expected the team to finish under .500 in the division and confidence in the team’s […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WI - JANUARY 8: The Green Bay Packers take the field before the NFC Wild Card game against the New York Giants at Lambeau Field on January 8, 2017 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Dylan Buell/Getty Images) | Getty Images What a difference a week makes. Heading into last Sunday’s game against the Chicago Bears, Green Bay Packers fans were still pretty down about their team. Despite a win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers the week before, Cheeseheads still overwhelmingly expected the team to finish under .500 in the division and confidence in the team’s overall direction hovered at around 25 percent. Beating your biggest and oldest rivals in a blowout fixes a lot of concerns, however, and that’s exactly what the Packers did with a 31-7 shellacking of Ben Johnson’s crew. As a result, fan sentiment has bounced back dramatically, starting with expectations for the team to make the postseason now that they are sitting at 3-2 and squarely in the playoff hunt in the NFC. With Green Bay currently holding the #5 seed in the far-too-early NFC playoff picture, we at Acme Packing Company felt it time to take the temperature of our readers on their level of playoff expectations. Sportsbooks like FanDuel still think it’s less than a 50/50 shot for the Packers to make the postseason — that book has Green Bay’s odds at +156 — but Packers fans, at least, have a much more optimistic view of the team now that they have a dominant win on the books. That’s right, a full two-thirds of those who responded to our survey say they think the Packers will be playing meaningful football past Week 18: Interestingly, however, there is a small group of fans who are not confident in the team’s overall direction despite thinking that they will be a playoff team. Our confidence index sits at just 59%, up massively from the 24% rating a week ago but still lagging behind the playoff expectations. If you’re one of those who expect a playoff berth but still aren’t confident in the team’s direction, we want to know why. Is it simply a matter of expectations? Are you defining “the right direction” as requiring the team to land a top seed and be a top-level Super Bowl contender? Or is it something else? Please let us know in the comments if you’re one of those fans and what your thought process was in voting that way.

title: ESPN: Josh Jacobs has spoken to the NFL in their investigation
summary: According to ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler, the NFL has had a discussion with Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs, which is an important piece of information now that he’s been reinstated by the league and removed from the commisioner exempt list. Here is Fowler’s relevant quote on the subject and the corresponding video, which touches […]
full_text: (Photo by John Fisher/Getty Images) | Getty Images According to ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler , the NFL has had a discussion with Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs, which is an important piece of information now that he’s been reinstated by the league and removed from the commisioner exempt list . Here is Fowler’s relevant quote on the subject and the corresponding video, which touches on multiple league-wide topics beyond just Jacobs’ standing with the NFL: They ruled that he is off the commisioner exempt list starting on Monday. So, to start Week 7, he can go back to the team facility with the Packers, work his way back into the lineup for Week 7. Now that doesn’t mean that the investigation into his domestic incident is over. I’m told that is ongoing, but I talked to the attorney of the woman in the case, who said she has not participated in the investigation part. She has not been interviewed, due to privacy concerns. Josh Jacobs, I heard, has talked to the NFL. So a lot of legwork is done. They key here, Kevin, is the video that does exist, parties involved are trying to keep the video from being released. The police locally are trying to get it released. Does it ever come to light is the question? If it does, the league could step back in and create a longer suspension. Running through QBs ailments (Penix, Caleb, Hurts) as well as the latest on Josh Jacobs @SportsCenter with @KevinNegandhi pic.twitter.com/VHmPG3G2nM — Jeremy Fowler (@JFowlerESPN) October 16, 2026 This is the first time that it’s been reported that Jacobs has been interviewed as part of the league’s investigation. Previously, reports stated that Jacobs had not talked with the NFL — at those points in time. Here is why Jacobs’ talk with the league is a pretty important piece of information: When Ray Rice was suspended in 2014, the league initially suspended Rice for two games, after he had his discussion with the league about his domestic incident. When the video of Rice’s domestic violence incident was released to the public, the NFL punished Rice further, giving him an indefinite suspension. When Rice appealed the second suspension, on the grounds that he was already punished once for the same personal conduct violation, a judge ruled in Rice’s favor , stating that the league had to reinstate Rice back into the league and pay him out for games missed because he never misled the league during his interview during the NFL’s investigation. In short, Rice was truthful with the league, so the league had no basis to punish Rice more severely, just because a video caused a public reaction that the NFL did not want to deal with. In the eyes of the judge, the video did not change whether or not the league had all the information they needed to make their initial suspension of Rice, even if the NFL wanted to escalate the suspension due to the public’s reaction to the video. Because of the lessons learned in the Rice case, the league has taken a different approach with the Jacobs case. Instead of suspending Jacobs initially, they allowed him to spend six weeks on the commisioner exempt list — which is technically not a suspension, as Jacobs continued to get paid while he was unavailable for the Packers. The NFL only gets to press the suspension button once for the same personal conduct violation, as long as they aren’t misled during their investigation, but the league appears to be maneuvering in a way to reserve its right to suspend Jacobs in case the video in this dispute causes a negative public reaction — even if Jacobs was being truthful with them in their investigation up to his return in Week 7. Their one chance to hit the suspension button is still preserved. Financially, Jacobs has not been punished directly by the league in any way up to this point, but the NFL will likely announce an official suspension for the running back when the dust finally settles on the fate of the video. As a reminder, time on the exempt list will count as time served toward a suspension. Both Jacobs and the victim in the case are suing the Hobart-Lawrence Police Department to keep the video sealed , and the filing claims that the police department has 20 days to respond from October 14th. — Update: I have received an email from Brian Glicklich, the CEO of Digital Strategy Ltd., a self-described crisis communications and reputation management firm , who sent the following statement on behalf of attorneys Clarence F. Duchac III, David Z. Chesnoff and Richard A. Schonfeld — Jacobs’ representation: Josh has dedicated the last several months to bettering himself, and he accepts responsibility for his actions. He is excited to get back to work and on the field with his teammates. Josh is grateful for the support he is receiving from his teammates, coaches, the Packers organization, and the greatest fans in the world. Since there are ongoing legal matters, he will not have any further comment.

title: How the Packers’ defense is pressuring into interceptions
summary: The Green Bay Packers defense is climbing out of the bottom of the NFL’s worst defenses after a lopsided Week 3 loss to the Falcons, turning in a five-turnover performance in Week 5. They ranked 26th in EPA per play after Week 3 and now rank 14th after Week 5. While their run defense EPA […]
full_text: (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers defense is climbing out of the bottom of the NFL’s worst defenses after a lopsided Week 3 loss to the Falcons, turning in a five-turnover performance in Week 5. They ranked 26th in EPA per play after Week 3 and now rank 14th after Week 5. While their run defense EPA per play and run defense success rate allowed remain below league average, the Packers defense is surviving on the strength of their pass defense. In week five, they forced Tyson Bagent and Case Keenum into three interceptions. The quality of quarterbacks faced might not be anything but below average, but the pass coverage unit shows on tape that they are sound in their assignments regardless, meaning they don’t give up ground or space easily within their play calls. First interception The first interception came with 5:39 remaining in the first quarter on a 2nd-and-10. Tyson Bagent was the Bears starter this game until Keenum took over late in the game. Bagent brought the offense out in an 11 personnel shotgun formation to run a 3×1 dagger concept Ben Johnson has used to carve up opposing teams in the secondary. The Packers are playing cover-8 “trix” once the formation motions to a 3×1. In cover-8, the coverage plays cover-2 to the trips passing strength while the backside safety keys in on the final #3 receiver or the deepest crossing route. Luther Burden is the receiver sent in motion running the dig route from behind the bunch receivers who are running deeper crossing routes across the field. Bagent is looking for the dig route and tried to rip the pass over Javon Bullard gaining depth in the vertical hook under the dig. Bullard tipped the pass up, allowing safety Xavier McKinney to run under the tipped ball from his deep half safety zone. Second interception Bagent’s second interception came with 41 seconds left in the third quarter and down 23-7 on a pass intended for Colston Loveland. The pass was intercepted by McKinney again. The Bears started in an empty 3×2 formation with trips to the right. Bagent is targeting Loveland running the dig route on a two receiver wrap concept with a short curl route under the dig. The intent is to pull up the curl flat player to the curl route and hit the dig in the window between the curl flat and weak hook defender. The Packers are playing cover-3 strong buzz rotation with the safety buzzing down to the strong hook toward the nickel, what Gannon would “Ralph” rotation (rotation to the right to the nickel). McKinney, as the strong hook defender, reads Bagent’s eyes the whole way and with no one threatening his zone, McKinney works to the middle of the field to play the pass to Loveland. Bagent is late on the throw, has to try to fit the pass over the hook defender, and throws it too far in front of Loveland and right into the hands of McKinney, who started from the far hash. Third interception The third interception came with 12:58 left in the 4th quarter. Case Keenum was in for Bagent, who drove the offense into the red zone before turning it over on a hurried throw with pressure in his face. The Bears were in an empty 3×2 formation again here on 4th and goal from the 9-yard line. Keenum tried to hit Rome Odunze on a double move over the middle but Ty’Ron Hopper came racing over from his quarter/flat zone to intercept the pass. The defense is in red zone quarters where they first show pressure and a cover-0 look. Hopper and Zaire Franklin back out of the blitz but Keenum is already changing the protection to slide right in case he gets a free runner off his right edge. The result is disastrous, though. The protection slide away from Lukas Van Ness proved to be costly. Van Ness came off the offense’s left edge untouched as the left tackle took his block inside to the inside rusher. Van Ness forced Keenum to drift away from the pocket and throw across his body to Odunze. Hopper read his eyes the whole way and came over from his zone to make the interception at the goal line where he eventually returned it out to the 20-yard line. The Packers coverage will be tested on Sunday night as the Cowboys come into Green Bay eager to get back on track after a brutal loss to the Buccaneers in week 5. The Cowboys like to throw deep, and the combination of CeeDee Lamb and Dak Prescott is nothing to scoff at.
author: Rich Madrid

title: 3 Big Picture Thoughts From Pittsburgh: What NEEDS to Be Fixed vs. Tennessee
summary: The Colts had a somewhat predictable loss in Pittsburgh last week. Given the rest edge, it was easy to tell that the Colts would have a large mountain to climb. A win, in my mind, would have been quite impressive. The Colts had to come back from London and then go on the road to […]
full_text: The Colts had a somewhat predictable loss in Pittsburgh last week. Given the rest edge, it was easy to tell that the Colts would have a large mountain to climb. A win, in my mind, would have been quite impressive. The Colts had to come back from London and then go on the road to play a team that had an embarrassing loss on Thursday night. That being said, it some ways even uglier than I thought it would be, particularly on defense. 1.The Communication on Defense hasn’t improved, and it’s very concerning Jaylen Warren scores his first TD this season. …. an 80-yarder! pic.twitter.com/AYVvPrb9vu — Underdog NFL (@UnderdogNFL) October 11, 2026 This was a rep that was an immediate red flag. No throw to the flat should ever go for a score, so the first thing we can call out is the tackling. Obviously the tackling and effort to fly to the football is less than ideal. Mooney Ward should be fighting to get off the block. But what’s even more concerning is how the Colts got there in the first place. This is as basic a look as you can possibly get in the NFL. It’s 2×2 and there’s no change of strength motion, no direct picks or rubs, it’s a static look. Warren is the hot into the flat. He is the “Fast #3”. In zone match coverages, there has to be answer for the RB running fast to the flat. Some defenses will “push” the flat to the nickel since he’s better leveraged to make that play. Others will ask the LB to match that flat. The issue in this case, is that both Walley and Bryce Boettcher are playing techniques assuming the other is on the same page. They weren’t and Warren is an uncovered hot. Lou Anarumo in his press conference alluded to Bryce Boettcher having a technique issue on the play, which would suggest that it was his responsibility to “peel” and take the RB into the flat. Nick Saban, Kirby Smart, Dan Lanning defenses often “push” a Fast #3 in Rip/Liz or 3 match coverage, so maybe he reverted back to what he was used to doing at Oregon. Either way, it’s not good and it’s pretty concerning. It’s on the coaches and it’s on the young players. I have never installed a NFL defense, but I do feel confident in saying that this is a look that probably should be mastered early into training camp. 2.As a result, the Colts are already abandoning their plan to get younger on defense. That is also concerning. The Colts signed Germaine Pratt to the practice squad, who actually had some moments of really good football for the Colts. I think back to the Chiefs game in particular. That being said, I struggle to find another way to look at this other than the coaches are simply waiving the white towel. Does that mean the players the Colts drafted just aren’t good enough? Does it mean the coaches aren’t coaching well enough? Maybe both? But if Germaine Pratt plays meaningful reps on Sunday, there’s no other way to look at it than a failure and directly contradictory to the company line this offseason: We need to get younger and faster on defense. This just adds to a laundry list of weird construction of defense this offseason. When the messaging and the on-field product deviate this much from each other, it’s usually a red flag that there’s more at play— the Colts just don’t want to admit it. My best guess is that this system is such a departure from what the Colts have scouted for in Chris Ballard’s tenure, that the front office and the defensive staff just can’t get on the same page for what they are looking for. 3.I think Daniel Jones took a step in the right direction and can still play better. I found it a bit odd the amount of critics Daniel Jones got after the loss on Sunday. That’s not to say the box score was overly generous to him, or that he was lights out. But I thought he took a step in the right direction. The Colts definitively lost the battle up front, could not run the ball, and had a lack of receiver talent that has plagued them all season. Plain and simple, Daniel Jones can be good enough to win you games, but dropping back 40+ times with no run game is not a winning formula. Unless you are an elite of the elite, most QBs need a proper run game to survive. Look at Sam Darnold. I would make the argument that for the most part, Darnold is the same QB he was last year. But without Price and a proper run game, things look different. He’s in an offensive infrastructure that exposes him to more hits and tougher tight window throws when the offense is behind the sicks. The same applies to Daniel Jones and the vast majority of QBs in the league. In my opinion, the Colts need to do more to help him out. Part of that is scheme, but part of that is just the talent around him. I am not closing the book on Daniel Jones playing better, especially as he has more reps under his belt to trust the achilles.

title: Colts need to do what they do best and punch down
summary: The Indianapolis Colts are receiving a much needed gift on Sunday when they host the Titans from Lucas Oil. Nothing is for sure, but the Colts should handle the Titans without too much drama. Expect Jonathan Taylor to run wild and the defense to look strong again. The Titans have been a punching bag for […]
full_text: The Indianapolis Colts are receiving a much needed gift on Sunday when they host the Titans from Lucas Oil. Nothing is for sure, but the Colts should handle the Titans without too much drama. Expect Jonathan Taylor to run wild and the defense to look strong again. The Titans have been a punching bag for the league so far, and with the way the Colts punch down, they have a great opportunity to get back to .500. Under Shane Steichen, the Colts hold a 7-25 (.219) record against teams over .500. That’s not good. What’s even worse is that the majority of those wins happen early in the year. When the going, and their opponent, gets tough, the Colts get going. That inability to beat good teams is what has kept the Colts out of the playoffs during Steichen’s tenure. This team hasn’t risen to the occasion and folds under pressure. Luckily, the pressure will be lighter this week. The Colts can’t lose if they want to keep this season alive because a loss to the Titans could result in a cleaning out of top Colts coaches and personnel. That brings some pressure, but the Titans are 0-5. Steichen’s record against that type of team is 19-5 (.792). It’s great to win the ones you should, but the Colts also have to find a way to win in the toss-ups and marquee matchups as well. Punching down may be enough for the Colts to claw back against the Titans this week. What about the 5-0 and well-rested Minnesota Vikings? Let’s try not to even think about the road contest against the 4-1 Jaguars. If you believe in stats, and if nothing changes, it isn’t looking good. The Colts need to win on Sunday and start playing up to the competition. Punching down only works when you’re better. The Colts might have a hard time finding too many more opportunities where that’s the case.

title: How much is Jonathan Taylor worth on the trade market?
summary: This is the first part of a three-article series looking at the hypothetical trade value of three of the Colts’ biggest stars. We’re starting with Jonathan Taylor. This is not an argument that Indianapolis should trade any of them. In fact, the answer in most cases will probably be the opposite. The idea is to […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PA - OCTOBER 11: Jonathan Taylor #28 of the Indianapolis Colts rushes against the Pittsburgh Steelers in the first half at Acrisure Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Justin K. Aller/Getty Images) | Getty Images This is the first part of a three-article series looking at the hypothetical trade value of three of the Colts’ biggest stars. We’re starting with Jonathan Taylor. This is not an argument that Indianapolis should trade any of them. In fact, the answer in most cases will probably be the opposite. The idea is to look at what would happen if the Colts received serious interest around the trade deadline and determine what each player should realistically be worth. Taylor is the obvious place to start. He is 27 years old, coming off a 1,585-yard season and remains one of the best running backs in football. He has nearly 8,000 career rushing yards, three Pro Bowls and a First-Team All-Pro selection. Even during a relatively inefficient start to 2026, Taylor has six rushing touchdowns through five games and remains the centerpiece of the Colts’ offense. Running backs, however, are difficult to value in trades. The position has been devalued across the league, Taylor has accumulated an enormous workload and a team acquiring him would eventually have to pay the expensive portion of his new contract. So what is he actually worth? The recent trade market gives us a floor and a ceiling There are very few useful running back trades because very few players of Taylor’s caliber ever become available. D’Andre Swift was traded from Detroit to Philadelphia in 2023 for a future fourth-round pick and a swap of seventh-round selections. Swift was only 24 and had averaged 4.6 yards per carry over his first three seasons, but Detroit had just drafted Jahmyr Gibbs and clearly no longer viewed Swift as part of its future. Jay Ajayi provides another useful floor. Philadelphia acquired him from Miami for a fourth-round pick in 2017. Ajayi was also only 24 and was less than a year removed from a 1,272-yard Pro Bowl season. Neither player was Jonathan Taylor. Swift was a good player who had never topped 617 rushing yards in a season before being traded. Ajayi had one excellent season and a much shorter résumé. Taylor has been one of the best running backs in football for most of his career and has already produced multiple seasons that neither player approached. If Swift and Ajayi were worth fourth-round picks, I have a difficult time seeing any scenario where a fourth is enough for Taylor. To me, that establishes the absolute bottom of the conversation rather than his actual value. The much more useful comparison is Christian McCaffrey. San Francisco acquired McCaffrey midway through the 2022 season for a 2023 second-round pick, third-round pick and fourth-round pick, plus a fifth-round pick in 2024. That is obviously a massive haul for a running back, and Taylor probably would not get quite that much. McCaffrey was 26 when San Francisco acquired him, roughly a year younger than Taylor is now, and his receiving ability made him uniquely valuable. He was essentially an elite running back and high-end receiving weapon in one player. Taylor is also carrying considerably more mileage, which becomes important when projecting what a contender would actually be buying. Still, Taylor belongs much closer to the McCaffrey end of this spectrum than the Swift end. How much high-level football does Taylor have left? I have written about the “running back wall” several times because running backs tend to have a much more dramatic decline curve than most positions. In my most recent update , I used approximately 3,300 combined college and NFL touches as the baseline point where heavily used backs tend to begin declining. It is not a magical number where a running back suddenly becomes bad. There is roughly a 600-touch standard deviation around it, meaning some players fall off much earlier and others remain productive well beyond it. Taylor is now around 2,800 combined touches between Wisconsin and Indianapolis. At his current workload, he is on pace for close to 390 touches this season, which would put him a little above 3,100 by the end of the year. Using the 3,300-touch baseline, he would probably reach the historical wall sometime during the 2027 season. That sounds concerning until you put it in the context of a deadline trade. A team acquiring Taylor around the middle of this season would get the remainder of 2026 and all of 2027 before age and workload become a major concern. Even if he crosses the 3,300 threshold sometime next season, that number is an average rather than an expiration date. Taylor is also a better athlete than the average running back included in these studies. I would feel comfortable projecting roughly another season and a half of high-level Taylor, with 2028 becoming the uncertain year. That still has considerable value to a contender. Teams making deadline trades are generally not worried about what a player will look like four years from now. They are trying to win a Super Bowl in the current window. If Denver, Green Bay or another contender believes Taylor could materially improve its chances over the next two postseasons, what happens when he is 30 is not particularly relevant. And even if the decline begins during the back half of the contract, the acquiring team controls him through 2028. Taylor does not have to remain the best running back in football for the entire deal to provide value. His contract is actually helpful for a deadline trade Taylor signed a two-year, $44 million extension before the season that keeps him under contract through 2028. The expensive portion of the new deal essentially begins next year. A team trading for him during 2026 would have a relatively inexpensive immediate cost. Taylor’s 2026 base salary is $6.98 million, and Indianapolis has already paid the signing bonus. An acquiring team would only be responsible for the remaining portion of his base salary and applicable bonuses for the rest of this season rather than taking on the Colts’ prorated signing-bonus charges. That makes fitting him under the cap at the deadline fairly easy. The bigger commitment comes afterward. Taylor is scheduled for roughly $16 million in cash in 2027 and approximately $18 million in 2028. That is premium running back money, but a contender trading meaningful draft capital for Taylor would obviously be doing so because it considers him a premium running back. The contract also provides certainty. A team is not trading a second-round pick for a rental that could leave four months later. It gets Taylor for three playoff pushes. Who could actually want him? There has to be a market for any trade-value projection to make sense, and I can see several teams where Taylor would provide a major upgrade. Denver might be the cleanest fit. The Broncos are 4-2 and have one of the better defenses in football, but the offense remains inconsistent. They managed only 168 total yards in Thursday night’s win over Seattle, with the defense again doing most of the heavy lifting. J.K. Dobbins is their veteran lead back, but his extensive injury history makes him difficult to rely on as the centerpiece of a championship run. Taylor would give Sean Payton a legitimate workhorse and take pressure off Bo Nix on a team that appears capable of winning now. Denver also retains its own first-, second- and third-round picks in 2027, so the draft capital is there. Green Bay is fascinating for a different reason. The Packers have always placed a major emphasis on the running game in recent years, but Josh Jacobs has created uncertainty. He rushed for 929 yards at 4.0 yards per carry last season, a noticeable step down from his best years, and he has yet to play in 2026 after spending the start of the season on the commissioner’s exempt list. He is now eligible to return, but his long-term future in Green Bay is hardly…

title: Chiefs need to stay on their toes against winless Chargers
summary: It’s hard to call a division matchup a trap game, but the (4-0) Kansas City Chiefs must avoid overlooking the winless Los Angeles Chargers on Sunday afternoon. According to Tom Pelissero, formerly of NFL Network, now with The Ringer and Netflix, the Chargers are “rejecting trade calls” because the team believes it is close to […]
full_text: (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s hard to call a division matchup a trap game, but the (4-0) Kansas City Chiefs must avoid overlooking the winless Los Angeles Chargers on Sunday afternoon. According to Tom Pelissero, formerly of NFL Network , now with The Ringer and Netflix , the Chargers are “rejecting trade calls” because the team believes it is close to turning it around after an 0-5 start. There are no plans for “a fire sale.” That narrative could change if the Chiefs take care of business this weekend, but if Kansas City lets Los Angeles get its bounceback performance and pick up a win in the AFC West along the way, it could be the turning point the Chargers need to regroup. Head coach Andy Reid understands the Chargers’ desperation. A Reid-led Chiefs team once started 1-5 before ripping off enough consecutive wins to make the postseason in 2015. During his press conference on Friday, Reid warned that Kansas City needs to stay alert and avoid getting caught off guard by an offensive mind looking to manufacture a win with a lengthy injury report . “Well, you expect the unexpected,” Reid said when asked about Chargers offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel. “He’s a sharp mind and very creative, so you’ve got to be on your toes. He does a nice job. (Chargers Head Coach) Jim (Harbaugh), likewise. I mean, you have two guys in there that are real good football guys, offensive minds.” Los Angeles will be without its two starting offensive tackles — Joe Alt and Rashawn Slater — along with its top wideout this year: Tre Harris. It’s hard to know what the unit could look like with all the injuries, and the Chargers could play into the ambiguity to pull off a major upset. With their season at a clear pivot point ahead of a Week 7 bye, Los Angeles will go all-out for a win in Arrowhead Stadium on Sunday. On offense, defense and special teams, the Chiefs must be prepared for anything, because the Chargers will play like they have nothing to lose.
author: Ron Kopp Jr.

title: Kingdom Keys: 3 Keys to a Chiefs victory over the Chargers in Week 6
summary: Following an early bye week, the Kansas City Chiefs return to action Sunday against the winless Los Angeles Chargers. Kansas City is 4-0, while Los Angeles has lost its first five games and is averaging fewer than 17 points. But the Chargers remain a dangerous divisional opponent — especially for a Chiefs team potentially missing […]
full_text: (Photo by Kirby Lee/Getty Images) | Getty Images Following an early bye week, the Kansas City Chiefs return to action Sunday against the winless Los Angeles Chargers. Kansas City is 4-0, while Los Angeles has lost its first five games and is averaging fewer than 17 points. But the Chargers remain a dangerous divisional opponent — especially for a Chiefs team potentially missing two important wide receivers. Rashee Rice missed the first two practices of the week with hamstring and knee injuries. Tyquan Thornton is sidelined after dislocating his ankle against the Las Vegas Raiders. That places additional responsibility on Kansas City’s young pass-catchers as it attempts to remain undefeated. Here are three keys to a Chiefs victory in Week 6. Offensive key: Young receivers — and Travis Kelce — must win their matchups The Chargers’ record shouldn’t overshadow their ability to pressure opposing quarterbacks. Los Angeles has recorded 11 sacks through five games, ranking in the top half of the league despite its winless start. With Kenneth Walker III leading one of the NFL’s most productive rushing attacks, the Chargers will likely emphasize stopping the run and forcing Kansas City’s young receivers to beat man coverage. That makes this an important game for Xavier Worthy, Jalen Royals and Cyrus Allen. Andy Reid can help them by leaning on play-action, pre-snap motion and route combinations that create natural separation. However, those receivers will eventually have to win individual matchups and find openings when Los Angeles drops into zone coverage. Patrick Mahomes needs dependable targets who can keep the offense on schedule, especially on third down. Travis Kelce should also have a larger role . He was targeted only four times against the Raiders, finishing with two receptions for 15 yards. Chargers safety Derwin James will not play because of his hamstring injury, so Kansas City must exploit his absence in the middle of the field. Kelce doesn’t necessarily need another 100-yard performance, but he should be one of Mahomes’ primary answers under pressure. If Kelce controls the middle and the young receivers consistently separate outside, the Chargers will have a difficult time committing additional defenders to Walker. Defensive key: Sack Nation must return The Chiefs have created pressure but haven’t consistently finished plays. Kansas City enters this matchup with only four sacks — the fewest in the NFL — and a league-low sack rate of 2.6%. Its 24% pressure rate is closer to the league average, showing defenders are reaching the pocket but not taking quarterbacks to the ground. Against Las Vegas, the Chiefs recorded 10 quarterback hits but failed to sack the quarterback for the third straight game. This is the week that must change. Quarterback Justin Herbert has already been sacked 17 times, including five times in last week’s loss to Denver. The Chargers are also dealing with extensive injuries along their offensive line. Starting tackle Rashawn Slater is on injured reserve, while tackle Joe Alt and guard Kayode Awosika missed the first two practices this week. The Chargers were forced to start four rookies along the line against Denver. That gives Chris Jones, George Karlaftis, and the rest of Kansas City’s defensive front its best chance to finish the pressures it has been generating. Karlaftis produced 11 pressures and seven quarterback hits against the Raiders , while Jones has yet to record a sack this season. The goal should be at least three sacks and consistent hits on Herbert. Steve Spagnuolo can attack Los Angeles’ inexperienced blockers with twists, simulated pressures and carefully timed blitzes. More importantly, Kansas City’s front four must win enough matchups to prevent Herbert from becoming comfortable. Pressures matter. This week, however, the Chiefs need to turn them into drive-ending sacks. X-factor: Avoid the trap-game mentality The Chargers are 0-5. The Chiefs are undefeated, rested and playing at home. That combination makes it easy to see this game as an automatic Kansas City win. It is not. Los Angeles is still a division rival with an experienced quarterback. A winless team would love nothing more than to earn its first victory by handing an undefeated rival its first loss. The Chiefs’ coaching staff must ensure the players approach this matchup with the same urgency they carried into their early-season games against Denver and Las Vegas. Kansas City cannot allow turnovers, penalties, or defensive breakdowns that keep the Chargers within one possession late. The Chiefs should play aggressively from the opening drive, build an early advantage, and continue attacking rather than becoming conservative. The longer an underdog remains within striking distance, the more confident it becomes. Kansas City must stay focused — and keep its foot on the gas — for all four quarters. The bottom line The Chiefs cannot expect Kenneth Walker III to carry the offense every week, especially when the Chargers will likely build their defensive plan around slowing him down. Kansas City’s young receivers must create separation, while Travis Kelce needs to control the middle of the field—especially if Derwin James cannot play. Defensively, the Chiefs must exploit Los Angeles’ depleted offensive line by turning recent pressures into at least three sacks and several hits on Justin Herbert. Most importantly, Kansas City must respect its winless division rival and play with urgency from beginning to end. If the Chiefs accomplish those three things, they should avoid the trap, improve to 5-0 and continue strengthening their early position atop the AFC West.

Like Hunter, Tonga has started every game on defense this season. Like Hunter, Tonga has played only limited offensive snaps this season. Tonga has two carries; Hunter has two catches. Both have picked up one first down. Hunter plays a little bit more on offense, but not much more: Hunter has played 6.8 percent of the Jaguars’ offensive snaps, while Tonga has played 4.2 percent of the Chiefs’ offensive snaps. Cooper, 28, was placed on the list Aug. 30 and was ineligible to play or practice with the team during the first six weeks of the season. His placement on the list was the result of two June arrests stemming from a pair of domestic incidents with his then-girlfriend. Cooper is facing multiple charges, including a second-degree felony assault charge, and is currently scheduled for a trial date in March. When he comes off the list next week, Jacobs will have missed the first six games of the season, and those games would count toward any suspension. However, if Jacobs ends up getting suspended for more than six games, he will have to miss additional games to make up the difference. There is still a chance Hurts eventually ends up on injured reserve, if that is the direction the medical information leads them. title: Chargers-Chiefs Game Preview: 3 things to watch in Week 6
summary: It’s Chargers-Chiefs this week and as much as I’d like to be able to say this one is for sole possession of first place in the AFC West, I cannot. One team is winless and the other is undefeated. This one does not look good on paper. By records alone, it also doesn’t look like […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 27: Defensive co-ordinator Chris O'Leary and inside linebacker coach Sean Spence of the Los Angeles Chargers celebrate a stop of the Los Angeles Rams on fourth and goal during the first half in a preseason game between the Los Angeles Rams and the Los Angeles Chargers at SoFi Stadium on August 27, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Harry How/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s Chargers-Chiefs this week and as much as I’d like to be able to say this one is for sole possession of first place in the AFC West, I cannot. One team is winless and the other is undefeated. This one does not look good on paper. By records alone, it also doesn’t look like a fun watch for anyone that isn’t already a fan of either team. But hey, it’s a divisional matchup that has given us plenty of entertaining watches over the last decade. More than likely this one will still do the same. That said, here are three things I’ll be watching closely when these teams take the field on Sunday. 1.) What will the offense look like just one week before the bye? There’s a very strong chance the Chargers simply play it safe with their numerous injuries and use this week as one more opportunity to see what the bottom of the roster has within them. Wide receivers Ladd McConkey, Quentin Johnston, and Brenen Thompson are all hobbled and have been limited through the first two practices this week. Tre’ Harris is in even worse shape as he has been a DNP thus far. KeAndre Lambert-Smith just had his 21-day window activated and it looks like he’s trending to return this week. That development may lead the Chargers to take a cautious approach with their top guys just one week from the bye. Let’s just be honest, the offense honestly looks no better no matter who is out there unless it’s a healthy McConkey. He hasn’t been healthy since Week One and it’s about time we let him get to 100 percent before he steps back out on the field. Right now, Justin Herbert’s healthy receivers are Theo Wease, Derius Davis, and Marquez Valdez-Scantling. On the practice squad, they have Gary Jennings and the recently-signed Luke Grimm. Jennings is out of game day elevations which means he’d have to be signed to the active roster in order to participate against the Chiefs. With Alec Ingold now on IR, Jennings could take that spot if the team chooses. As for the offensive line, will they send out four rookies for another week? Will veteran Daniel Brunskill learn the offense enough to start at right tackle for Alex Harkey? We’ll have to see come game day. UPDATE: Both Ladd McConkey and Quentin Johnston were removed from the final injury report meaning Justin Herbert will have his two top wideouts back this Sunday. 2.) Will Omarion Hampton continue to see his snaps share decrease? Hampton played only 31.7 percent of the offense’s snaps against the Broncos, although he did receive over 40 percent of the running back carries. With each week, Hampton is playing less and less. Kimani Vidal’s huge 42-yard touchdown rumble will not do him any favors in getting back anywhere lose to workhorse duties. It also doesn’t help that Mike McDaniel continues to force Keaton Mitchell into the game plan to run sweeps to specifically the right side. Defenses know what’s coming when either back is in, which can’t be good for a Chargers offense that already isn’t fooling anyone in anyway. The Chiefs have a great defense. Their linebackers can fly, hit hard, and blitz. Chris Jones is still a menace along the interior and George Karlaftis is an ascending pass rusher. They’re about to face a very young Chargers offensive line and it may not even matter which running back is in. Hampton, in my opinion, is still the Chargers’ most talented back. I don’t think he’s a timeshare guy and his ability to punish deep into the fourth quarter was an aid to the Bolts last season as they closed out games with the ball in their hands. It’d be nice to get back to that kind of football. But seeing how things are going, we may never see that again (at least, maybe until next year?). 3.) Can Chris O’Leary’s defense continue their strong start against another elite offense? After a rough outing in Week One against the Cardinals, O’Leary’s unit has been one of the best in the entire league the past four weeks. Check out these numbers: Chris O’Leary’s #Chargers defense over the last 4 games: – 5th in EPA/play – 7th in success rate – 5th in dropback/EPA – 11th in EPA/rush – 6th in dropback success rate – 14th in rushing success rate pic.twitter.com/agcgGawueE — Guilty As Charged Podcast (@GACPodcast17) October 12, 2026 Despite not having Derwin James and Donte Jackson in their past two games, they’re still a top-1o unit in EPA/play, success rate, and dropback/EPA. The efficiency is insane for a group that’s far and away the leader in most drives started within their own territory (18!). Compared to the Saints who are second with 11, that’s even more unreal. They got Josh Allen and the Bills to turn the ball over five times and helped put a lid on both Sam Darnold and Bo Nix the past two weeks. Now they will face Patrick Mahomes and the revitalized Chiefs offense that now features Kenneth Walker and a highly-productive rushing attack. O’Leary doesn’t need the team to win this game for it to be a personal “W” in his book. If the defense does their part, records a turnover or two, and helps keep this one close, no one will be able to say another word about his group not pulling their weight.

(Photo by C. Morgan Engel/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Los Angeles Chargers are facing off against the Kansas City Chiefss in Week 6 at Arrowhead Stadium hoping to secure their first win of the season. The Chargers have lost their first five games and have been arguably the more disappointing teams in the league. However, the Chargers can turn things around with a win against the undefeated Chiefs. Per FanDuel Sportsbook , the Chargers are an underdog by 7.5 points. Let’s take a look at some predictions for the game. Over/Under: 41.5 Only one of the five games so far this season has seen a Chargers game score more than 41.5 points. That came in Week 4 against the Seattle Seahawks, but against an offense like the Chiefs, which has the potential to break out on any given Sunday, this number could hit. That said, based on how the Chargers’ offense has performed and the Chiefs’ desire to make it more of a defensive game, I like the under in this one. Prediction: Under Chargers +7.5 FanDuel is giving the Chargers 7.5 points to start the game. The Chargers lost by more than a score in each of their first two weeks, but have kept things close in the last three. Their 23-17 loss against the Denver Broncos in Week 5 was the closest margin in a game this season. That being said, playing on the road against the Chiefs is an incredibly daunting task, especially for a team that is dealing with as many injuries as Los Angeles is. The line is fair, and I believe the Chargers will still have a tough time beating the spread. Prediction: Chiefs -7.5 Final Score The Chargers are massive underdogs here for good reason. They are one of the three winless teams in the league, going up against one of the three undefeated teams. They also have to do this on the road while Kansas City is coming off a bye week. title: Rams represent ‘Super Bowl-sized’ game for the Cardinals
summary: The Los Angeles Rams are just trying to right their ship in time to still compete for the NFC West with the San Francisco 49ers and Seattle Seahawks, but for the Arizona Cardinals this Sunday’s game is about more than the playoffs. It’s about finally trying to establish themselves as the fourth team in the […]
full_text: The Los Angeles Rams are just trying to right their ship in time to still compete for the NFC West with the San Francisco 49ers and Seattle Seahawks, but for the Arizona Cardinals this Sunday’s game is about more than the playoffs. It’s about finally trying to establish themselves as the fourth team in the NFC West that anybody will acknowledge. The best division in the NFL is a “three-team division” to most people, with the Cardinals serving as two easy wins for everybody else. Lose either of your games to the Cardinals? Well, that could spell doom — and gloom — for that NFC West team. Not to mention ridicule. The Cardinals beat the L.A. Chargers in Week 1, a game that many considered an upset at the time. “Are the Cardinals a sleeper in the NFC?” they said. They beat the Chargers and the Chargers are good. Well, it turns out everybody beats the Chargers because the Chargers are 0-5. Since then, the Cardinals are 0-4. They haven’t won a game since Week 1 and they’ve allowed an average of 37 points per game in the last four weeks. They’ve lost by an average of 17 points. It wasn’t that people expected Arizona to win the Super Bowl, or even make the playoffs, but being the worst team in the NFL over the past month has to have some people on the Cardinals worried about their jobs. Will Mike LaFleur even survive to see year two? That’s why this game against the Rams is, in many ways, LaFleur’s Super Bowl. In lieu, of course, of an actual Super Bowl. Hired off of Sean McVay’s staff with the intention to built an acceptable offense, LaFleur wasn’t handed much. He inherited Jacoby Brissett, Marvin Harrison, Trey McBride, and Michael Wilson. The team drafted Jeremiyah Love with its first pick. Since then, Harrison has been traded to the Texans. Love is having typical rookie struggles behind a so-so offensive line. Brissett is his usual self, averaging just 5.6 yards per attempt and throwing an interception at a rate of 2.5%, which isn’t good. The Cardinals may be vying for the number one pick, but unfortunately for them they’ve already won a game. The Rams should win this game. If they don’t, it won’t be the Cardinals who have egg on their face. That’s why LaFleur and Brissett will do everything in their power to keep it competitive. Defensive coordinator Nick Rallis may not survive another week if he gives up 40 points. Arizona wants it bad enough. Will that matter?
author: Kenneth Arthur

summary: The Los Angeles Rams look to take advantage of home cooking for a second straight week, hosting the Arizona Cardinals on Sunday October 18. full_text: The Los Angeles Rams look to take advantage of home cooking for a second straight week, hosting the Arizona Cardinals on Sunday October 18. Kickoff from SoFi Stadium is set for 1:05 p.m. PDT. Last Monday night, L.A. (2-3) spilled the beans in their home kitchen, losing an overtime heart breaker to the Buffalo Bills 37-34, while the Cards (1-4) were smacked around by the Detroit Lions 45-21. Through the first five games, the Rams offense has only been generally efficient. Other than the fourth quarter, the L.A. offense has appeared to sputter. Over the last three games, the Rams have went pass-happy, throwing 50+ passes in each and they now lead the NFL in, not only passing yards (1538), but total yards as well (2122). The run game has also been solid, considering its limited usage, with 4.6 yards per carry a solid number. There has been a small disconnect between the yardage points scored. L.A. has scored at a 23.8 clip, down a touchdown per game from last year’s final tally, but in line with what the Rams have done since the Sean McVay and Matthew Stafford union. It hasn’t been a case of the Rams just churning yards between the 20’s. Their touchdown scoring rate from the red zone is 65 percent rate, 9th best in the league, but that rate does drop to 35.7 percent for any type of score over all drives overall (19th best). Since L.A. has a good third down conversion rate, 7th in the league at 44.6 percent, what’s the disconnect? It appears the Rams have had problems just as they cross mid-field. A good measure of that boils down to the weak kicking game. Missing makeable medium length field goals doesn’t just affect that individual drive, it also creates a situation where coaching decisions are compromised. Having to limit the mid/long field goal attempts forces going for it on unfavorable fourth down plays. Hopefully, newly acquired placekicker Blake Grupe can help alleviate some of those concerns and the Rams can get hitting on all offensive cylinders. Here’s how to follow the game! title: Rams Reacts: Fans blame Sean McVay for special teams problems
summary: The Los Angeles Rams have had problems on their specials teams for years, and fans are blaming Sean McVay as the reason. Nearly 57% of fans surveyed are putting the heat on McVay for the special teams woes. According to the data below McVay is taking more of the blame than Bubba Ventrone, and more […]
full_text: The Los Angeles Rams have had problems on their specials teams for years, and fans are blaming Sean McVay as the reason. Nearly 57% of fans surveyed are putting the heat on McVay for the special teams woes. According to the data below McVay is taking more of the blame than Bubba Ventrone, and more blame than Harrison Mevis. The Rams are one of if not the worst special teams units across the board. The unit most recently cost them on Monday Night Football against the Buffalo Bills with a poor opening kickoff leading to three points for Buffalo. Later, a missed Harrison Mevis kick and finally a blocked kick to basically end the game in Buffalo’s favor. McVay’s done plenty right , but if you ask the fans, they are burned-out on McVay getting the special teams so wrong. When it comes to betting at FanDuel , if the Rams are favored by 3 points or less, maybe bet on the other team. The Rams can’t guarantee three points to win a game, cover the spread or save their season. Are the Rams the best tw0-win team in the NFL? 65% of fans surveyed seem to think L.A. is the strongest 2-win team with the most potential. The data says expect the Rams to end the season with the best record out of all the other two-win teams across the league. Whereas, the Rams may be the best two-win team in the league, L.A. had much bigger dreams than being the strongest two-win franchise five weeks into their season. The Rams want to make the playoffs; they want to win the Super Bowl. The Rams still can do this, but they are falling well behind the San Francisco 49ers. Whereas you may want to check FanDuel and bet on the Rams winning more games than not, you also may want to avoid placing any bets on L.A. winning the whole thing, for now. Are you confident the Rams are headed in the right direction? The football season be like a pendulum with big swings back and forth. Last week ,after a win, fan confidence was above 70% , This week, after a loss, fan confidence sits at 33%. The Rams are favored to beat the Arizona Cardinals this week, but imagine if L.A. drops this game? Where will fan confidence be then? It’s been an uphill battle for the team that was expected to be the best in the NFL in 2026. The Rams haven’t looked like the best team in the NFL, their own conference, or their division. They look like a team that’s 2-3. They also look like a team that could be 4-1, or 3-2, but their 2-3. Might be no better time to bet the over on wins for L.A. at FanDuel. May have been the right time to bet the under from the start, or to bet the under again. Bet responsibly.
