title: Bills, Raiders a battle between two keen offensive-minded head coaches
summary: Joe Brady and Klint Kubiak represent a changing of the guard for the NFL. The Buffalo Bills’ and Las Vegas Raiders’ head coaches, respectively, are a pair of hotshot offensive play callers who ascended to the lead role of their franchises this past offseason. And through five games of the 2026 campaign, the neither team […]
full_text: (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images Joe Brady and Klint Kubiak represent a changing of the guard for the NFL. The Buffalo Bills’ and Las Vegas Raiders’ head coaches, respectively, are a pair of hotshot offensive play callers who ascended to the lead role of their franchises this past offseason. And through five games of the 2026 campaign, the neither team regrets the decision to go with offensive coordinators-turned-first-time lead men. The ascension of Brady, the 37-year-old who served as Buffalo’s offensive coordinator last season, appeared inevitable after the Bills dismissed then-head coach Sean McDermott in January following the team’s 33-30 overtime loss to the Denver Broncos in the AFC Division Round of the playoffs last season. Brady has picked up where he left off as he remains the play caller and head coach title as Buffalo (4-1 overall) is the top-ranked scoring offense (164 total points) and fourth-highest yards gained (1,981) in the NFL so far. The Bills red zone offense is the sixth-best with 15 touchdowns on 21 trips in the area between the opponent’s 20-yard line and end zone (a 71.4 percent success rate). Last season, Brady was the architect of Bills’ fourth-best scoring (481) and yards gained (6,397) offense. The red zone performance was impressive too in 2025 as Buffalo scored 43 touchdowns on 65 visits (66.2 percent success rate). #Bills HC Joe Brady, in the nicest and kindest way possible, put RB James Cook on notice over his fumbling issues. Brady said there will be consequences if it continues, including fewer carries. pic.twitter.com/LLv8bKI6k0 — Ari Meirov (@MySportsUpdate) October 13, 2026 Flipping to Kubiak, the 39-year-old has breathed much-needed life into an anemic Raiders offense that ranked dead last in points scored and yards gained in 2025 under a different regime. While many want to forget the abysmal 2025 campaign, the Silver & Black produced just 241 total points and 4,168 total yards which ranked 32nd out of the 32 teams in the league. Currently, Las Vegas (3-2) sits with the eighth-highest scoring offense (132) and 14th-most yards gained (1,678) through five games with Kubiak at the helm and with the play sheet, providing tangible data on why minority owner Tom Brady, general manager John Spytek, and the rest of the Raiders’ decision makers were deliberate and patient to interview and eventually hire Kubiak. There’s areas of opportunity for the Raiders head coach, however, such as a ground game that’s been neutralized and is in the bottom run of the league rankings (28th in yards gained at 402; 27th in rushing touchdowns at just two). Another blemish for Kubiak’s offense is red zone performance as the team has scored just 10 touchdowns on 18 visits (55.6 percent success rate) which ranks 20th in the NFL. That noted, Kubiak’s system has super veteran Kirk Cousins on-point as Raiders quarterback and is using elite tight end Brock Bowers all over the field. The synergy Kubiak has in Las Vegas is clearly lacking from his former team, the Seattle Seahawks (3-3). The Raiders head coach was Mike Macdonald’s offensive coordinator in Seattle and the Seahawks offense has struggled creating that rhythm Kubiak had as he orchestrated the third-best scoring offense (483) and eighth-best yards gained (5,973) for the 2025 Super Bowl champions. The Week 6 clash between the Bills and Raiders inside Allegiant Stadium features two young coaches in their respective AFC divisions (East for Buffalo, West for Las Vegas). And if both can continue their impressive debut seasons and beyond, are the changing of the guard from older and established coaches. Maxx Crosby speaks on the Raiders loss to the Patriots, what Klint Kubiak’s message was, & playing the Bills & Rams the next 2 weeks “The fans should be disappointed. We got whooped, but there are good things on film & things to get better at” pic.twitter.com/OXqBop5hNb — ShifftttyyyQB1✞🏴‍☠️ (@raiders1022) October 14, 2026 But first comes Sunday’s matchup where the Raiders are looking to rebound to keep pace in the AFC West while the Bills are eager to trample another opponent to remain in the AFC East lead. Kubiak heaped praise on Buffalo during his media sessions this week and he made it clear his offense must stay on the field and score points against the high-powered Bills. “Yeah, well, you’ve got to get first downs to stay on the field. So, going three and out and punting the ball back is not the way to go,” Kubiak said. “So, you’ve got to sustain drives. A big part of sustaining drives is not being one-dimensional. So, that’s a part of our team that we got to improve.” Keeping quarterback Josh Allen on the sideline as much as they can will help Las Vegas, especially as the Raiders defense has struggled mightily in the red zone (14 touchdowns allowed on 18 visits; 28th in the league). And Brady is well aware of the Silver & Black’s penchant to create turnovers — even though the Raiders have only one takeaway the last two weeks after forcing nine in the first three games of the season. Ball security is a must for Buffalo as running back James Cook and Allen have four fumbles, apiece. “Right now, we’re putting the ball in harm’s way, and we know that’s the way that we lose football games is we turn the ball over,” Brady said. “James has put the ball on the ground. He’s doing so many good things running the football, and I don’t want to lose sight of how great he is running the ball right now, but we’re putting the ball on the ground, and it’s negating all the positive. “And I have all the confidence in him. That’s why I put him right back out there. But obviously at some point there has to be consequences when we’re putting negative stuff out there. James knows. It’s important to him, but that can’t happen, and it’s going to cost us football games, and it almost cost us that one. So, it’s got to improve, or the carries are going to decrease.” Kubiak said Dont'e Thornton Jr. is "getting closer" to being activated from IR. On what he saw from him this week: "I'm impressed. He's looking good. He's getting back into football shape. Really doing a great job in the meeting room. He's putting himself in position." https://t.co/GcZhA4y0EO — Sam Warren (@samwarren83) October 16, 2026 While both Kubiak and Brady are younger head coaches, the inherent roster differences between the Raiders and Bills is quite the advantage for the Bills. There’s just simply more talent on Brady’s roster than Kubiak’s due, in large part, to Buffalo’s sustained success of seven-straight winning seasons from 2019-25. Las Vegas has only one season in Sin City where they were above .500 — a 10-7 record in 2021, in comparison. That said, stranger things have happened and it’s not out of the realm of possibility for Las Vegas to get a much-needed victory at home. Quotes of Note “Yeah, that’s the best tool. You know, the guys are visual. You can only tell them so much. If you show them, it definitely helps get your point across. That’s definitely something that I like to do, a lot of coaches on our staff like to do. But you got to make the correction somehow, someway. So, whatever hits the player’s brain the fastest you got to use that technique.” —Las Vegas Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak on how game film from last Sunday’s loss helps his team. “Benefits? I don’t know if there are benefits from getting your butt whooped, but you got to know yourself in your area, your strengths and your weaknesses on defense.” —Las Vegas Raiders defensive coordinator Rob Leonard when asked if last Sunday’s game tape benefits the team.
author: Ray Aspuria

title: Raiders Mailbag: Is Spencer Burford offensive line’s biggest problem?
summary: It’s funny how two weeks can dramatically change the tune of an entire season. The Las Vegas Raiders have gone from a feel-good story as one of the biggest surprises in the NFL to feeling like the sky is falling. Back-to-back losses, including an embarrassing blowout in New England last week, will do that. Part […]
full_text: (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s funny how two weeks can dramatically change the tune of an entire season. The Las Vegas Raiders have gone from a feel-good story as one of the biggest surprises in the NFL to feeling like the sky is falling. Back-to-back losses, including an embarrassing blowout in New England last week, will do that. Part of the reason is the Raiders’ offensive line continues to be an issue, as it’s a major point of emphasis in this week’s mailbag (again) heading into Week 6 against the Buffalo Bills . Q: I’ve seen a couple of other guys on Raider Twitter saying that Spencer Burford has been the best guard still, and his PFF grades are more affected because they mostly help the other side. Sorta similar to DJ Glaze. I think Marcus, in one of the TDLs, said he was the best run blocker for that game. He seems to get beat a lot in pass pro every game, though. What do you think about that? Do you feel run or pass pro is more important and that affects the choice? It kinda seems like the guards have all been bad, but at some point the decision is if they are gonna be bad anyway, then you might as well work on the upside of Caleb Rogers or Trey Zuhn III. Also, if the Raiders are gonna throw Fernando Mendoza in there, they’ve gotta protect him better, right? A: When it comes to pass protection versus run blocking at guard, I tend to lean toward the running game . Of course, both are requirements of the position. However, in my opinion, pass protection is easiest at guard — compared to the other two offensive line positions — since they (typically) aren’t responsible for setting the protection and doing the thinking for a group like a center is. Also, guards have help on both sides with a center and a tackle to their left and right, and interior pass-rushers don’t have as much space to operate, unlike blocking on the edge. So while it’s ideal to have a guard who can do both at a high level, personally, I’ll sacrifice some pass-pro issues for a high-level run blocker. Burford is decent in the running game and has had a couple of good outings in that department. For some context, Pro Football Focus gave him a 73.9 run-blocking grade against the Saints and an 81.0 against the Chiefs. One of those two is the game Marcus referenced. However, Burford has a 56.6 mark for the season. To be clear, I’m not trying to say PFF grades are the end-all, be-all; I’m just using them to contextualize the level of “good” versus “bad” and Burford’s performance. The problem is, and this is true pretty much regardless of what website or metric you’re using, he’s given up the most pressures ( 18 ) of any guard in the league and has the fourth-lowest pass protection grade (26.6). To me, just being decent or slightly above-average as a run blocker isn’t worth the liability he’s been when protecting the quarterback, even given my preference for the position. Also, as you mentioned, Mendoza is going to take over at some point. Having a young quarterback shifts the goalposts because putting the future of the franchise behind bad pass protection is organizational malpractice. That’s where even I would say it makes more sense to give a guy like Zuhn, who doesn’t bring much as a run blocker but was good in pass protection at tackle in college, so the rookie signal-caller doesn’t get killed. I think the narrative that Burford was getting less help was true during the first three weeks of the season. However, in the last two games, he’s been getting a lot more help from Kolton Miller in pass protection. When the Raiders want to push the ball down the field, Miller has been staying closer to the line of scrimmage a little longer so that he can help slow the defensive tackle down. More on this in the next question; that’s also part of the left tackle’s issues. At the end of the day, both guards have left something to be desired. Jackson Powers-Johnson continues to be inconsistent, especially as a run blocker, but he’s at least been solid in pass protection. So, he and Burford both could get replaced, and it wouldn’t surprise me if Klint Kubiak does that soon. But, in my opinion, Kubiak at least has to give someone else a shot at left guard. The thing to keep in mind about Burford is that the only reason he started games during his last two years in San Francisco was because of injuries. On top of that, Ben Bartch was the 49ers’ starting left guard in Weeks 1 and 2 before getting injured, and they turned to Connor Colby before Burford after Bartch went down last season. I get the “scheme fit” and “familiarity with the system” line of thinking, but Burford didn’t have the track record to be unchallenged for the starting spot in training camp. If you ask me, it’s time for Kubiak to try someone else at that spot. Q: What is going on with Kolton Miller? Is he injured, or is FatherTime finally catching up with him? A: I got this question last week and defended Miller, saying he only had one bad game at the time. Then, he went out and had another bad game. (Thanks for having my back, Kolton, LOL!). So, I definitely think left tackle is something to monitor for the rest of the year, especially as we creep closer to the offseason and start thinking about team needs. The 31-year-old likely doesn’t have that many years left, after all, and he certainly needs to play better. However, picking up where I left off above, I don’t think it’s a coincidence that Miller’s struggles began the week after Burford gave up a season-high six pressures and posted a 4.0 PFF pass-blocking grade against the Saints. As previously mentioned, the left tackle has been giving the guard more help in pass protection, and the clip Marcus posted below is a good example. This was a bad sack by Cousins. He had Tucker open, and I'm not sure why he came off it. Then just stares down Bowers. Knocked the Raiders out of field goal range. pic.twitter.com/qt56gT2KwL — Marcus Johnson (@TheMarcJohnNFL) October 12, 2026 The endzone view (which starts around the 20-second mark) gives you a good look at what I’m talking about when I say Miller has to stay closer to the line of scrimmage at first. Notice how he doesn’t get much depth on his pass set initially and extends his inside arm. That’s to give the defensive tackle (No. 97) less space to operate and potentially get another hand on the DT to help slow his momentum down for Burford. Compare Miller’s pass set to DJ Glaze’s on the other side. Since the center is turning to the right and able to help JPJ, Glaze doesn’t have to worry about assisting the guard and can get depth immediately. Whereas Miller has to hang tight for a second and then rush to get depth, throwing his footwork and the whole process out of whack because the process has to be sped up. On top of that, Burford loses on the high side of the rush, forcing Kirk Cousins to step up in the pocket. As a result, the edge rusher works back inside and Miller, who can’t see where the quarterback is, gives up a sack. Don’t get me wrong, Miller has to do a better job of staying engaged on the block and staying in front of inside moves is part of playing tackle. But the point I’m making here is that his assignment is more difficult because the guy next to him isn’t getting the job done. So, both guards are getting help in this example. However, one of them was brought in to be a reliable veteran who knows the system, and the other had to fight to retain his starting spot during training camp. Again, a case could be made for both guys to get replaced, but I don’t know how anyone can justify Burford’s level of play this season. And when it comes to Miller, he definitely needs to pick it up, too. But I’d like to see how he plays with someone else next to him. Q: I like outside zone running, but maybe the line, which we thought was suited for it, really isn’t. Why not move JPJ to left guard, where he had played better in the past, and try Evan Neal at right guard and run more power/gap? We need some…

title: Las Vegas Raiders-Buffalo Bills FEED topic: How will offensive line respond?
summary: Heading into their Week 6 matchup against the Buffalo Bills, the 2026 version of the Las Vegas Raiders’ offensive line hasn’t looked very different than last season. The Raiders are averaging just 3.0 yards per carry as a team and, according to Pro Football Focus, 240 of Ashton Jeanty’s 291 rushing yards (82.5%) have come […]
full_text: (Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Heading into their Week 6 matchup against the Buffalo Bills , the 2026 version of the Las Vegas Raiders’ offensive line hasn’t looked very different than last season. The Raiders are averaging just 3.0 yards per carry as a team and, according to Pro Football Focus , 240 of Ashton Jeanty’s 291 rushing yards (82.5%) have come after contact. Additionally, quarterback Kirk Cousins has been under pressure on 41.0% of his dropbacks in Las Vegas’ last two games, per PFF . As a result, head coach Klint Kubiak suggested some changes to the Raiders’ trenches could be coming during his press conference on Monday after the team’s 45-17 loss to the New England Patriots. “We have to look at everything,” Kubiak replied when asked about a potential shuffle to the offensive line, via Silver & Black Sports Network’s Jesse Merrick . “We have to improve there. It’s something I’ve been saying for multiple weeks now that’s not getting done, and so, as a coaching staff, it falls on me. It falls on me to get it fixed.” The Athletic’s Sam Warren added that Kubiak confirmed other linemen will get more opportunities moving forward. In other words, the coach is publicly calling the position group out, and it’s up to them to respond. No one should feel like their spot is safe at this stage, leading to questions about what changes could be in store for Sunday’s game against the Bills. Left guard Spencer Burford seems like the most logical choice to get replaced. Burford has really struggled in pass protection, giving up the most pressures (18) of any guard this season, per PFF . Additionally, his 56.6 run-blocking grade doesn’t inspire much confidence and is tied for 56th out of 81 qualifiers (minimum 85 snaps). Then again, the other guard, Jackson Powers-Johnson, has a case to get replaced, too. Powers-Johnson has been stingier in pass protection with just nine pressures surrendered in four games. However, he’s been a problem in the running game with the fifth-worst run-blocking grade (43.8) at his position. The third-year pro has struggled with consistency throughout his career and had to fend off second-year pro Caleb Rogers during training camp to remain in the starting lineup. That sets up another potential swap. On top of that, Kolton Miller and Tyler Linderbaum were viewed as steadying presences on Las Vegas’ offensive line heading into the campaign. However, both have left something to be desired. Miller has been charged with 12 pressures over the last two weeks, and Linderbaum’s 63.1 PFF grade for the season ranks 19th among centers. The latter isn’t “bad” per se, but it isn’t what the organization bargained for when it made him the highest-paid interior offensive lineman in NFL history, and by a wide margin at that. Granted, it’s highly unlikely that those two are in danger of losing their respective spots at this stage. But there is certainly room for improvement. Long story short, the only Raiders offensive lineman who has met or exceeded expectations so far this season is right tackle DJ Glaze. The 2024 third-round pick has been solid in the run game with a 62.8 mark and has made tremendous strides in pass protection, yielding just seven pressures. That gives the Silver and Black a silver lining in the trenches, but the rest of the group has some work to do and, as noted above, changes could be coming. Rogers had a rough showing in his one start this year, filling in for an injured Powers-Johnson against the Kansas City Chiefs. But that’s a small sample size, and it isn’t like the current first-string guards are getting the job done. The Texas Tech product has exclusively played right guard under Kubiak, but he did get run on the left side during the preseason a year ago. Also, JPJ and Burford have experience playing on both sides of the line to expand the combinations that the Raiders can deploy in the trenches. Meanwhile, rookie Trey Zuhn III was cross-trained at just about every offensive line position during training camp but has only been used as an extra lineman/jumbo tight end for 12 snaps during the regular season. He could factor into the mix at guard too, and maybe even left tackle if need be, since that was his primary college position. Granted, Zuhn missed last week’s game with a knee injury and was limited in this Wednesday’s practice. Also waiting in the balance is second-year offensive tackle Charles Grant, whose only significant regular-season action came in last year’s Week 18 contest against the Chiefs. So, for this week’s game day discussion on The FEED , we’ll be keeping tabs on the Raiders’ offensive line, starting with who is on the field. The game kicks off at 1:25 p.m. PST and will air on CBS (check your local listings). I look forward to talkin’ some ball with y’all!

title: NFL draft prospects 2027: Players to watch for Florida State vs. Miami
summary: Week 7 of the college football season is here, and it brings a key Florida in-state rivalry game. The Florida State Seminoles head from Tallahassee to South Florida today to face the Miami Hurricanes. This game obviously has plenty of meaning for our community, with so many people having attended or become fans of either […]
full_text: CLEMSON, SOUTH CAROLINA - OCTOBER 03: Darian Mensah #10 of the Miami Hurricanes warms up during the first half of a football game against the Clemson Tigers at Memorial Stadium on October 03, 2026 in Clemson, South Carolina. (Photo by David Jensen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Week 7 of the college football season is here, and it brings a key Florida in-state rivalry game. The Florida State Seminoles head from Tallahassee to South Florida today to face the Miami Hurricanes. This game obviously has plenty of meaning for our community, with so many people having attended or become fans of either team. It felt like the right time to bring in the Miami Dolphins’ perspective and take a closer look at some of the 2027 NFL Draft prospects who could be on the field today. The game kicks off at 7 p.m. Eastern on ESPN and Disney+. Florida State 2027 Draft prospects Duce Robinson, wide receiver (Senior) – Robinson is a huge target – like a bigger-than-the-Dolphins-tight-ends huge target. Listed at 6-foot-6 and 230 pounds, Robinson uses his size to give his quarterback a receiver who will fight for contested passes in a huge catch radius. If he gets his hands on the ball, it is going to be a catch. He is not the most precise route runner, and he does not have the speed to pull away from anyone, so he relies on his size to make the catch rather than speed to create separation. He is probably a day-two prospect who can excel as a possession receiver and redzone target. Charles Lester III, cornerback (Junior) – Lester is likely a developmental outside cornerback with good size. He is 6-foot-2 and 195 pounds, but he still needs to develop his technique, especially against faster, smaller wide receivers. He needs to clean up his work when receivers cut, but he can coach that up this year and in the NFL. He still has eligibility, so a 2027 return to college is not out of the question, but he could transition to the league, probably as a day-two pick. For Miami, where cornerback depth is a question mark, Lester could be an ideal option. Ja’Bril Rawls, cornerback (Senior) – Another cornerback with good size (6-foot-1, 180 pounds), Rawls is behind his teammate in draft potential, but the potential for success in the NFL is there. He probably needs to add strength, and his frame suggests he can do that without sacrificing speed. He has the versatility to slide back to safety, which might be the better option. He is not the best tackler, and he will need to clean that up in the NFL, especially if he is expected to step up in run defense. A developmental defensive back option who should contribute on special teams, Rawls is likely a day-three prospect who could rise to the end of day two. Quintrevion Wisner, running back (Senior) – The former Texas running back moved to Florida State this year after three seasons in Austin. He carried the ball 226 times for 1,064 yards in 2024, but he played only nine games in 2025 due to a hamstring injury. He has 29 carries for 141 yards this season, but is buried on the depth chart, and he has to prove he can be a receiving option out of the backfield before he can be considered a feature running back at the NFL level. He is a day-three depth running back option who can contribute on special teams. Micahi Danzy, wide receiver (Redshirt sophomore) – Danzy is the smaller receiver on our FSU prospects list, but that is only because Robinson is ridiculously large. Danzy is listed at 6-foot-1 and 195 pounds, and he can line up in multiple roles among the receiving corps. He has track speed, setting the FSU school record in the 400, and started his college career as a running back. He has 19 receptions for 139 yards and two touchdowns this season. He uses his speed to his advantage but needs to keep building his route tree. He is probably a day-three prospect who could use his speed to battle his way into a day-two consideration. Miami 2027 Draft prospects Darian Mensah, quarterback (Redshirt junior) – Mensah is a modern college football player who bounces between teams; he started at Tulane, then spent a year at Duke before moving to Miami this year. He throws with anticipation and makes good decisions, but he does not always work through his progressions and still has to prove he can handle pressure. He does not have the strongest arm and throws great short-to-medium passes, but the ball can die on longer throws at times. He could be the first quarterback off the board this year, potentially as the number one overall pick. Xavier Lucas, cornerback (Junior) – Lucas might be the ideal press-corner for the NFL. He has the size (6-foot-2, 200 pounds) to disrupt receivers at the line of scrimmage and the speed to keep up with the league’s vertical threats. He contests passes well, using his size to break up jump balls, but he is more likely to knock the ball away than to come away with an interception. He is a liability on run defense, with seemingly no interest in getting his nose into the mess in front of him; he also needs to clean up his tackling. Lucas has missed the last month of the season with an undisclosed injury, but he is expected to return for tonight’s game. He is probably a day-two prospect who is clearly not a finished product and will continue to grow in the NFL. For a Dolphins team in need of defensive secondary help, Lucas could be a key target. Note: Lucas is the basis of the lawsuit from Wisconsin against Miami. Lucas played his freshman year at Wisconsin under a two-year Name, Image, and Likeness contract. He tried to transfer to Miami for his second season, but Wisconsin refused to enter him into the transfer portal, citing his contract. Lucas dropped out of Wisconsin and enrolled at Miami without entering the NCAA’s transfer portal, and Wisconsin is alleging tampering by Miami to entice Lucas to transfer. Damon Wilson II, edge (Senior) – The Dolphins will likely be highly interested in edge rushers in the 2027 Draft, and Wilson could put himself on the board. At 6-foot-4 and 250 pounds, Wilson has the size and athleticism needed to succeed in the NFL. He uses both speed and power to attack offensive tackles, but he needs to add counter moves to get off the block if his initial move does not win. He also needs to improve his edge-setting against the run. He has the flashes to be great in the NFL, but he hasn’t shown the consistency yet. He broke out last year at Missouri with a nine-sack season, and he has tallied 3.5 sacks through the first five games this year, including 2.5 sacks against Clemson a couple of weeks ago. If he can keep up that production, he will be a second-round target who could slide into the end of the first round. Samson Okunlola, offensive tackle/guard (Redshirt Junior) – Okunlola’s potential is projected based on limited playing time at Miami. He did not get regular snaps until last year, when he rotated at left guard all season. He was clean, did not allow a sack, and showed he could be relied on in big spots. He slid out to left tackle this year, and he has been successful there as well – though he has had a penalty issue that needs to be cleaned up. He could bring that versatility to the NFL, allowing teams to use him as either a guard or tackle as needed. At 6-foot-6, 330 pounds, he still brings athleticism to the line and could be an effective mover to lead block in running situations. He is probably a day-two prospect who could start as a depth option at tackle and guard before settling into a starting role as a guard on the line. Ryan Rodriguez, center (Redshirt Senior) – A sixth-year college player, Rodriguez has played both guard and center at Miami. He has had injury issues, including needing surgery in 2022 and 2024. He is 6-foot-2 and 300 pounds, which is smaller than most NFL interior linemen, but Miami’s All-Pro center, Aaron Brewer, is 6-foot-2 and 290 pounds, so that might not be a major concern. He has to prove he can withstand the pressure of an entire season and anchor the line,…

title: 5 Things I Think I Think About the Miami Dolphins After Week 5
summary: Welp, another week, another loss. Sure, a seven-point loss to the Bengals isn’t particularly encouraging (though let’s be honest, that score was closer than a lot of us might have predicted). But there were still a few developments worth discussing. Some are positive. Some are frustrating. A few are both. Here are five things I […]
full_text: Welp, another week, another loss. Sure, a seven-point loss to the Bengals isn’t particularly encouraging (though let’s be honest, that score was closer than a lot of us might have predicted). But there were still a few developments worth discussing. Some are positive. Some are frustrating. A few are both. Here are five things I think I think after Week 5. The defense is better than people give it credit for. When you’re 0-5 and coming off a four-touchdown torching by Joe Burrow, nobody wants to hear about defensive rankings. But hear me out: This unit is statistically better than people might think. The Dolphins enter Week 6 ranked 15th in passing defense, 16th in rush defense, and 17th in total defense. They’re also tied for sixth in yards allowed per carry (3.7). Now, before we start organizing a ticker tape parade down Flagler Street, this unit has obvious problems too. They’re 24th in points allowed, 27th in takeaways, and near the bottom of the league in third-down defense. Also, amazingly, they’ve played only one game in which they managed to record at least one sack. The lack of defensive pressure is a serious problem. But considering how young this roster is, the defense has at least shown signs that it can be part of the foundation moving forward. Could Ollie Gordon be the answer at running back? OK, pitchforks down, people. I’m not saying Ollie Gordon is better than De’Von Achane. But: Is it possible he’s a better fit for the offense right now? Let’s go to the box score: De’Von Achane Oliver Gordon III Game 1, @ Las Vegas Raiders 11 for 36 yards rushing, 4 for 30 yards receiving, no TDs Bupkis Game 2, @ San Francisco 49ers 20 for 74 yards rushing, 3 for 19 yards receiving, no TDs 3 for 7 yards rushing Game 3, vs. Kansas City Chiefs 3 for 17 yards rushing 17 for 41 yards rushing, 1 TD, 3 for 14 yards receiving Game 4, @ Minnesota Vikings DNP 9 for 100 yards rushing, 1 TD Game 5, vs. Cincinnati Bengals DNP 18 for 88 yards rushing, 1 TD It’s obviously a small sample size, but the Gordon fisherman has 236 yards rushing and 3 touchdowns on 47 attempts (5.0 yards per carry). Achane was averaging 3.7 yards per carry on 34 carries, with 49 receiving yards, and no touchdowns. How could this be? One possibility: Achane is a lightning bolt who thrives on speed, angles and getting to the edge. That style of running works best with perimeter and second-level blocking upfield. Gordon is a 225-pound bowling ball* who wants to lower his shoulder and get north-south. If you told me Gordon’s physical style is easier and less complicated for this young offensive line to block for, I’d believe it. It’s something to think about. * I say “225-pound bowling ball” with love. I’m a huge Ollie Gordon fan. There are just so many self-inflicted wounds. The Dolphins don’t need opponents to make life difficult. They’re doing a pretty good job of that themselves. The special teams disaster continued with an 81-yard return against Cincinnati to start off the game. Three plays later the Bengals are in the end zone. Next play, Jaylen Wright muffs the kickoff (which he recovers and returns, but that’s not the point — it Takes No Talent to catch a kickoff!). Later, we get a 25-yard penalty for kicking the ball short of the landing zone. The landing zone is 20 yards long by 53 1/2 yards wide. That’s over 1,000 square yards! How much bigger do we need to make the landing zone for Riley Patterson to kick into it?! And this is just the first quarter — I’m not even getting into strip sacks or missed extra points later in the game. For every takeaway the Dolphins defense has secured this season, the offense has given away two. Add in penalties (7 in the Bengals game!), missed assignments and blown coverages, and it’s hard for any rebuilding team to overcome that kind of weekly damage. I know, this is part of the growth process for a very young team. Suffice it to say, Miami is making things much harder than they need to be. OK, fine, let’s talk about Malik Willis. The numbers aren’t pretty. On the season, Willis is 24th in the league in completions, 32nd in completion percentage, 25th in passing yards, 29th in passing touchdowns, 33rd in yards per attempt (reminder, there are still only 32 teams) and 31st in passer rating. Even when you factor in his good (but could be better) rushing performance, that’s still not great. That said, I have no interest in benching him. This season is about evaluation. Willis is a relatively inexperienced quarterback playing behind a young offensive line, without De’Von Achane and top receiver Caleb Douglas. It’s clear the offense is not clicking, some of which falls on Willis, but that includes rookie receivers not being where they’re supposed to be. None of that excuses what was easily Willis’ worst game of the season. Against the Bengals he missed open receivers, passed over check-down options, took (another) unnecessary sack by running out of bounds behind the line of scrimmage and turned the ball over three times. Perhaps most concerning, this was the third straight game in which he’s put the ball on the ground. The part that worries me isn’t the bad game as much as the repeated mistakes. That’s why I’d keep playing him. The Dolphins need to find out exactly what they have over the next 12 games, if Willis can be someone to build around. But if the same issues continue, the conversation won’t be whether Miami drafts a quarterback in 2027. It’ll be how early. The Dolphins may actually have a foundation to build on. Putting the quarterback position aside: Maybe it’s just me, but it feels like an identity to this team is starting to emerge: A defense that’s quietly been pretty good, even with Kenny Grant missing the season’s first month. And that’s largely without any sort of pass rush to speak of, which speaks well of how good they’ll be in the future. Ollie Gordon emerging as a legitimate contributor. Before the last two games, it was fair to wonder whether Ollie Gordon had a future as a meaningful NFL contributor. These past two games have shown that maybe the Dolphins have someone to build around with Achane in the running back room. Young players across the roster getting meaningful snaps. Maybe that’s the most exciting part — what the future might hold for the team. The combined record of the Dolphins’ first five opponents is 20-6, and you can make the argument that playing against tough competition only accelerates this young team’s growth. Sure, it’s an 0-5 team. But they’re playing good teams close, they’re getting meaningful snaps for young players, and they’re finding more than a few pieces worth building around. That’s not a winning season, but maybe it’s the beginning of a foundation.

title: NFL Picks and Predictions, Week 6
summary: It may be an off week for our Minnesota Vikings, but we’re not resting, as it’s time for our staff of learned (pronounced learn-ed) pro football blowhards to pass along who we are picking in this week’s games around the National Football League. As always, we start by putting up our tally of how all […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - OCTOBER 4: A detailed view of an NFL logo on the field prior to an NFL football game between the Detroit Lions and Carolina Panthers on October 4, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images It may be an off week for our Minnesota Vikings, but we’re not resting, as it’s time for our staff of learned (pronounced learn-ed) pro football blowhards to pass along who we are picking in this week’s games around the National Football League. As always, we start by putting up our tally of how all of us are faring so far this season. You can break things down by any of the picks we make, whether it’s straight-up, spread, or over/under picks, and you can look at any individual week or the entire season. My picks are particularly embarrassing across the board, but I’m putting them out there anyway because they make everyone else look good. With that, here are our picks for this week, ladies and gentlemen. As always, we remind you that the numbers-based picks like over/unders and spread picks may vary from person to person based on when each individual selector punches their picks into the system that Tallysight supplies to us. title: Bye Week Breather
summary: The Minnesota Vikings improved to 5-0 with a convincing (if frustrating) victory over the New Orleans Saints. A 23-13 final was fine, but the game should have been at least 29-7, more like 33-7. But a win is a win; in the end, that’s all that matters. In the first part of the 2026 season, […]
full_text: The Minnesota Vikings improved to 5-0 with a convincing (if frustrating) victory over the New Orleans Saints. A 23-13 final was fine, but the game should have been at least 29-7, more like 33-7. But a win is a win; in the end, that’s all that matters. In the first part of the 2026 season, when the Vikings seem to be catching most of the breaks, they get another: a bye. A Week 6 bye didn’t look all that appealing before the season, but it couldn’t have come at a better time. Injuries abound, and a week off is just what the doctor ordered to get healthy before what will certainly be the most daunting stretch of the schedule. After Week 5, the next five opponents have a combined 17-8 record, including the current Super Bowl favorite, the 49ers, and the Bills. Other than the Vikings, of course. Duh. HOW WE GOT HERE Aaron Jones, Sr., RB1: Jones has shouldered the burden while the passing game found its footing amid Jordan Mason’s absence. All the while, he’s been banged up himself. Since Week 1, he’s surpassed 100 all-purpose yards in every game except the win over the Buccaneers, where he had 92 yards. He’s currently 5th in the NFL in carries and 6th in rushing yards. His 410 rushing yards so far are one less than the Vikings’ combined net passing yards in weeks 1 through 3. At age 31, his performance so far projects to nearly 1,400 rushing yards. He likely won’t reach that total because Mason is set to return, but we wouldn’t be sitting at 5-0 right now without Jones leading the way. Kyler Murray, Ascending: The performance against the Saints was exactly what it needed to be and more. Murray built on his outstanding 4th quarter against the Dolphins to put together his first complete game: 24 of 30 for 229 yards, a touchdown, and an excellent 109.6 QB rating. What really pushed the excitement level to 11, however, was his 51 rushing yards in key situations, moving the chains and extending drives. It’s exactly what we envisioned when we signed him in the offseason. Injuries delayed it a bit, but the trend is our friend. If Murray keeps improving in the coming weeks, the sky is the limit for what this team can achieve this year. Why? Because… Vikings Defense, Historic (Potentially): With another week making an opposing quarterback look more uncomfortable than I do at a Taylor Swift concert, Brian Flores’ group has laid the early foundation for a potentially historic unit. With roughly 30% of the season in the rearview, the Vikings have allowed just 12.8 points per game (11.6, excluding the Saints’ fumble-recovery TD). Advanced analytics from the usual sources rank them #1 in the following categories: EPA/play allowed, points per drive, red zone conversion rate, pressure rate, and sack rate. This is on top of their high rankings in traditional categories: passer rating allowed (#1), completion percentage (#1), turnover differential (#1), takeaways (2nd), sacks (3rd), and yards per pass attempt (7th). Folks, I watch a lot of football. I rarely miss a primetime NFL game, and I have the four-screen Sunday Ticket setup when the Vikings aren’t playing. It’s a tremendous source of annoyance for my wife. One of many, actually. You’re not supposed to play defense this well in 2026. Years of rule changes favoring offenses and quarterbacks, along with the salary cap and other factors, have made defensive dominance far tougher than it was 20 years ago. The 80s and 90s? Forget it. The defense the Vikings are playing now shouldn’t be happening in the modern NFL. I’m not ready to call this defense historic yet, but if it handles the upcoming gauntlet of potentially dangerous, high-powered offenses (Lions, Bills, Packers, 49ers) in a similar fashion, then, yeah, I’m declaring it the best NFL defense over multiple seasons since the Legion of Boom in Seattle and the best Vikings defense since the Purple People Eaters. Will Reichard, Modern-Day Elvis. No one since The King of Rock ‘n’ Roll has reshaped pop culture and redefined their chosen field. It’s bigger than Beatlemania. Paul needed John; John needed Paul; they both needed to be challenged by George; and Ringo had to steady the ship (and the beat). Will the Thrill needs no one. The charisma. The aura. He tosses out arrogant boasts, gets in players’ faces, and pushes away anyone who dares enter his orbit uninvited. Will Reichard is a vibe. It’s only a matter of time before he’s linked to some popular Gen Z actress or singer I’ve never heard of. Only one kicker has won NFL MVP: Mark Moseley in 1982. But that was a strike-shortened season, and he actually missed a field goal. After five weeks, the Thrill is your NFL MVP. He’s 15-for-15 on field goals (5-for-5 from 50+ yards) and 8-for-8 on extra points, for 53 points. For reference, that’s almost half the Vikings’ overall scoring (109 points). That said, it may not be the end of the world if he misses one, say, up 31-7 on the Jets in Week 17. Going into the postseason without missing a field goal brings back a particular memory. Am I the only Vikings fan whose mind is so warped and scarred by past heartbreaks that I even contemplate such a thing? THE ROAD AHEAD The Vikings have the NFL’s toughest remaining schedule (.568) when they return home from the bye. While the 49ers and Bills’ combined 9-1 record plays a role, it’s still very tough sledding ahead. Two Lions games and a trip to Lambeau Field still lie ahead, for instance. The good news is that, of the 12 remaining games, seven will be at U.S. Bank Stadium, and the 49ers game will be on a neutral field. With an improving, healthier offense driven by an increasingly comfortable Kyler Murray and the NFL’s best defense, there’s legitimate reason to support the loftiest expectations over the next few months. I don’t care if the ’72 Dolphins, ’85 Bears, and ’89 49ers were on the schedule. That said… HOW IT ENDS MATTERS Going 5-0 out of the gate is tremendous, but it doesn’t change the calculus for this season: playoff success. We’ve seen variations of this movie in the past decade, and I want no part of either previous outcome. Going 5-0 in 2016 got us to 8-8 and missing the playoffs. Two years ago, 5-0 became 14-3, and Vikings fans wished they’d missed the playoffs. I don’t care if we beat that and go 15-2. We must rip up the previous scripts and rewrite the ending. It may be Halloween season, but I’m done with horror movies. It’s time for one of those cheesy, feel-good Hallmark Christmas closing scenes. Kevin O’Connell needs it, and, most of all, a long-suffering, loyal Vikings fanbase needs it. It’s the 50th anniversary of our last Super Bowl appearance. Enough is enough. It’s time.

title: Patriots elevate safety Elliott Davison from practice squad, release running back
summary: Pro Bowl wide receiver A.J. Brown will make his official return versus the New York Jets after spending four games on injured reserve. But the New England Patriots announced an additional two moves on the eve of the AFC East meeting at Gillette Stadium. The organization elevated safety Elliott Davison for Sunday’s 1 p.m. ET […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - OCTOBER 11: Elliott Davison #27 of the New England Patriots reacts during the fourth quarter against the Las Vegas Raiders at Gillette Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images Pro Bowl wide receiver A.J. Brown will make his official return versus the New York Jets after spending four games on injured reserve. But the New England Patriots announced an additional two moves on the eve of the AFC East meeting at Gillette Stadium. The organization elevated safety Elliott Davison for Sunday’s 1 p.m. ET kickoff and also released running back Hassan Haskins from the practice squad. Davison, 24, reverted last week after appearing in his first NFL game beyond the preseason. The 6-foot, 190-pound safety recorded two tackles and one pass deflection during what became a 45-17 win over the Las Vegas Raiders. He handled 10 snaps on defense and 19 snaps on special teams in his debut as a standard elevation and now has a third and final call-up remaining before a move to the active roster would be required to take the field. Signed to the Patriots’ practice squad at the start of September before being released and re-signed , Davison originally entered the league as an undrafted free agent out of UTSA in 2025. The former Roadrunners defensive back logged all of his rookie year on the practice squad of the New Orleans Saints and cleared waivers following the 53-man cutdown deadline in August. Haskins, 26, departs from New England’s practice squad after returning to the fold last week. The 6-foot-2, 228-pound running back had visited Foxborough for a workout that became a contract ahead of the preseason opener. After being released as a vested veteran at the end of August, he spent two weeks on the initial practice squad before circling back amid October. Selected in the fourth round of the 2022 NFL draft at No. 131 overall, Haskins spent previous tours with the Tennessee Titans and Los Angeles Chargers. Through 44 games, the Michigan product stands with 76 carries for 229 yards, 18 catches for 119 yards, three touchdowns as well as one start in the backfield. He has handled 371 snaps on offense and 683 snaps on special teams in his career. The Patriots recently worked out three running backs and move forward with a full 53-man roster as well as one open spot on the 17-man practice squad. Head coach Mike Vrabel’s 3-2 club ruled out cornerbacks Carlton Davis III and Karon Prunty on the final injury report ahead of the divisional matchup.

full_text: Update 10/17/2026: Patriots activate A.J. Brown off injured reserve After an earlier report detailing their plans, the New England Patriots have made it official. Wide receiver A.J. Brown has been activated off injured reserve and rejoined their 53-man roster. Patriots activate WR A.J. Brown to the 53-man roster. pic.twitter.com/H8txrBvF9V — New England Patriots (@Patriots) October 17, 2026 Original story 10/17/2026: Patriots to activate A.J. Brown off injured reserve, per report The New England Patriots offense will have one of its best players back against the New York Jets. Wide receiver A.J. Brown, who spent the last four weeks on injured reserve, will be activated to the 53-man roster on Saturday. The expectation is that he will line up against the Jets on Sunday, according to a report by Ian Rapoport of NFL Network. Brown, 29, was moved to IR following the Patriots’ season opener against the Seattle Seahawks. After catching three passes for 26 yards in his debut with the team, he suffered an ankle injury in the third quarter. The issue was later diagnosed as a high ankle sprain, prompting New England to move him to injured reserve. After the requisite four weeks on IR, Brown returned to practice on Wednesday to open his 21-day activation window. Despite being a limited participant throughout the week, he has progressed enough to rejoin the active team this week. “I think he looks okay, like everybody,” head coach Mike Vrabel said about Brown on Friday. “Some good plays, some bad plays. We’re trying to see where his conditioning level is and see how he may feel here after practice today.” Apparently, he is feeling good. Brown now rejoins a receiving corps also featuring Romeo Doubs, DeMario Douglas, Kyle Williams and Efton Chism. The Patriots will host the Jets at Gillette Stadium on Sunday, 1 p.m. ET.

title: 5 questions and answers about Patriots vs. Jets
summary: The New England Patriots and New York Jets have trended in different directions since introducing their new head coaches last offseason. Whereas the former made the Super Bowl in 2025 and are again looking like one of the NFL’s better teams as of late, the latter went a combined 5-17 the last two seasons. On […]
full_text: The New England Patriots and New York Jets have trended in different directions since introducing their new head coaches last offseason. Whereas the former made the Super Bowl in 2025 and are again looking like one of the NFL’s better teams as of late, the latter went a combined 5-17 the last two seasons. On Sunday, they will cross paths again. Will it be more of the same after the Patriots swept the Jets last year? Or will New York manage an upset? To find out more about the Patriots’ opponent, we spoke with MacGregor Wells of Pats Pulpit’s sister site Gang Green Nation , the SB Nation community for all things Jets. 1. What’s changed about the Jets’ culture and on-field play in year two of Aaron Glenn? What’s gotten players to seemingly buy in? Well, you may be asking the wrong guy about culture stuff. I’m not really a big believer in culture. Sure, there are some teams that end up having a toxic culture, but for the most part, I’m a believer in talent. Put together a talented team that isn’t littered with divas and has a decent coaching staff and you’ll usually have a winning team. Put together an untalented team with a bunch of team captain types and you’ll usually have a losing team. The Jets players seem to like Glenn and his coaching staff. They seem to care about winning. But to me the biggest difference between this year’s Jets team and last year’s Jets team is the talent level has been raised considerably. That isn’t to say the Jets have a top of the NFL roster – far from it. But last year’s Jets team was starting a bunch of guys who were practice squad material. With all the additions in free agency and the 2026 NFL draft, the Jets defense has been almost completely overhauled, and the offense has added a competent quarterback, unlike last year’s three headed monster of Justin Fields, a washed up Tyrod Taylor, and practice squad dude Brady Cook. In addition the Jets have added some nice weapons on offense in Omar Cooper and Kenyon Sadiq, and they have Garrett Wilson back after missing all but seven games last year with an injury. Put it all together and last year the Jets were fielding arguably the least talented roster in the NFL. This year the Jets are fielding a roster that is maybe a little below NFL average, but certainly much better than last year’s dreck. To me, that’s the reason the Jets are more competitive this year. I’m not sure culture is that big of a factor. 2. Geno Smith has been one of the league’s most efficient and risk-averse passes in his return to New York, but how much of that has that come at the cost of downfield protection? How do you expect him and Garrett Wilson to challenge the Patriots’ defense? You kinda nailed the issue on the head here. Geno has yet to throw an interception. As a result the Jets have only lost the turnover battle once in the first five games, a big turnaround from recent Jets turnover-prone teams. That’s a very good thing, but it does come at a cost. Geno is looking for the dumpoff passes more than ever, and foregoing downfield shots. As a result the Jets passing offense can stagnate, with plenty of completions but few chunk plays. Geno has also been holding the ball too long, reluctant to pull the trigger, which has resulted in too many sacks and four Geno fumbles. As far as how the Jets might attack the Patriots, Christian Gonzalez is apparently going to play, so that will make things difficult for Garrett Wilson. Nonetheless, Wilson is by far the Jets’ best receiver, so I expect to see plenty of Wilson targets. How that battle plays out will go a long way towards determining how much success the Jets have on offense. I expect the Jets to try to move Wilson around the formation to free him from a Gonzalez matchup as much as possible. In general, the Jets would prefer to pound the ball on the ground. Breece Hall is out, so Braelon Allen will be the Jets’ bell cow on the ground in this game. Allen is fresh off his first 100+ yard rushing game in the NFL, and the Jets hope he can repeat that against the Patriots. If Allen is shut down and Wilson can’t get the better of Gonzalez or whoever is on Wilson, this could be a long day for the Jets offense. 3. Can Braelon Allen carry the rushing attack without Breece Hall? Braelon Allen is a very different back from Breece Hall. Allen is the kind of back who moves the chains and almost always gets positive yards, but he is nowhere close to the chunk play guy that Breece Hall is. Hall is also a much more productive receiver than Allen. Can Allen carry the rushing attack? Sure. He’s coming off a 110 yard rushing game just last week against the Cleveland Browns. In a way Allen better fits the Aaron Glenn ball control mindset, but there’s no denying he is unlikely to give the Jets the kind of big play presence Hall does. 4. What’s allowed David Bailey to be so productive so early and how can he continue to improve? Where do you expect him to line up in crucial moments? David Bailey is a very physically gifted pass rusher with a lightning quick first step. He is also pretty relentless in pursuit, never giving up on the play. The combination has led to five sacks in five games, but he still has plenty to work on. His technique is still raw and he does not have a plethora of go to moves if he doesn’t quickly beat you around the edge. He is still a developmental player who can be stymied by a tackle with quick feet who can handle Bailey’s speed. Bailey lines up on the edge on almost every down. He sometimes is asked to drop into coverage, which is rarely a good idea. He gives good effort, but he is miscast as a pass defender. 5. There are well-known veterans at all three levels of the Jets’ defense, but who are some under-the-radar defenders Patriots fans should know? I’ll give you three guys. Dane Belton is a former New York Giants safety who was signed this year in free agency. He spent most of his time with the Giants as a special teams dude, but with the Jets he has been a revelation as a starting safety. He is fast and fundamentally sound. He is a great tackler who wraps up and rarely misses a tackle. He is best used as a heat seeking missile against the run, but he has also held up fairly well against the pass. Belton’s been a really nice addition for the Jets at safety. On the defensive line the Jets added Kingsley Enagbare, an edge defender from the Detroit Lions, in free agency. Enagbare had a reputation as a strong defender against the run and setting the edge, but not particularly great at rushing the passer. With the Jets he has been surprisingly good in pass rush situations while continuing to do well against the run. At cornerback, last year’s third round draft pick Azareye’h Thomas had a quiet rookie year last season, starting just five games and not really standing out. This year Thomas has taken over as a starting outside cornerback, and he has held up well, with five passes defended in five games. Thomas also holds his own in run support. Going into this season Jets fans weren’t sure what the team had in Thomas, but he has gradually made many fans believe Thomas could be a long term starter at cornerback.

title: What activating A.J. Brown off IR means for the Patriots
summary: Injuries have been one of the stories of the season so far for the New England Patriots, but Saturday brought some positive news for once. Wide receiver A.J. Brown, who made his return to practice earlier this week, will reportedly be activated off the injured reserve list and officially rejoin the offense against the New […]
full_text: Injuries have been one of the stories of the season so far for the New England Patriots, but Saturday brought some positive news for once. Wide receiver A.J. Brown, who made his return to practice earlier this week, will reportedly be activated off the injured reserve list and officially rejoin the offense against the New York Jets on Sunday. Needless to say that getting Brown back is a positive for the Patriots offense and quarterback Drake Maye. Let’s dive a bit deeper, though. Positive development Since Brown went down in Week 1 with what was later diagnosed as a high ankle sprain, the Patriots continued to lose key contributors to injury. Wide receiver Mack Hollins, fullback Reggie Gilliam and guards Mike Onwenu and Greg Van Roten have all been moved to injured reserve as well. In addition, tight end Eli Raridon missed time due to injury, while left tackle Will Campbell and running back TreVeyon Henderson are facing unclear outlooks after sustaining respective knee and ankle injuries last week versus the Las Vegas Raiders. Only five weeks into the season, the Patriots have already had to overcome more substantial injuries than they had to deal with through all of 2025. Needless to say that getting some talent back — especially of Brown’s quality — is a positive development that should help the entire offense: he is the rising tide capable of lifting all the boats. Trickle-down effect With Brown set to rejoin the 53-man roster, the Patriots’ wide receiver group will look drastically different. After previously having four wideouts on the active team, he will add a starter-caliber fifth option: 53-man roster (5): A.J. Brown (1),Romeo Doubs (87), DeMario Douglas (3), Kyle Williams (18 | KR), Efton Chism III (86) Practice squad (3): Kyle Dixon (83), Cameron Dorner (88), Chandler Brayboy (81) Injured reserve (2): Mack Hollins (13), Jeremiah Webb (29 | season-ending) Brown returning to reclaim usual spot atop the depth chart means that the entire group will be shaken up below him. Romeo Doubs and Kyle Williams might see fewer opportunities at the X-receiver spot, while Efton Chism — who played a career-high 57 snaps against the Raiders last Sunday — might be used more as a package player again moving forward. In the meantime, the Patriots may no longer feel the need to carry three wideouts on their practice squad. They could instead decide to use one of those spots on one of the free agent running backs they recently had in town for tryouts Immediate impact TBD What speaks against the Patriots making a follow-up move involving a practice squad wide receiver, at least initially, is Brown not yet being cleared for full practice participation. Even though he will rejoin the 53-man team on Saturday, he was limited at all three sessions this week. This also means that it remains to be seen how actively involved the 29-year-old actually will be against the Jets. He played 91% of offensive snaps against the Seahawks before going down, but might not see the same playing time share on Sunday. The goal is to get him back to a full workload, obviously, but he might not be at this point just yet making his comeback after a four-week absence. Open roster spot filled The Patriots entered the weekend with one open spot on their 53-man roster. Brown will fill it, but it remains to be seen whether or not this is the only transaction taking place on the eve of the team’s Week 6 matchup with the Jets. Mike Vrabel and company could, for example, also activate offensive tackle Marcus Bryant off injured reserve. “He’ll be another guy that we’ll look at here in the morning to see about his elevation and see where that is and see how he feels after a few days of work,” said the Patriots’ head coach. Like Brown, Bryant made his return to practice this week and is eligible to return to the active roster at any point over the next three weeks. And with starting left tackle Will Campbell questionable because of a knee ailment, adding him to bolster the depth at his position might make sense — even if it will come at the expense of another player currently on the 53-man team.

title: Key matchups: Saints vs. Giants
summary: The New Orleans Saints have fallen to 1-4 and are now set to travel to MetLife to take on the 3-1-1 New York Giants. After their promising two-week start, the Saints have been dominated in their last nine quarters of football and are looking to get back on track against a team that doesn’t appear […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LA - OCTOBER 11: Chase Young #99 of the New Orleans Saints reacts after a play against the Minnesota Vikings during an NFL football game at Cesars Superdome on October 11, 2026 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints have fallen to 1-4 and are now set to travel to MetLife to take on the 3-1-1 New York Giants. After their promising two-week start, the Saints have been dominated in their last nine quarters of football and are looking to get back on track against a team that doesn’t appear to be a whole lot better than them on paper. But if New Orleans wants to get back in the win column, they’ll have to take advantage of these key matchups. Saints pass rush vs. QB Jameis Winston Saints fans may know it better than anyone other than Tampa Bay Buccaneers fans how to beat Giants quarterback Jameis Winston: make him make mistakes. Winston is coming off a big win in the team’s tie with the Washington Commanders, throwing for 326 yards and 3 touchdowns with a 61.1 completion percentage. It was Winston’s best game of the season, and his second consecutive 3-touchdown game. Winston, who has been less than accurate this season, has a 57.6 completion rate over his four starts and has thrown 3 interceptions. Carl Granderson is coming off a strong game, and Chase Young is having a stellar season, logging 4 sacks in 5 games. Granderson and Young will both need to show up on Sunday to disrupt the Giants’ quarterback. The Saints defense has struggled plenty this season, but is coming off a decent showing against the Minnesota Vikings. While Kyler Murray still completed 80% of his passes, he only threw for 229 yards on 24 completions and one touchdown. If the Saints’ pass rush finds success on Sunday, it will make Winston’s chances of making mistakes significantly higher, and New Orleans could finally win in October. QB Tyler Shough vs. Giants secondary Tyler Shough is coming off the worst game of his career, but luckily for him, he won’t face a defense as good as the Vikings for the rest of the season. Unfortunately for Shough, he’ll be facing one of the better pass defenses in the league against the Giants. New York has the seventh-ranked pass defense. The Saints’ philosophy so far this season has been relying on Shough’s arm to pull them out of poor position. New Orleans hasn’t been able to establish the run, and play-calling has been subpar at best. While it’s easier to say the Saints should take advantage of the Giants’ bottom-10 run defense, the Saints haven’t shown the ability to run the ball, and it’s more likely we’ll see a lot more of Shough throwing on Sunday. CB Kool-Aid McKinstry vs. WR Malik Nabers Contrary to public opinion, Kool-Aid McKinstry has been solid for the Saints in 2026. Don’t get me wrong, his lows have been low, and when he gets beat, it is noticeable. But McKinstry was tasked with the impossible job of covering Justin Jefferson in the loss to the Vikings and held his own. McKinstry will see another former LSU standout on Sunday against Malik Nabers, who logged 11 receptions for 121 yards and a touchdown last week. Winston looked to Nabers in must-have situations, and if the Saints’ pass rush becomes a problem on Sunday, it will likely be the same against New Orleans. Interestingly, the Saints haven’t allowed a 100-yard wide receiver so far this season, although some have been close. Brock Bowers has been the only player to pass 100 receiving yards. Limiting Winston’s best receiver could lead to mistakes, and McKinstry could be a big reason New Orleans comes out with a win.

title: College Players to Watch: Week 6
summary: The way the season is going for the Saints, all things are possible for this roster at this moment. full_text: STARKVILLE, MISSISSIPPI - OCTOBER 25: Kelley Jones #1 of the Mississippi State Bulldogs intercepts a pass during the first half against the Texas Longhorns at Davis Wade Stadium on October 25, 2025 in Starkville, Mississippi. (Photo by Justin Ford/Getty Images) | Getty Images The way the season is going for the Saints, all things are possible for this roster at this moment. So, when you’re watching college football games this weekend, here are a few players to watch, regardless of their position. Carter Smith is an offensive tackle who plays at Indiana, and with the way the offensive line has performed, it wouldn’t be a surprise if that’s where the Saints choose to make another investment. Smith is one of the best, and he will be taking on a really good edge rusher in Kenyatta Jackson, who plays for Ohio State. That game will be at 11 a.m. on Fox. Smith is currently ranked as the fifth-best offensive tackle on Mel Kiper’s Big Board. Smith has played against Jackson before, including in the 2025 Big Ten Championship Game, which the Hoosiers won 13-10. The Saints obviously need to have a true number-one corner, and Kelley Jones could be him. Jones plays for Mississippi State, and the Bulldogs will be playing the Tigers in Baton Rouge at 11 a.m. on ESPN. So far this season, Jones has allowed a completion percentage of only 28%. He is a true outside corner with size and range and is a consensus first-round selection. Jones will be tested by the LSU offense. The Tigers feature several talented receivers and one of the best passing offenses in the nation. If Jones can hold his own, he could help the defense take away one side of the field and make containing the LSU offense more manageable. Another edge rusher who is not getting a lot of headlines but is currently viewed as a first-rounder is Yhonzae Pierre. Pierre is currently ranked as the third-best edge rusher in the 2027 class. So far this season, Pierre has 2.5 sacks, 17 tackles, one interception, and a forced fumble. The Tide will be taking on the Volunteers at 2:30 p.m. on ABC. Pierre is going to be tested by the Volunteers, but not just in the passing game. Tennessee will be featuring DeSean Bishop, who is having an amazing season, especially with the uncertainty at the QB position. Bishop just ran for 138 yards on 19 carries against Arkansas, and the week prior, he ran for over 200 yards. If Pierre can hold his own against the run and play a complete game on the edge, it could get ugly in Knoxville for the Volunteers. What position group would you like to see the Saints address? What players are you watching this weekend? Share your thoughts in the comments.

title: Eagles QB Jalen Hurts placed on IR, will miss the Week 9 Giants game
summary: The Philadelphia Eagles have placed quarterback Jalen Hurts on the injured reserve. Hurts will now be out for the next four weeks, and his earliest possible return is after the New York Giants travel to Philly to take on the Eagles in Week 9. While Hurts will be eligible to return following the Eagles’ Week […]
full_text: Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts.﻿ | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Philadelphia Eagles have placed quarterback Jalen Hurts on the injured reserve. Hurts will now be out for the next four weeks, and his earliest possible return is after the New York Giants travel to Philly to take on the Eagles in Week 9. While Hurts will be eligible to return following the Eagles’ Week 11 bye, Adam Schefter reports that Hurts is considered sidelined indefinitely. The move is in response to the blood clot which has become an increasing concern for both Hurts and the Eagles. The blood clot was originally caused when he was cleated earlier in the season and he played through the injury in the Eagles’ Week 5 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars . However, tests have since shown that the clot has moved, sparking significant concern. ESPN is reporting that Hurts could be treated with blood thinners, and the average treatment course being six weeks. However, it’s possible that he could be sidelined for as long as three months, which would effectively be season-ending. The Eagles are tied with the Dallas Cowboys at 2-3 on the season, and 1.5 games behind the first place Giants. Philly’s season started as disappointing before quickly spiraling after the retirement of RT Lane Johnson , injuries to RB Saquon Barkley and WR DeVonta Smith , and the trade of OC Cam Jurgens . The loss of Hurts is yet another significant blow to the Eagles’ season. The Giants will have their own bye week in Week 8, and will play the Eagles immediately after in Week 9. That game is followed by a home game against the Washington Commanders in Week 10 on Thursday Night Football. Nobody wants to see an opponent deal with injury, particularly something as potentially serious as a blood clot. However, this turn of events is another opportunity for the Giants to extend their lead over the Eagles in the division.

title: Survey results: NY Giants’ fan confidence remains high
summary: To the surprise of, well, pretty much everyone, the New York Giants come in to Week 6 of the 2026 NFL season with sole possession of first place in the NFC East. The Giants have had at least a share of first place since their season-opening win, and have managed to expand their lead while […]
full_text: New York Giants quarterback Jameis Winston celebrates a touchdown with wide receiver Malik Nabers. | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect To the surprise of, well, pretty much everyone, the New York Giants come in to Week 6 of the 2026 NFL season with sole possession of first place in the NFC East. The Giants have had at least a share of first place since their season-opening win, and have managed to expand their lead while their division rivals have faded. Even the Giants’ Week 5 tie served to extend their lead by half a game. And yet, the Giants are still entering Week 6 as 1.5-point underdogs at home against the New Orleans Saints , per Fanduel . This marks the third time in three weeks that oddsmakers have held the Giants as underdogs against a team in last place, and the fifth time in six weeks that the Giants are underdogs. But while Las Vegas and the national media in general don’t have much faith in the Giants, Giants’ fans themselves remain very confident in the direction of their team. The 2026 season hasn’t been easy, with the team losing two of its most important players in QB Jaxson Dart and OLB Brian Burns . Even so, the Giants have managed to do what’s necessary to win, and have shown a level of resilience and execution in key situations that has been lacking in recent years. So it’s not all that surprising that a full 95 percent of Giants fans are confident that the team is heading in the right direction. Fan confidence took a big hit following the loss of Dart in the loss to the Rams, but it’s rebounded nicely and is holding steady at 95 percent, which is second only to San Francisco 49ers’ fan confidence (96 percent). Right now the biggest questions facing the Giants are whether they can keep things rolling. QB Jameis Winston has played like a Top-10 quarterback over the last two weeks, throwing for 576 yards, 6 touchdowns, and 2 interceptions in soggy games against the Arizona Cardinals and Washington Commanders. At the same time, WR Malik Nabers has had 17 catches for 233 yards and 2 touchdowns and TE Isaiah Likely has had 18 catches for 160 yards and 2 touchdowns. On the defensive side of the ball, the Giants have unleashed their athletic defenders with one of the NFL’s most aggressive blitz schemes. Over all, the Giants’ pass defense has been among the best in the NFL, forcing the fastest throws in the NFL, and is among the fastest to pressure in the NFL. The defense has been disruptive and opportunistic when their disruption causes mistakes. All that said, Fan Confidence doesn’t ask how good the team is, it asks whether the team is moving in the right direction. And the Giants do still have plenty of room for improvement. They need to get their run defense to be more consistent and give up fewer explosive plays on the ground. Improving their gap integrity while continuing to disrupt behind the line of scrimmage will go a long way toward shoring up their run defense. Meanwhile, they also need to improve their own ground game. While running the ball has been one of John Harbaugh’s and Greg Roman’s calling cards, the Giants haven’t done it well. They need better execution from their front seven as well as less predictability from the play callers. But the Giants can get there, and if the team ahs shown anything, it’s that they‘ve bought in to the coaching and aren’t willing to give up.
