title: Is losing getting to the Eagles?
summary: The crumbling usually starts like this. The subtleties surface like tiny lashing out spurts and the vacant facial expressions that take command when NFL teams are sinking without any answers available. General manager Howie Roseman may be feeling the sting of a three-game losing streak. Bleeding Green Nation recently learned he expressed frustration during an […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 28: (L-R) Head coach Nick Sirianni and executive vice president Howie Roseman of the Philadelphia Eagles talk prior to the game against the Chicago Bears at Soldier Field on September 28, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images The crumbling usually starts like this. The subtleties surface like tiny lashing out spurts and the vacant facial expressions that take command when NFL teams are sinking without any answers available. General manager Howie Roseman may be feeling the sting of a three-game losing streak. Bleeding Green Nation recently learned he expressed frustration during an impromptu gathering with local media over a benign question about the offensive line. Roseman has been seen at practices more often than usual. He stormed off the sidelines visibly upset, his face distorted after the 19-17 walkoff loss to Jacksonville in London last Sunday. Poor offensive coordinator Sean Mannion has worn the look of a man escaping from the spin cycle of a Maytag washing machine during the Eagles’ current three-game losing streak. How the team has been covered by media this season has also drawn significant displeasure from some inside the building. Is losing getting to them? They have every right to feel the way they do, with 24 players on the injury report this week and a team that seems headed to the loser’s pile, after the most successful four-year stint in Eagles’ history. The Eagles went four-straight double-figure winning seasons, which was the third time in franchise history the Eagles have done that behind the five-year runs of Andy Reid’s 2000-2004 teams and Buddy Ryan/Rich Kotite’s 1988-1992 teams. What made the most recent four-year run unique was it marked the most victories that the Eagles have ever had in a four-year span (50), over Reid’s 2000-2003 (46) or 2001-2004 (48) teams, or Ryan’s 1988-1991 (41) or 1989-1992 (42) teams. Plus, the Eagles won the Super Bowl during their most recent four-year victory run. The Reid and Ryan teams did not during their four years of success. Barring a miracle, or a miracle worker who can somehow cure the many ailing Eagles, the double-figure season winning streak looks like it will come to a screeching halt in 2026. You’re fooling yourself if you think the Eagles will reach the Super Bowl. This team, now kept together with Scotch tape and Super Glue, have no Super Bowl in sight this season. The front office may be getting nervous. They may be seeing the end to something special that is probably a reason why this team is in the state it is. In the last five years, the Eagles have played 95 games, the fifth most of every team in the NFL behind Kansas City (97), San Francisco (96), and Buffalo and the Los Angeles Rams (95 each). Success can also run down a team. It shortens the offseason for the body to heal, and that is compounded by the reduced conditioning time between seasons. Nagging injuries that every NFL player endures during the season linger longer. Roseman, a future Hall of Famer, has been the architect of winning. He is entitled to have a flop or two, which is what is happening here, knowing he had to fortify the offensive line, considering he knew before the season Lane Johnson was close to being finished, before announcing his retirement last week, and knowing Cam Jurgens and Landon Dickerson were close to finished, too, due to their bodies breaking down. Roseman knew, too, he could not rely on the highly dubious back line at safety with Andrew Mukuba and Marcus Epps, who are both ailing on and off the field. He still failed to address that. Over the last two drafts, Mukuba, linebacker Jihaad Campbell, receiver Makai Lemon and tackle Markel Bell have been the only regulars getting playing time. Tight end Eli Stowers, taken in the 2026 second round, has not sniffed the field, while Mukuba and Campbell keep making the same mistakes after playing a whole NFL season. Campbell’s play has deteriorated so much that his position may be in jeopardy by a growing role for Jeremiah Trotter Jr. Behind the scenes, this is where Nick Sirianni thrives, where he is actually at his best. The Eagles’ head coach does a great job of keeping the outside noise where it belongs—outside. The players keep playing hard for him, which seems there are no signs of cracking so far, especially in Week 5’s heartbreaking 19-17 setback to Jacksonville. The undermanned Eagles really had no right to be in that game and were eight seconds away from a strong statement that they still belong among the NFL’s elite. They don’t. Weak special teams, a unit assembled together from the faulty depth pieces Roseman provided this season, let them down. The 19-17 loss was the kind of gut punch that carries for months—maybe throughout a season. October is not over yet. The Eagles are entering Week 6 at 2-3 with the worst ahead. Behind closed doors, maybe the suits are sweating. It sure looks like it from here.

It also means you’re probably paying a bit more attention to NFL Draft lists. Here are some players to watch this weekend. Charlie Becker, Wide Receiver, Indiana v. Ohio State (12 PM ET on Fox) While everyone is rightfully talking about Jeremiah Smith as the best player in the country, he won’t be the only first round hopeful receiver in this ranked showdown. With Elijah Sarratt and Omar Cooper in the NFL, Charlie Becker has stepped up as Indiana’s most dynamic pass catcher. Becker is strong, dependable, and a good athlete. If Indiana wants to come out of this Big 10 showdown with a win, Becker will need to make some big plays. Princewill Umanmielen, Edge Defender v. Mississippi State (12 PM ET on ESPN) The Eagles are going to need some edge rushing reinforcements in the 2027 draft. Princewill Umanmielen had a really good junior season at Ole Miss and is following it up with a brilliant year at LSU. He’s a ferocious pass rusher and LSU will need every bit of his talents to slow down Kamario Taylor. Dejaun Lane, Cornerback, Tennessee v. Alabama (3:30 PM ET on ABC) Alabama is coming off a tough loss to Georgia and needs to rebound against Tennessee if they want to stay in the playoff race. The Crimson Tide offense has a lot of juice, and Dejaun Lane will be tasked with slowing them down. The athletic, long armed cornerback will need to keep Ryan Williams Coleman in check if the Vols want the upset. Austin Simmons, Quarterback, Missouri v. Ole Miss (3:30 PM ET on SECN) While we’re all panicking about the Eagles quarterback health, here’s a mid round name to know. Austin Simmons went from losing his job to Trinidad Chambliss to being one of the best quarterbacks in college football. Simmons has good size and tools, and has looked really confident in the Mizzou offense this year. He’s been accurate, poised, and creative. This game has the makings of a shootout and Simmons will have plenty of opportunities to impress. Leonard Moore, Cornerback, Notre Dame v. BYU (7:30 PM ET on ABC) Could you imagine getting a stud corner to play across from Quinyon Mitchell with Cooper DeJean in the slot? Leonard Moore might be one of the two best defenders in the country. He’s a great athlete who can run with anyone and bring it in run defense. BYU’s offense has been causing problems all season and will challenge Notre Dame’s defense. Moore having a great game will solidify his high draft stock and help the Irish get a big win.

title: Eagles Film Preview: Scouting the Panthers’ offense
summary: Each week, I’ll publish two film-room previews: one focusing on the offense and one on the defense. These are primarily film-based, focusing on the schemes, tendencies, and matchups that could shape Sunday’s game, with all statistics coming from the Fantasy Points Data Suite. I also record a video version for Patreon, where I break down […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - OCTOBER 04: Bryce Young #9 of the Carolina Panthers and Tetairoa McMillan #4 react after a touchdown during the second half of a football game against the Detroit Lions at Bank of America Stadium on October 04, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by David Jensen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Each week, I’ll publish two film-room previews: one focusing on the offense and one on the defense. These are primarily film-based, focusing on the schemes, tendencies, and matchups that could shape Sunday’s game, with all statistics coming from the Fantasy Points Data Suite . I also record a video version for Patreon , where I break down the plays in greater detail and where you can further support my work. Yet another week watching an opponent’s offense and thinking, “Well, this looks quite fun.” The Panthers have a quarterback playing very good football, two talented receivers, and creative ways to get their best players favorable matchups. They also have an offensive line that can make the whole thing fall apart. Bryce Young is doing a lot to overcome that, but the Eagles’ defensive front has opportunities this week. Vic Fangio’s challenge is getting after Young without giving this passing game the isolated downfield matchups it wants. Pass Game Young is playing with real confidence. His release is excellent; he’s throwing with anticipation, and he’s placing the ball accurately enough to give his receivers opportunities to make plays after the catch. He’s also doing this without putting the football in harm’s way very often. Nine touchdowns and two interceptions through four games reflect the combination of aggression and control that shows up on film. This is absolutely a vertical passing offense. Young isn’t standing back there looking for a checkdown on every snap. He’s willing to attack outside the numbers, throw into tight windows, and give his receivers opportunities when the coverage leaves them isolated. Here, Jalen Coker wins downfield, and Young hits him in stride. If the Eagles are going to play single-high coverage, their corners had better be comfortable turning and running. Panthers' Offense All22 Thread. 1) Yet another quite fun offense I got to watch! Bryce Young is playing very well, and they funnel much of their passing game through two fun wide receivers & Darren Waller. Here is Jalen Coker winning downfield, and Young hitting him in stride.… pic.twitter.com/AadWEcpYAo — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) October 15, 2026 Coker deserves proper attention alongside Tetairoa McMillan. He has caught 18 of his 22 targets for 222 yards and two touchdowns, despite playing in only three games. He’s a big receiver who can win outside, contribute after the catch, and do some of the physical work this offense asks of its receivers. This isn’t a passing game where you can tilt everything toward McMillan. Darren Waller is the other receiving weapon who stood out, particularly in the red zone. The Panthers can spread the defense out and let him work against a linebacker or safety, and his option routes give Young an answer based on the defender’s leverage. They also use him on crossing concepts, where his size gives Young a target even in tight coverage. The Eagles’ linebackers and safeties will have some difficult coverage assignments if the rush doesn’t get home. I like the variety in this offense. You get the familiar under-center outside-zone action with a boot off it, but there are also boots and keepers from the gun, RPOs, empty formations, and spread passing concepts. They can condense the formation and threaten the run or spread everyone out and make the defense declare its intentions. Young looks comfortable operating within those different structures. It’s a fun offense to study. 2) As mentioned, Darren Waller is the other weapon to keep an eye on, especially in the red zone. The Panthers like to spread the defense out and can do a bit of everything on offense. You will see the standard outside zone under center boot action, but a lot of passing comes… pic.twitter.com/8gr8kuezFz — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) October 15, 2026 McMillan, though, is the player who can take over a game. He’s playing like a true WR1. He is strong at the catch point, can go up and get the football, and take over a game if you let him. The Panthers move him and Coker around to create favorable matchups rather than leaving them in the same positions all afternoon. Against single-high coverage, Young will give McMillan opportunities downfield. According to Fantasy Points Data, Young ranks fourth in attempts against single-high safety coverages, with 755 yards and six touchdowns, despite having played only four games. That matches what I saw. The Panthers see those outside opportunities and go after them. For the Eagles, I wouldn’t play a ton of single-high this week, which is where Young is at his most comfortable. 3) Tetairoa McMillan has made the leap and is playing like a true WR1. They move him and Coker around the field to create positive matchups. Coker is tall, but McMillan is very strong at the catch point and can go up and get it. Young will test defenses vertically with McMillan… pic.twitter.com/4vsXXNRoIm — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) October 15, 2026 However, the protection is a significant problem. There are plays where the Panthers look completely overwhelmed, including against pressure looks, and their willingness to keep attacking downfield can make those failures look particularly ugly. They don’t always take the immediate underneath answer. Sometimes they want the shot, and the protection simply doesn’t give Young enough time. Individual blitzes have caused some awful breakdowns, but Young has generally punished the blitz this season. The offense is averaging +0.35 EPA per dropback against blitzes, and only one of its ten sacks has come against a blitz. The other nine came against non-blitz looks. The Eagles should have opportunities to get home without constantly sending pressure. This is a week to trust the front 4. Young’s production drops from +0.41 EPA per dropback in a clean pocket to −0.02 under pressure. Make him operate under pressure while keeping enough defenders back to contest the throws he wants. I would play a ton of split-safety coverages while rushing 4. 4) However, the offense does have a clear issue, which is pass protection. They have struggled vs. the blitz, but also with just 4 pass rushers. This play might look a little familiar. They will take shots vs. pressure looks, rather than take the easy checkdown every time,… pic.twitter.com/62VixfCAfk — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) October 15, 2026 Their use of empty makes this offense particularly interesting. Young loves throwing from empty, and the Panthers are happy to attack vertically from it. Many offenses use empty to get the ball out quickly and spread out underneath defenders. The Panthers can do that, but they will also ask their receivers to win downfield with only five blockers protecting. Young’s use of empty has always been unique. The Eagles won’t face many similar challenges this year. Young is 17-of-22 for 237 yards from empty, averaging 10.77 yards per attempt, behind only Brock Purdy. It’s a small sample, but it supports how dangerous these plays look. And, once again, McMillan is a major part of it. Spreading the defense out can make it easier for Young to identify his best matchup, and he’s accurate enough to take advantage. Personally, I would want Fangio to show pressure against these formations and then change who actually rushes. Simulated pressures could test the protection while preserving seven defenders in coverage. The Eagles don’t have to send six just because the Panthers have emptied the backfield. They need those five blockers to sort out the rush correctly and give Young a less comfortable picture behind it. 5) However, what makes this offense really interesting is their use of empty. Germie Bernard and Pat Friermuth will see an increased role, but regardless of the options at receiver, the Steelers offense must execute better on early downs and convert more third downs, plain and simple. Second down isn’t better with a success rate of 40.9%, but third down is where the number craters at 39.4%. The overall success rate on first down through fourth comes to 42.7%. That number is good for 19th in the NFL. The two teams behind Pittsburgh are the Giants and Jets. If the Steelers are to make a run during this five-game stretch, they have to execute better on early downs and put themselves in striking distance on third down. title: NFL fines 49ers player for crucial uncalled illegal hit on Jaxon Smith-Njigba on final drive
summary: While the Seattle Seahawks are just two days removed from an agonizing overtime loss against the Denver Broncos, there’s a considerable development from their previous defeat to the San Francisco 49ers that just feels like pouring salt on the wounds. Remember when Jaxon Smith-Njigba took a big hit from 49ers safety Malik Mustapha on Seattle’s […]
full_text: While the Seattle Seahawks are just two days removed from an agonizing overtime loss against the Denver Broncos, there’s a considerable development from their previous defeat to the San Francisco 49ers that just feels like pouring salt on the wounds. Remember when Jaxon Smith-Njigba took a big hit from 49ers safety Malik Mustapha on Seattle’s final drive of the game? It was 1st and 10 at midfield, two plays before JSN couldn’t come down with a long ball from Sam Darnold. JSN was shaken up after Mustapha’s hard hit, and no penalty was called for hitting a defenseless receiver. Well, the NFL has fined Mustapha $6,998 for a “hit on the defenseless player” violation. That is as close as you can get to a public admission that the on-field officials made an incorrect no-call. Had a flag been thrown, Seattle would’ve been at the 49ers 35-yard line and in game-tying field goal range. Wow. The NFL fined 49ers safety Malik Mustapha for a "hit on a defenseless player." More specifically, the hit on JSN on Seattle's final drive. A penalty would've put the Seahawks in game-tying field goal range. pic.twitter.com/1DCt4NiTVs — Mookie Alexander (@mookiealexander) October 17, 2026 Now, this in no way means the Seahawks would’ve forced overtime or won the game, especially not when the Seahawks offense was a sack or turnover waiting to happen all afternoon. But in isolation, missing this call likely would’ve changed how the game ended. It’s a big miss by the referees and there’s no way around it now that the NFL says this should’ve been a penalty. No one else from this game was fined. Elijah Arroyo could’ve been dinged extra for his personal foul penalty after he punched at Renardo Green at the end of Sam Darnold’s second interception, but closer inspection indicates that Arroyo was clearly trying to punch the ball out simultaneous to Green going to the ground.

title: Seahawks injury update: Jadarian Price expected for ‘sooner rather than later’ return
summary: The Seattle Seahawks need running back help in the worst way. It’ll be at least two weeks until Jadarian Price is eligible to return from injured reserve, while Zach Charbonnet has a chance to play against the Kansas City Chiefs in Week 7. Mike Macdonald had no update on Charbonnet’s progress (or, maybe, no update […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks need running back help in the worst way. It’ll be at least two weeks until Jadarian Price is eligible to return from injured reserve, while Zach Charbonnet has a chance to play against the Kansas City Chiefs in Week 7. Mike Macdonald had no update on Charbonnet’s progress (or, maybe, no update he was willing to share), but it’s worth noting that Charbonnet must be activated this upcoming week or else he reverts to injured reserve for the rest of the season. Seattle opened his 21-day practice window on Oct. 1, prior to the Week 4 win over the Los Angeles Chargers. Once that window expires, the Seahawks either have to place him on the 53-man roster or end his season. The latter is obviously not happening unless there’s some unbelievably worrying setback, so we’re left to turn our attention to Price. Mike Macdonald revealed a little bit of a timeline as far as Price’s return during his Friday morning show with Brock and Salk on Seattle Sports 710 . “He’s doing great,” Macdonald said. “We should be looking at a sooner rather than later return after this [Kansas City Chiefs] game.” Price has been out since the start of Week 4 with a chest injury, which he aggravated in practice after getting the initial injury in Week 2 against the Arizona Cardinals. The rookie out of Notre Dame has had a couple of costly fumbles , but since George Holani and Emanuel Wilson have also since lost a combined three fumbles, he’s hardly the only culprit. Price has offered some explosiveness in the run game in a limited sample size, and his speed is what the main running back room lacks. In an ideal world, Charbonnet is back in Week 7 and Price is back in Week 8, at which point the running back room should be a lot stronger.

title: Mike Macdonald sticking with Sam Darnold as Seahawks starting quarterback
summary: The Seattle Seahawks, for now, will stick with their Super Bowl winning quarterback amid ongoing struggles with turnovers and accuracy. Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald told Seattle Sports 710 and later reporters on Friday that there won’t be a pivot to Drew Lock, who started and performed well against the Arizona Cardinals and otherwise doesn’t […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks, for now, will stick with their Super Bowl winning quarterback amid ongoing struggles with turnovers and accuracy. Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald told Seattle Sports 710 and later reporters on Friday that there won’t be a pivot to Drew Lock, who started and performed well against the Arizona Cardinals and otherwise doesn’t have any turnovers through (essentially) two games played. “We have a great backup quarterback in Drew,” Macdonald told Seattle Sports. “Drew is a tremendous quarterback. He’s a starting-level quarterback, and [I understand] that we didn’t turn the ball over when Drew played, and then we’ve had takeaway issues [with Sam starting]. “But right now, I think these things we have to attack as if they’re in our control, and then we can move it forward. Sam’s played great football for us this year the majority of the time, and there’s other times where, and he’ll be the first to tell you, he needs to take care of the football.” Darnold acknowledged on Thursday night following his catastrophic two-interception showing against the Denver Broncos that the turnovers, of which he has a league-leading seven picks, are hurting the team. “I just think it’s ‘BS,’ you know, for me to keep turning the ball over,” Darnold said. “It’s not fair to our defense, not fair to our special teams’ group, not fair really to the entire team. So I have to be better that way.” “We have a lot of faith in Sam,” Macdonald said at his press conference. “Sam has played great football for us. He’s done a lot of great things this year. He’s obviously turned the ball over more than we want to. There are things on our end that can help him play better football and he’s part of the solution rather than the opposite.” It’s not surprising that Macdonald didn’t get off the plane and immediately declare Drew Lock the starter. We’ve sort of been here with Mike when Geno Smith had his turnover issues in the 2024 season, namely against the Los Angeles Rams in a 26-20 overtime loss. He never benched Geno for Sam Howell, and now we’ve got another conversation brewing with Darnold and Drew Lock. If Darnold continues to struggle against the Kansas City Chiefs, a QB change really should not be out of the question. It’s less of, “Is Drew Lock suddenly a franchise quarterback?” and more of, “Is Drew Lock going to be less of a liability than Sam Darnold?” at this point in what is on course to be a very disappointing season. A highly anticipated Sunday night showdown with Kansas City, in part because of Ken Walker’s return to Seattle, now has an even bigger storyline to watch.

title: The cracks in the Seahawks offense last season are now chasms under Brian Fleury
summary: The Seattle Seahawks offense stinks. Ignore the points scored, which do not accurately reflect the underlying statistics, the Seahawks offense is bad. It may cost them a playoff berth, and it’s pretty much already cost them the NFC West title barring some humongous San Francisco 49ers collapse. Seattle sits at 3-3 after a brutal 17-14 […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks offense stinks. Ignore the points scored, which do not accurately reflect the underlying statistics, the Seahawks offense is bad. It may cost them a playoff berth, and it’s pretty much already cost them the NFC West title barring some humongous San Francisco 49ers collapse. Seattle sits at 3-3 after a brutal 17-14 overtime loss to the Denver Broncos. The Seahawks’ three losses are by a combined eight points, but the turnover margin in those games is a combined -7. That’s not going to get it done. Sam Darnold has played poorly enough to justify talks about benching him. The running game is both banged up and an absolute mess. If not for Jaxon Smith-Njigba, the Seahawks would look like an offense befitting of their 1990s throwbacks, because Seattle’s offenses for much of the early 1990s were an impossible watch. New offensive coordinator Brian Fleury is taking a lot of heat for the way this unit has cratered coming off a Super Bowl season. I’m not going to excuse Fleury whatsoever for this atrocious offensive slide, but I think there’s something bigger at play that stems from the tail-end of last season under Klint Kubiak. The warning signs for the Seahawks offense were there last year For those of you who are new to Field Gulls and/or don’t remember, I wrote a big article right before the season finale against the San Francisco 49ers . Seattle had won six consecutive games but the high-flying, high-scoring offense from the first half of the season noticeably dipped during the win streak. I’m not going to just quote myself in huge blocks and make this article a lot longer than it needs to be, so here are the CliffNotes (MookNotes?) of what I observed at the time: The passing game clearly declined in efficiency from the Los Angeles Rams loss onward . The run game improved, which was a relief, but Sam Darnold’s hot start noticeably cooled and it was more than just the four-interception disaster against LA. His sack rate would’ve been worse if you took the Rams game out, actually. They were also a much more explosive offense pre-Rams loss. Teams started blitzing Sam Darnold more and stacking the box less . Four of Darnold’s six highest blitz rates faced were from Week 11 onward, most notably the onslaught from Brian Flores’ Minnesota Vikings. Even the Carolina Panthers blitzed on over half of Darnold’s dropbacks. Darnold was one of the most blitzed QBs at the time (and generally performed well), but teams were sending extra heat more often. In terms of stacked boxes (8+ defenders in the box), the Seahawks went from facing stacked boxes north of 35 percent of the time to barely 30. Opposing teams stopped fretting about the running game and wanted Sam Darnold to beat them. Sam Darnold’s weaknesses were exposed in pure dropback situations . When Sam was slinging it, the Seahawks were the best play-action passing team in the NFL. Put him in a spot without the play-action and things get a whole lot worse. At the time of last year’s article, Darnold was 23rd in EPA/dropback on non-PA throws, with most of his interceptions coming in those scenarios. Seattle scored a lot of points by living off short fields. The Seahawks still scored at a healthy clip in part because they were getting defensive and special teams touchdowns, as well as really short fields that the offense couldn’t screw up. They led the NFL in touchdown drives starting at midfield or better from Week 12 onward. From Weeks 1-11, the Seahawks scored touchdowns on about 25% of their drives when starting inside their own 30. They scored touchdowns about 10% of the time from Week 11 onward, which ranked 28th. The running game showed signs of improvement . The rushing EPA was markedly better while the success rate was only moderately better. Seattle’s passing game dropped considerably but the rushing attack found some juice as the season progressed. A great sign for how they ended up performing in the Super Bowl. My buddy Griff (cmikesspinmove on Twitter and BlueSky, one half of the Seattle Overload podcast ), provided some more perspective on how flat the passing offense in particular was after Darnold’s torrid start. Can't let Kubiak off the hook (or Sam if that's how you want to look at it) SB run made it easy to gloss over that the pass EPA from weeks 11-18 2025 was 23rd. That Kubiak offense fell off hard. https://t.co/rN26dQTffM — under zone x (@cmikesspinmove) October 16, 2026 Things have only gotten worse for the Seahawks in 2026 The Seahawks offense is not good at virtually anything right now even though Jaxon Smith-Njigba is having a dominant season . They rank 25th in EPA/play, 18th in EPA/pass (almost certainly propped up by Drew Lock’s showing against the Arizona Cardinals), 31st in EPA/rush, 9th in sack rate, 16th in net yards/attempt, 28th in third-down conversion rate, 18th in red zone touchdown rate, and 16th in yards per play. Sam Darnold is playing like a bad quarterback in play-action or dropback . Darnold is 24th in EPA/play on play-action passes, heavily hampered by his three interceptions and no touchdown passes, and 25th in EPA/dropback on non-PA throws, right behind Bo Nix. So nothing is working for Darnold and his turnovers are absolute game-sinkers. Defenses are stacking the box even less than last year and Seattle can’t take advantage. While fully acknowledging the Jadarian Price and Zach Charbonnet injuries, Seattle cannot run the ball explosively. The stacked box rate is 23.6%, 15th in the NFL and nine percentage points lower than 2025. The Seahawks rank 25th in EPA/rush against light boxes, and their yards after contact against light boxes is 19th after being 11th in 2025. Over the past two games, the Seahawks faced stack boxes at a 15% clip, and the Seahawks running backs put up zero explosive runs against the San Francisco 49ers and three against the Broncos. Yes, Sam Darnold is still getting blitzed a lot , and he’s the literal worst QB when pressured . Darnold has been blitzed on almost 37% of his dropbacks, fifth-highest rate in the NFL. Last year is was 34.8%, so it was already high and now it’s even higher. When he’s pressured, he is essentially a non-functioning quarterback. This is his EPA/dropback. Dead last. Keep in mind that Darnold was 30th in this same stat last year, so this is a two-year trend of the same problem. When he’s under duress he is at his worst, and the offensive scheme and pass protection only exacerbates his chronic weakness. The Seahawks still cannot consistently score touchdowns without reasonably good field position . Seattle has now had 40 drives at or inside of its own 30-yard line this season. Only five of those have turned into touchdowns, which ranks 26th (via Stathead ). Their touchdown drives during this ugly three-game stretch have traveled 23, 65, 20, 68, 24, 23, and 67 yards. They’re average TD drive length from Week 4 onward is 41 yards. When Drew Lock started against the Cardinals, they did have 86-, 80-, and 70-yard touchdown drives, while Darnold had 90- and 80-yard TD possessions against the Washington Commanders. That’s it. But the pattern from late last year has bled into this year: Seattle’s offense is stuck when it isn’t starting possessions effectively a couple of first downs away from field goal range. You cannot live like that. The running game is horrendous . I’ve already given some stats earlier in this section, but when Kenneth Walker III and Zach Charbonnet (up until his injury) caught fire it saved the offense. That’s not happening with Emanuel Wilson and George Holani. So if the passing game structure is broken and there is no running game as a fallback option, you are screwed. We have to be honest with how much Klint Kubiak protected this offensive line . Hawkblogger had this great question and stat about Seattle’s max protect usage. Last year they were first, this year (prior to last night) they were 27th. That means a lot more responsibility belonging to the offensive line than previously…

title: 49ers safety fined for uncalled hit on final drive vs. Seahawks
summary: The San Francisco 49ers were able to escape last weekend with a 32-29 road win over the Seattle Seahawks, as they got a go-ahead field goal and forced a turnover on downs on the final drive of the game. Well, it turns out there was an uncalled penalty for an illegal hit on the drive […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - OCTOBER 11: Malik Mustapha #6 of the San Francisco 49ers in action during the game against the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field on October 11, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Alika Jenner/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers were able to escape last weekend with a 32-29 road win over the Seattle Seahawks, as they got a go-ahead field goal and forced a turnover on downs on the final drive of the game. Well, it turns out there was an uncalled penalty for an illegal hit on the drive by Malik Mustapha, and he was fined $6,998 for a hit on a defenseless receiver. The hit came on 1st & 10 and the 50-yard line on Seattle’s final set of downs. The Seahawks had just gotten a 35-yard completion to Jaxon Smith-Njigba on the first play of the drive to set them up at midfield with 1:13 remaining in the game. On the following play, Smith-Njigba was targeted on a slant, but a hard hit from Mustapha jarred the ball loose. Seattle would then have incompletions on second and third down, and their fourth-down completion came just a yard short, forcing a turnover on downs, Well, the NFL deemed Mustapha’s hit ‘‘a hit on a defenseless player’ when issuing the fine, although the play was not flagged for a penalty in real time. Had that been called, Seattle may have had 1st & 10 at the 49ers 35-yard line with over a minute left, needing only a field goal to tie. Instead, the 49ers are now 5-0, while the Seahawks are 3-3 following their loss to the Denver Broncos on Thursday Night Football.

Seven players didn’t practice for the 49ers on Friday: Nick Bosa (calf), Mike Evans (ribs, Achilles), Gracen Halton (quad), Romello Height (hamstring), Deebo Samuel (hamstring), Marques Sigle (ankle), and Garrett Wallow (hamstring). Of that group, Bosa, Samuel, Sigle, and Wallow were all ruled out. Evans and Halton seem to have a solid shot to play. Six others were limited: Christian Kirk (calf), Colton McKivitz (illness), Siran Neal (neck), Upton Stout (shoulder), James Thompson (ankle), and Mykel Williams (knee). Of the bunch, McKivitz and Thompson were cleared off the injury report, while the rest are considered questionable. On the Commanders side, four players are out, while nine others are questionable. The biggest loss is running back Jacory Croskey-Merritt, who missed all week with a groin injury. Additionally, outside linebacker Javontae-Jean Baptiste, quarterback Marcus Mariota, and defensive end Charles Omenihu will all be out for Monday’s game. Wide receiver Stefon Diggs, defensive tackle Javon Kinlaw and linebacker Jordan Magee were among the questionable players for the Commanders. All three practiced in limited fashion on Saturday. Heading into the game the 49ers are 7.5 point favorites against the Commanders. Kickoff is set for 5:15 PM on Monday night on ESPN.

title: A look back at some of the 49ers’ biggest midseason trades under Kyle Shanahan
summary: The San Francisco 49ers have a knack for making blockbuster trades midseason. The odds are even higher when they have a good team and a “missing piece” to put them over the edge. 2026 carries a certain caveat: the 49ers are injured, but they expect a good majority of their players back. That leads us […]
full_text: Oct 31, 2017; Santa Clara, CA, USA; San Francisco 49ers general manager John Lynch (left) and quarterback Jimmy Garoppolo (middle) and head coach Kyle Shanahan (right) speak during a press conference at Levi's Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Stan Szeto-USA TODAY Sports | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The San Francisco 49ers have a knack for making blockbuster trades midseason. The odds are even higher when they have a good team and a “missing piece” to put them over the edge. 2026 carries a certain caveat: the 49ers are injured, but they expect a good majority of their players back. That leads us to wonder what piece they would actually need , knowing most of their players aren’t out for the season. The trade deadline isn’t until November 10, but that won’t stop the speculating. Rather than make guesses, it seemed like a good time to look back at some of the midseason trades the Shanahan regime made over the years. This won’t be every midseason trade of the 49ers, but it will be a few of the notable ones. Jimmy Garoppolo Year Acquired: 2017 From: New England Patriots Cost: Second-round pick Final Year on the Roster: 2022 Some have a bit of a revisionist history when it comes to Jimmy Garoppolo’s time with the 49ers. Acts like stepping out of bounds during a scramble or being counted on to throw a boneheaded interception just about every game. The thing is, Jimmy G was actually seen as the future at one point, and he backed it up. Garoppolo was drafted by the New England Patriots in the second round of the 2014 NFL draft and served as Tom Brady’s backup. It was widely believed Garoppolo’s pick was seen as the heir apparent. In 2016, Garoppolo filled in for a suspended Tom Brady after the Deflategate suspensions and looked very impressive in his 1.5 games until getting injured (this is going to be a running theme). It was only a game and a half, but it was a good game and a half. Things heated up in 2017, with numerous teams like the Cleveland Browns coming up as possible destinations, but the Patriots wouldn’t trade him. Then on that fateful Halloween day, the 49ers made a move for Garoppolo. Their quarterback room wasn’t impressive, containing Brian Hoyer and a rookie C.J. Beathard—who was starting in place of the ineffective Hoyer. It was almost certain Kyle Shanahan would get then-Washington Commanders quarterback Kirk Cousins the following offseason once the team was done using franchise tags to keep him from leaving the organization. Garoppolo was seen as an alternative if that didn’t happen, and at best a quick rental to see what he could do. A quarterback coming in midseason as a starter is usually a bad idea, especially when Garoppolo is going from the Erhardt-Perkins system the Patriots ran to the West Coast terminology Kyle Shanahan used. Week 12 sped that up when CJ Beathard got injured in the final minute of a home game against the Seattle Seahawks. The 49ers were done at this point; the score was 24-6, and they just wanted to get out of there with little injuries. In that minute, the possibilities of Garoppolo were put on full display: the perfect QB sneak, the quick release, and some Jimmy G magic : a touchdown as time expired. The 49ers went to 1-10 following the loss, but didn’t lose another game that season. Despite his inexperience, Garoppolo offered some of the best quarterback play the 49ers had seen in years. He signed a record-breaking deal in the offseason and finally, FINALLY, the quarterback position was figured out. Kirk Cousins was an afterthought, though some stirred the pot, thinking the 49ers might still find a way to get him. Then in Week 3 of 2018, Garoppolo tore his ACL. The 49ers turned in another losing season. Garoppolo returned in 2019, but something was off—though you didn’t really notice it because the 49ers were delivering a season no one expected, one that had a trip to the Super Bowl waiting for them. With a rookie Deebo Samuel and an acquired Emmanuel Sanders (we’ll get to him), Garoppolo had a powerful offense to work with. Looking back, you almost want to ask if the 49ers were winning despite Garoppolo. You knew something was up in the NFC Championship Game when Garoppolo threw only eight times. Back then, the simple argument was that the 49ers’ run game was so good there was no reason to throw. Looking back, there might have been a deeper reason. In the Super Bowl, Garoppolo had a chance to win the game, but overthrew Sanders as the 49ers blew a 10-point lead. While Garoppolo wasn’t a bad quarterback, the way he played in that game, after all the money the 49ers gave him two years earlier, brought a big microscope. It wasn’t an immediate benching, but he was paid to win games like that or at least give a better effort. Garoppolo battled injuries for the rest of his time with the 49ers. The organization traded three draft picks in 2021 to draft Trey Lance, though Garoppolo was still under contract. It’s all good Garoppolo still started that season, but Lance stepped in when Garoppolo suffered an injury or two. When 2022 training camp began and Garoppolo remained on the roster, everyone knew it was a matter of time before he was off the roster. Moving on was almost a certainty (with him even telling the fans goodbye in the final game of the previous season), but that Trey Lance pick wasn’t looking so hot, so they kept Garoppolo on as the backup. Lance had an ankle injury in Week 2, and Garoppolo was the starter again. Then Garoppolo got a foot injury, and the 49ers went to their third quarterback. Some kid named Brock Purdy. The Jimmy G saga was officially over following the 2022 season. If that’s a lot about a single pick, it’s because that’s how exhausting Garoppolo—and the arguments for and against him—was at quarterback. When he started, he looked like the franchise player the 49ers were missing. Unfortunately, after his ACL tear, a statue would have made quicker movements. While he might not have been one of the best quarterbacks in 49ers history, I do think he was one of the most important. That touchdown against Seattle was more than just a garbage-time score. It signaled what was coming with Kyle Shanahan. It would be a few years until the 49ers lucked into Brock Purdy, and until then, Garoppolo made the 49ers competitive. He darn-near won them a Super Bowl. This is one of those trades that was well worth both the pick and the deal that followed in Garoppolo’s salary. Record-breaking, sure, but the 49ers won with Garoppolo. And they weren’t winning with anyone else under center (despite what some may say). Emmanuel Sanders Year Acquired: 2019 From: Denver Broncos Cost: Third and fourth-round picks Final Year on the Roster: 2019 The 49ers had just about everything. They had a filthy defense helmed by Nick Bosa and DeForest Buckner; they had a decent running game with Matt Breida (and later Raheem Mostert); the wide receivers were a bit iffy. Dante Pettis was a bit of a reach, Kendrick Bourne was more a third-down receiver, and Marquise Goodwin was fast, but his getting injured was a matter of “when.” Enter Sanders. While he debuted against the Carolina Panthers and was mostly quiet, his second game against the Arizona Cardinals showed you this was a good pickup: 112 yards receiving, a touchdown, and immediate rapport with Garoppolo. Sanders gave the wide receiver group a shot in the arm and had instant trust from the quarterback. Unfortunately, while Sanders earned his quarterback’s trust, the quarterback failed to connect on a crucial deep pass that could have altered the NFL as we know it. Sanders left in the offseason and signed with the New Orleans Saints. A classic definition of a “rental,” the 49ers’ passing game would have had deeper issues in 2019 without him. Christian McCaffrey Year Acquired: 2022 From: Carolina Panthers Cost: Second, third, and fourth-round pick Final Year on the Roster: Still on the team After the 49ers had a brutal loss to the Atlanta Falcons, Kyle Shanahan decided to…

Height’s designation is an illness, so the hope is that he’s fine, with the game still 72 hours away.” 49ers’ John Lynch says he’s shopping before NFL trade deadline; Kittle asks about Khalil Mack (paywall) “When asked on KNBR on Friday morning about the 49ers possibly trading for Mack, 35, Lynch said “a lot of people ask me that” before revealing Kittle posed the question Thursday. “It’s usually Kittle because he asks about everything, which I love,” Lynch said….“I just like to chirp him and ask what he’s interested in and see if he’ll give me anything,” Kittle said. “So he didn’t really give me a lot yesterday. But me, (fullback Kyle Juszczyk), (left tackle) Trent (Williams), we’ll chirp him just to see if he’ll actually tell us anything. I think he tells Trent the most. Not me, though.” Examining the 49ers’ early-season feat: Generating pressure without Nick Bosa (paywall) “This year, Osa Odighizuwa already has 15 pressures after just five games while rookie Gracen Halton has seven. Odighizuwa’s 12.8 percent pass rush win rate ranks 12th at his position among those who have played five games. Halton’s is 9.6 percent, a rate Odighizuwa says ought to climb as Halton, a fourth-round pick, continues to improve his technique. Halton missed Thursday’s practice with a quadriceps injury. “He’s very raw now,” Odighizuwa said. “So you’re just seeing nothing but upside when you’re watching him play. So it’s exciting stuff.” John Lynch states 49ers trade discussions have ramped up ahead of deadline “Just because the flow of the trade deadline is approaching, yes,” he said. “That’s our job to do that, to talk with our counterparts around the league. We receive calls, we make calls, just to see where the market is at.” Raheem Morris, Klay Kubiak, Brock Purdy share updates ahead of 49ers-Commanders “It was a lot of fun. I’ll give you a quick story. I remember people asking me, ‘How was it coaching [former NFL WR] Julio Jones?’ I said, ‘It’s easy. Good catch, Julio’ (laughter). No, all joking aside, you were able to take your defensive analysis and bring it to those guys while you were learning how to be a good offensive coach and the detail and everything that’s required. That goes into scoring touchdowns and staying on the field and manufacturing first downs. Being around Kyle that first year on offense, it was really the philosophy of what we’re trying to do on football games and how we’re going to go out there and attack people. I had so much fun being able to be over there with the likes of Kyle Shanahan, [Green Bay Packers head coach] Matt LaFleur, [Arizona Cardinals head coach] Mike LaFleur was on that staff, [Los Angeles Chargers offensive coordinator] Mike McDaniel. It was a bunch of really great coaches that were teaching me the backend. And in the frontend, you had all the guys on the front end like [assistant head coach/offensive line coach] Chris Foerster and those guys just teaching you what it was like in the run game and what the rules were and everything that was required to go out there and accomplish what we wanted to get accomplished. You can’t help but bring that back to defense when you had to go back over there. So, when I was able to go back and really formulate how I see the game, how I feel the game, how you want to make your players feel the game, that philosophy really helped me a lot to grow. I think everything from the beginning was really helpful for me when it came to offensive football.” 49ers Week 5 Trench Grades: The duality of it all (paywall) “This week was defined by Gracen Halton dominating and Connor Colby getting dominated. After an encouraging start, Colby is officially a problem. Seattle attacked him, and what’s particularly cool is that I was able to really track that effectively. Because I logged Byron Murphy II and Leonard Williams as elite players (same for Demarcus Lawrence in the run game), we were able to identify that Seattle got Colby isolated against one of that elite pairing consistently. And he consistently lost. It’s one of the cooler reflections of tape to data thus far this season…..Keion White was a menace, and Romello Height is very clearly starting to cook, club and all. Mykel Williams also had a basic bull rush pressure that became White’s sack. It’s worth noting that Williams exclusively played on the edge this week. That’s easing him back into it. I would be stunned if that doesn’t change as the season goes.”

title: 49ers injury updates: Kyle Juszczyk practices in full; 2 rookies miss
summary: The San Francisco 49ers injury report saw a couple of changes Friday. Here were the players who did not participate during Friday’s practice: Nick Bosa missed for the second day in a row. With the 49ers playing on a short week after Monday and then having a bye, it’s setting up like he’ll play against […]
full_text: (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers injury report saw a couple of changes Friday. Here were the players who did not participate during Friday’s practice: Mike Evans (ribs, Achilles) Gracen Halton (quad) Romello Height (hand, illness) Deebo Samuel (hamstring) Marques Sigle (ankle) Garret Wallow (hamstring) Nick Bosa (knee, calf) Nick Bosa missed for the second day in a row. With the 49ers playing on a short week after Monday and then having a bye, it’s setting up like he’ll play against the Atlanta Falcons and then have a week off. Wide receiver Mike Evans didn’t practice for the second day in a row. This is likely how it’ll be with Evans this year. Even if he doesn’t practice, he’ll still suit up on game day. Defensive tackle Gracen Halton missed a second straight day with a quad injury. That’s suboptimal, given the injuries at the position. The 49ers are as thin as you can be at the position. The silver lining is that James Thompson was listed as limited, although that’s not a 1-for-1 swap. Rookie Romello Height was a new addition after practicing in full on Thursday. Height’s designation is an illness, so the hope is that he’s fine, with the game still 72 hours away. Fullback Kyle Juszczyk was upgraded to a full participant. If he only misses one game, that’s impressive. It looked like he’d miss multiple games when Juszczyk was lying on the field and grabbing his knee. Here were the limited participants: Siran Neal (neck) Upton Stout (shoulder) Colton McKivitz (illness) James Thompson (ankle) Christian Kirk (calf Mykel Williams (knee) Carer Willis was listed here on Thursday with a toe injury, but is no longer on the injury report. Juszczyk and Thompson were the only changes here.

Armstrong was fined $11,941 for unnecessary roughness, stemming from a face mask penalty that occurred with 9 minutes, 47 seconds left in the first quarter. He was also charged with a defensive holding call that was also questionable. Going back to the Amik Robertson penalty … looked like holding, not PI. full_text: UPDATE: This story has been updated after the release of the official Commanders injury report. Running back Bill Croskey-Merritt didn’t practice all week due to a groin injury and won’t be available to play the San Francisco 49ers on Monday night. Head coach Dan Quinn ruled him out during his Friday press conference. That fact was confirmed later Friday afternoon, when Washington released its official injury report . That’s a blow, considering Croskey Merritt got revved up with a strong performance in a Week 5 tie versus the New York Giants. Quinn said that Croskey-Merritt re-injured the groin originally hurt in August, which makes recovery a bit tougher. “That’s harder, on the same injury,” Quinn said. “We’ll work really hard to get him back.” While fellow rushers Austin Ekeler (chest) and Rachaad White (shoulder) have been banged up, both backs were cleared to play San Francisco. Another positive is that Jeremy McNichols was a full participant all week and should be ready to come off IR and play. “Having a combination of guys,” Quinn said, “is what we’ll lean on right now.” Quinn also told reporters that quarterback Marcus Mariota (knee), edge rusher Javontae Jean-Baptiste (pec) and defensive lineman Charles Omenihu (groin/ankle) have been ruled out versus San Francisco and won’t make the trip to the Bay Area. Washington has a long list of questionable designations, including receiver Stefon Diggs (hamstring), defensive lineman Javon Kinlaw (ankle/knee) and center Lucas Patrick (illness). Receiver Terry McLaurin (hamstring) and safety Nick Cross (illness) were cleared to play. Cornerback Trey Amos, linebacker Jordan Magee and McNichols are all questionable (as is customary for those with open practice windows) while waiting to come off IR. If any of them are to play Monday, Washington must add them to the active roster and make corresponding moves. title: How Commanders can keep run game going without Bill Croskey-Merritt
summary: Bill Croskey-Merritt isn’t a true feature back, but there’s no doubt that he’s the primary Commanders rusher.   He has taken 57% of carries by running backs through five games and leads his position group in rushing yards by more than double.   While his 3.6 yards per carry is inefficient by any standard, losing […]
full_text: Bill Croskey-Merritt isn’t a true feature back, but there’s no doubt that he’s the primary Commanders rusher. He has taken 57% of carries by running backs through five games and leads his position group in rushing yards by more than double. While his 3.6 yards per carry is inefficient by any standard, losing him for any stretch calls for some adjustment. The Commanders must make some on Monday night against the 49ers, a game he’ll miss with a groin injury. Dan Quinn said it’s a ‘re-injury’ of a groin issue suffered in late August that kept him out until the regular-season opener. “That’s harder, on the same injury,” Quinn said. “We’ll work really hard to get him back.” Washington has the benefit of a Week 7 bye to get Croskey-Merritt right. That could set him up to miss just one game. Or maybe not. The Commanders must find new ways to generate a steady ground game on Monday at least. Quinn said Washington will lean on a group of ball carriers, though all of them are dealing with injury in some way or another. Recent signing (and old friend) Austin Ekeler has a chest injury and was in a non-contact jersey during the practice. Rachaad White has battled a shoulder injury for a few weeks, and was in a non-contact jersey on Thursday. Both guys were cleared to play on Monday night, via the team’s official injury report . And veteran Jeremy McNichols has been on injured reserve thus far recovering from a quadriceps issue but seems poised and ready to return. This is one of the more professional ball players in terms of how he works and what he can bring,” Quinn said. “As we get to Monday – he has had a very good Monday, and we’ll decide from there.” Washington should have the backs available to carry the workload, but they must be efficient while facing San Francisco’s No. 11-ranked run defense . Can they be efficient as standard ball carriers? White and Ekeler are sitting at (roughly) four yards per carry. McNichols hasn’t seen game action to this point. It’s possible. The outer flanks have been good rushing locations from a blocking standpoint and all those guys have the speed and agility to run well outside. It’s hard to call any of those three tough interior runners, which could be an issue. All of those guys are good pass protectors and receivers out of the backfield. The Commanders haven’t used that avenue much to this point, with running backs (including Croskey-Merritt) with a combined 17 catches for 83 yards. Finding them the ball in space could be important, considering their potential explosiveness in the passing game. There’s also the Jayden Daniels factor to consider here. He is Washington’s most dangerous and dynamic rushing threat on designed runs, zone-reads and scramble plays. We saw how good Daniels is in that arena during Week 5, when he had 103 yards and two touchdowns on nine carries. We could see more of those designs in this one to keep the 49ers off balance. “We’re lucky the teams have to account for the quarterback in our run game as well,” offensive coordinator David Blough said in a Thursday press conference. “So, we’ll continue to lean into that and, you know, grow it as the season progresses.” The Commanders will use a committee in the backfield and capitalize on Daniels’ speed, but White’s logically the leading rusher. Ekeler has been with the team but a few weeks and is coming off a torn Achilles from early last year. And McNichols hasn’t played yet. White has been a high-volume carrier in the past, with 272 carries representing Tampa Bay in 2023 , with 990 rushing yards and six touchdowns. He has generally split time, however, but hit 17 carries twice in the past two seasons. The Commanders are at their best with high rushing volume, which Blough has been committed to achieving. Can they get there without Croskey-Merritt? That will be key to keeping the 49ers at bay.

Quinn noted the growth he’s seen from Daniels this year coming back from injury, running a new offense, and he said there’s an elevated presence about him that’s very easy to see. full_text: Purdy throws to a WR | AP Photo/Jed Jacobsohn It’s week 6 of the NFL season and the 1-3-1 Washington Commanders will be facing a 5-0 San Francisco 49ers team on the road at Levi’s Stadium in Santa Clara, CA this coming Monday at 8:15 p.m. ET. The 49ers, Vikings, and Chiefs are the only undefeated teams in the NFL through 5 weeks. Of those unbeaten teams, the 49ers have probably had the most difficult schedule, having played the Seahawks, Rams, and Broncos. It seems like people discounted the 49ers in the offseason due to how gutted by injury their roster has been the last few years, but they are reminding people this year that they are one of the best-coached and most-talented rosters in the NFL. On offense, the 49ers are coached by HC Kyle Shanahan and OC Klay Kubiak, with Shanahan calling the plays. Washington fans don’t need an introduction to Kyle Shanahan, but his offense relies heavily on pre-snap motion, an outside-zone run game, and a high rate of play action. It also relies heavily on versatile players, including TEs and WRs who are able and willing to block downfield. The 49ers offense ranks near the top of the league in explosive play rate ( 3rd in the NFL, 1st in the NFC ) largely by chaining small, well-executed plays together with the occasional unexpected big play to avoid third-and-long situations and leave all options on the table on every down. On the field, the 49ers are led by QB Brock Purdy, who only needs 5 more passes to qualify for the highest career passer rating of any QB in NFL history (we can look forward to the booth pointing out that fact during the game). In addition to Purdy, the 49ers have All-Pro players in TE George Kittle, RB Christian McCaffrey, WR Mike Evans, LT Trent Williams, and FB Kyle Juszczyk. The result has been an offense that is 7th-highest in yards and 3rd-highest in points scored this season. On defense, the 49ers have been led by DC Raheem Morris, former DC of the Rams (2021-2023) and HC of the Falcons (2024-2025). Morris has reportedly simplified the playbook on defense , leading to quicker reactions and more confidence in his defensive players. The 49ers like to run multiple fronts, with a mix of 3-, 4-, and 5-man fronts and mostly zone coverage. The 49ers defense is anchored by 1st-team All Pro players EDGE Nick Bosa and LB Fred Warner, each one of the best at their position. The result has been the NFL’s 10th-best defense against the run and 10th-best defense against the pass in terms of yards allowed, but most importantly giving the 4th-fewest overall points allowed. Overall, the 49ers are fielding one of the NFL’s best units on offense and defense this year, though they will be suffering somewhat from the suspension of LB Dre Greenlaw . I asked Jason Aponte of Niners Nation five questions about the state of the 49ers and what to look for in this game. 1) There has been some controversy about how well the 49ers have been drafting. What do you think about the 49ers in the draft and how have your young players been looking in games? While the 49ers have had issues turning their first-round picks into immediate, impact players, Mykel Williams is still very young and looked impressive in his first action on Sunday. De’Zhaun Stribling was the toast of the town until his unfortunate injury, but the 49ers still view him as a big piece of the offense moving forward. This latest draft class has seen huge contributions from DT Gracen Halton, LB Jaden Dugger, and RB Kaelon Black. Meanwhile, Marques Sigle was coming into his own at safety before his injury. CB Renardo Green is increasingly looking like a star, and CB Deommodore Lenoir is homegrown as well. The offensive line includes three 49ers draft picks: Dominick Puni, Colton McKivitz, and Connor Colby. I’d say the idea of the 49ers drafting poorly is far more dramatic than reality. Let’s not forget hitting on Brock Purdy. #49ers HC Kyle Shanahan really liked that they were able to trade back & not reach during the 2026 NFL Draft pic.twitter.com/nHeIKGxFxI — 49ers & NFL News 24/7 (@49ersSportsTalk) April 25, 2026 2) Washington fans are very familiar with LT Trent Williams, but tell us about the rest of the 49ers offensive line and how they’ve been performing this season? The offensive line has been one of the bigger surprises in 2026. Williams is as stellar as ever after delivering a clean sheet against Seattle’s defensive line. RG Puni and RT McKivitz have been excellent, and C Jake Brendel is enjoying his best season at center through five weeks. LG Colby did struggle on Sunday against Seattle, but Byron Murphy tends to do that to anyone. All in all, the 49ers offensive line moved Seattle off the line on their final drive, which gave the 49ers the lead and the win by running the football inside with duo runs. That, in itself, is a huge statement. 3) Washington’s GM Adam Peters came from the 49ers. What can you tell us about him? Adam Peters’ time with the 49ers is hard to nail down. On the one hand, there was a narrative out there that every late-round gem unearthed by the 49ers was Peters’ doing, but nobody knows that for certain. On the other hand, the number of 49ers players who didn’t work out and became Commanders could be a signal of how much Peters was involved, I.E., Javon Kinlaw. There is no doubt someone was working the PR machine for Peters, because the narrative became that every successful draft pick was Peters doing and every unsuccessful pick was John Lynch and Kyle Shanahan’s fault. Nobody knows for sure, but for some reason, that is how he was remembered, and I feel like the reputation wasn’t warranted. 4) Who is one 49ers player on offense and one player on defense that Washington fans probably don’t know much about, but should? One player Washington should know about is running back Kaelon Black from Indiana. Christian McCaffrey is the star of the show, but given the injuries to the wide receiver room, I can see Shanahan playing a run-first, close-to-the-vest type of game to get a victory on Monday night. If the 49ers get to 30 carries, they will most likely win, and Black would be in line for 10-15 opportunities. Black feeds on rhythm and needs more touches to get going, but if the 49ers get to the magic 30-carry number, Black will likely be a big part of that and could help put Washington on ice. 5) How should Washington go about gameplanning this matchup on both sides of the ball? A proper game plan for Washington on offense would be ball and clock control. Jayden Daniels did significant damage on the ground against the Giants, and his mobility will be a pain to contain, but keeping long drives alive while keeping the 49ers offense on the sideline could tip the scales in this game. Punctuating those drives with touchdowns puts pressure on the 49ers offense, especially with limited time with the ball. Defensively, choking off the run game would be ideal, but with the way Brock Purdy is playing, it may not matter. Forcing Purdy to drop back a ton isn’t as solid a plan as it sounds, but making any offense one-dimensional is the best idea. You can force the 49ers to throw the ball more, but leaning on McCaffrey, Mike Evans, and George Kittle isn’t some sort of death sentence. A companion article to this with my answers to Jason’s questions is linked here . Thanks again to Jason Aponte for taking time out of his day to answer our questions about the 49ers.

That’s a +5 turnover differential for the Commanders, tied for second-best in the NFL, even though the team has only won once this season. This is unusual, as teams in the top five in that category tend to be better positioned to win. 💪💪💪 @Redwire | #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/ifCOL1n4a8 — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) October 17, 2026 Washington got that lone win by turning three takeaways into 20 points in a 33-31 win, despite Seattle heavily outgaining the Commanders. That game should serve as an example moving forward of what happens when they take advantage of opponents’ mistakes. Against Indianapolis, however, Washington forced two turnovers but managed just three points off those opportunities in a 30-13 loss. The Commanders enter Week 6 ranked 30th in scoring defense, allowing 29.8 points per game. Washington is 25th against the pass, allowing 242.5 yards per game. The team’s offense averages 23 points per game, good enough to rank 17th in the league. Monday, Washington faces the 49ers, who average 30.8 points per game but only have a +2 turnover differential and a 5-0 record. That’s the difference between these two teams. Washington has done a good job taking the ball away, but when you’re allowing nearly 30 points per game and failing to consistently capitalize on those extra possessions, even one of the NFL’s best turnover margins isn’t going to save you. title: Dan Quinn, hot seats & 18%: Commanders fan reaction to the Giants tie
summary: A child of the last millennium When I was a young kid — near the middle part of the 20th century — we didn’t have the Super Bowl. The NFL’s championship game wasn’t officially called the Super Bowl until January 1969, just months ahead of the first Apollo moon landing, and the name was retroactively […]
full_text: ASHBURN, VA - AUGUST 12: Head coach Dan Quinn of the Washington Commanders speaks with the media during a joint practice at BigBear.ai Performance Center on August 12, 2026 in Ashburn, Virginia. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images A child of the last millennium When I was a young kid — near the middle part of the 20th century — we didn’t have the Super Bowl. The NFL’s championship game wasn’t officially called the Super Bowl until January 1969, just months ahead of the first Apollo moon landing, and the name was retroactively given to the first two AFL-NFL championship games that had been played in calendar years 1967 and 1968. Back then, in my early childhood, before the Super Bowl era of the NFL had begun, the league’s origins didn’t really feel very far in the past — after all, the National Football League had been born at about the same time as my father! Even major league baseball wasn’t much older than my grandfather . Somehow, as a late-postwar ‘baby boom’ kid in the early 1960s, I still felt a connection to games and players of decades past that, today, are barely even considered relevant to the modern games and the digital age. But I was that nerdy kid who used to read books about the history of football and baseball with incredible voracity ( though not too nerdy; I also played all the sports I read so much about ). I knew all about Ty Cobb, Bronco Nagurski ( who could only be stopped ’with a shotgun as he’s leaving the dressing room’ ), Babe Ruth, Jim Thorpe, Red Grange, the Nippy Jones shoe-polish pitch that happened a scant 3 years before I was born, and the cry of “Say it ain’t so, Joe” from the 1919 World Series. Knowing all that about my childhood connection to the (then) not-so-distant early days of American professional sports, it’s probably not surprising that an apocryphal saying about baseball reverberates with me; here it is, paraphrased from an episode of The West Wing : “They say you’re guaranteed to win 54 games and guaranteed to lose 54 games, but it’s the 54 in the middle that decide the pennant. I just wish somebody would circle those games on the calendar so we’d know when to try.” Data, inertia, and the fluid-54 The humor in that wry statement about the baseball season is obvious, I hope, but there’s also a more universal truth in there as well; specifically, that there’s a certain amount of inertia in data samples, where the real action is in the fluid middle, not at the more static extremes. Let me try to explain what I mean. Reacts surveys Over the years that I’ve been responsible for authoring the Hogs Haven Reacts surveys and publishing their results, the weekly in-season confidence question has often made me think of this longstanding observation about wins, losses, and that fluid middle-54 in major league baseball. I guess what I mean is that — with respect to our Hogs Haven surveys — even when things are generally going well for the team, a certain percentage of fans will express a lack of confidence; by the same token, even when things are going poorly, a certain percentage of fans seem to remain optimistic in their outlook about the team. Most of the time, it seems to me, the story I end up writing is focused on the thoughts of survey respondents who comprise that fluid middle — the fans whose optimism or pessimism (in a given week) is driven largely by the team’s W-L record and recent on-field performance. It’s their constantly-changing mood that I typically find myself attempting to capture, understand, and explain from week to week. Captain Jack In some seasons, that middle group has been so large that it reminded me of the movie, Pirates of the Caribbean: At World’s End , where Jack Sparrow gets the entire crew to sprint back and forth across the deck in unison, rocking the Black Pearl until it completely flips over. Entrenched Pollyannas and Cassandras This season, the confidence (or lack of confidence) has been slightly more stable than that. On each end — the “Pollyannas” and the “Cassandras” — there has been a stable group comprising about 15% to 20% of survey respondents who’ve either maintained confidence despite problems (Pollyannas), or, alternately, have remained pessimistic even when good things have happened (Cassandras). That has left about 60% to 70% of survey respondents swinging back and forth in response to the latest news — an impressively large group, to be sure, but not enough to — metaphorically speaking — flip over the Black Pearl . There’s a surprising amount of ballast at each end of our survey. Surprisingly, not a total loss of faith Reading many of the headlines this week in the wake of the tied game vs the NY Giants, I had the feeling of a cataclysmic disaster taking place in Ashburn; a complete loss of faith based on the final 12 seconds of that overtime contest. These survey results don’t really reflect that, though. The 18% of survey respondents still professing to have confidence in the team’s direction isn’t significantly different than the result following the Week 2 loss to the Cowboys in Dallas. Honestly, I’d been expecting the survey results this week to show an absolute meltdown in confidence to near-0%. Instead, roughly 1 in 6 survey respondents continue to see a team headed in the right direction. Visit our partners at FanDuel Cassandra’s view We know which issues are of concern to the 82% who lack confidence. The Cassandras argue that Quinn has mismanaged critical game situations, failed to mentor or assist his rookie offensive coordinator (David Blough), and relies on high energy/passion over sound X’s and O’s. They (mostly) want Quinn fired immediately. Opinions on GM Adam Peters are more nuanced and divided, with many commenters urging patience, pointing out that he inherited a legacy of mediocrity and mismanagement, and feeling that AP deserves at least a couple more seasons to finish building the foundation, while critics argue the roster remains one of the lowest-rated in the league, pointing to poor pass-rush production, lack of player development, and questionable durability among free-agent additions. A number of critics have noted that other heavily injured teams (like the 49ers) have managed to stay competitive, leading some to question the team’s conditioning, depth, and overall roster quality. How about Pollyanna? But what things are on the minds of the Pollyannas that comprise 18% of this week’s survey respondents? For many, having a true dual-threat franchise quarterback is the primary reason to believe the team is heading in the right direction. Fans praise Jayden Daniels’ vision, recent enhanced willingness to protect himself from injury, and pure football speed as an elite foundation for the rest of the roster. Others advocate for patience with young offensive coordinator David Blough, arguing that detours and growing pains are an expected part of a long-term rebuild. A number of those who continue to express confidence in the direction of the team also seem more inclined to see a method to the manner in which Adam Peters is building the roster, along with improving roster-building skills from year to year for the 3rd-year GM. Differing perceptions of time and achievement When I try to analyze the dynamic at work in these survey results, I think an important factor that separates the Pollyannas and Cassandras is their relative perception of time — as in, how long it should take the leadership (owners, GM, coaches) to shed the dysfunction of the Snyder era, re-build the hollow roster left behind by Ron Rivera, and field a consistent playoff contender on the field. Those still seeing the team through burgundy-colored glasses seem to perceive a construction project underway that isn’t complete, but has that strong foundation mentioned above in Jayden Daniels. They tend to see 2025 as an outlier driven by some poor roster decisions that haven’t been repeated, and a plague of injuries that also adversely impacted the Commanders in Weeks…
