title: NFL Week 6 predictions: Upsets, fantasy sleepers, stat lines, TD scorers, more
summary: First touchdown of 2026 for Drake London? Aaron Rodgers climbing the NFL record books? The Texans pulling an upset? Let's predict 15 things for Week 6.
full_text:
Week 6 of the  2026 NFL season is underway after the Broncos beat the Seahawks in overtime Thursday night . But what will happen in the remaining 13 games? We have 15 predictions from our NFL experts.

 First, betting analyst Pamela Maldonado picks three underdogs who could win outright. Then, analytics writer Seth Walder projects stat lines for three players. Fantasy football writer Eric Moody suggests three sleepers, and analyst Matt Bowen predicts three players who will find the end zone. Finally, analyst Ben Solak lays out three wild-card predictions.

 Could the Texans pull off an upset in London? How many sacks will Chiefs defensive tackle Chris Jones have against the Chargers? Could Rams tight end Tyler Higbee be a sneaky play in fantasy? Will Falcons wide receiver Drake London find the end zone for the first time this season? And will Aaron Rodgers move up in the NFL record books against the Bucs? Let's make 15 big predictions for the Sunday and Monday action.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Upset picks | Projected stat lines 
 Fantasy sleepers, surprises 
 TD scorers | Other predictions 

 
 

 Maldonado predicts three upsets 
 

 Dallas Cowboys +1.5 (+102 moneyline) at Green Bay Packers 

 The Packers have allowed the eighth-fewest passing yards per attempt this season, but this matchup presents a much tougher test than the backup quarterbacks they've faced in the past two weeks. The Cowboys convert nearly half their third downs and lead the league in the percentage of possessions producing points. Green Bay can hit big plays, but the Cowboys have enough on offense with Dak Prescott , CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens to answer.

 
 

 

 New York Giants +1.5 (+108 moneyline) vs.  New Orleans Saints 

 The Giants have a way to make this Sunday easier for quarterback Jameis Winston . They can run against a struggling Saints defense, then move tight end Isaiah Likely out wide for easy throws over smaller defenders.

 On the other side, Saints QB Tyler Shough has struggled even when he has time to throw. So New York doesn't need to constantly pressure him to get stops. That gives the Giants enough to keep this close and win at home.

 
 

 Houston Texans +3 (+120 moneyline) vs. Jacksonville Jaguars 

 Jacksonville's defense is allowing just 14 points per game, but opponents are still finding room to throw. The Jaguars allow 7.7 yards per attempt and 93.2 yards per game to No. 1 receivers, giving QB C.J. Stroud and WR Nico Collins a matchup to attack in London on Sunday .

 Houston can also pressure  Trevor Lawrence  without blitzing or disguising its coverage, making it harder for the quarterback to read the defense. That gives the Texans a way to get stops while leaving more players in coverage.

 

 

 Walder predicts three stat lines 
 

 Sauce Gardner , CB, Indianapolis Colts : 28 coverage snaps, 3 targets, 0 receptions allowed 

 Gardner has had a rough season, allowing 1.3 yards per coverage snap and 10.3 EPA when targeted. But I think most of that has been due to on-ball results, rather than Gardner putting himself in poor position throughout the route.

 Gardner has allowed a plus-19% completion percentage over expected, while spending 24% of the time in tight coverage (fourth most among outside CBs with at least 100 coverage snaps). And my own player tracking analysis indicates Gardner has been in good position before the ball is thrown. All of this is to say that his start to the season might be a blip, and a game against the Titans is just what he needs to turn the results around.

 
 

 Chris Jones , DT, Kansas City Chiefs : 1.5 sacks, 5 pressures, 26% pass rush win rate 

 Jones has the privilege of facing Chargers right guard Cole Strange in Week 6 , which ought to present more than enough opportunities for Jones to get at QB Justin Herbert . Strange has just a fourth percentile pass block win rate this season; Herbert is taking sacks at a massive 9.7% clip.

 Jones' season is off to a quiet start with zero sacks and a 59th percentile pass rush win rate at defensive tackle. He can kickstart his year against Strange -- and have an even bigger day if right tackle Joe Alt ( neck ) is out again.

 

 
 

 Michael Wilson , WR, Arizona Cardinals : 34 routes, 6 targets, 2 receptions, 12 receiving yards 

 Marvin Harrison Jr . was traded  to the Texans, so Wilson is in for a production explosion, right? That might happen ... but only after this week against the Rams .

 Wilson could see a healthy dosage of  Trent McDuffie  -- if the Rams' top cornerback plays (he is questionable with a groin injury). McDuffie is allowing 0.4 yards per coverage snap in 2026 -- well below the 1.1 average for an outside cornerback, per NFL Next Gen Stats. Plus, he has spent 28% of his time in tight coverage, which puts him third in that stat -- one spot above the aforementioned Gardner.

 Wilson has a 93 catch score in ESPN's receiver scores , which means he's good in contested catch situations. But he is struggling to get separation from defenders (47 open score). It is likely going to be a tough afternoon for him.

 

 

 Moody predicts three fantasy sleepers 
 

 Kirk Cousins , QB, Las Vegas Raiders (41.8% rostered in ESPN leagues) 

 Cousins disappointed with just 13.7 fantasy points against the Patriots last week , but he has averaged 18.5 fantasy points per game this season. He has a favorable matchup against a Bills defense that has allowed the fourth-most fantasy points per game to quarterbacks and the most to wide receivers.

 
 

 Kendre Miller , RB, New Orleans Saints (21.9%)

title: Ravens believe Browns' Todd Monken wants 'to kick our tail'
summary: When Cleveland's coach takes the sideline Sunday, Baltimore players will face off against their fiery former OC.
full_text:
OWINGS MILLS, Md. -- Many in the Baltimore Ravens ' locker room believe Cleveland Browns coach Todd Monken is not being entirely truthful about Sunday's reunion.

 Monken, who was Baltimore's offensive coordinator the previous three seasons, insisted this week that there are no added emotions in facing his former team. But the Ravens feel they know exactly what this game means to the usually fiery Monken.

 "If I know Todd the way I think I know Todd, he will want to kick our tail," Ravens cornerback Marlon Humphrey said.

 Despite great success in 2023 and 2024, Monken exited Baltimore nine months ago amid conflicting reports about his relationship with players, especially with quarterback Lamar Jackson , who isn't expected to play Sunday because of an ankle injury. During the 2025 season, when the offense dropped to the middle of the NFL, there were anonymous sources who voiced the players' discontent with Monken's playcalling.

 

 In the offseason, Monken stressed there were no issues between him and Jackson. After Monken was hired by the Browns in January, he received congratulatory texts from Ravens players, including Jackson.

 Now, after leading the Browns (3-2) to their best start in five years, Monken is facing the Ravens (4-1) in an early-season battle for first place in the AFC North ( 1 p.m. ET, CBS ).

 "He might not say it in the media, but to the team he definitely talks a lot of trash and lets them know [that] he wants to beat us," Ravens running back Derrick Henry said.

 During his time in Baltimore, Monken elevated the Ravens' offense to new heights. In 2023, he helped Jackson to his second NFL Most Valuable Player award. The next season, Monken led the Ravens' offense to its first No. 1 ranking in the NFL.

 But in 2025, the Ravens unraveled in a disappointing 8-9 season. With Jackson struggling with injuries, Baltimore finished with 311.8 yards per game, which was its fewest in eight years.

 Ravens wide receiver Rashod Bateman said he felt Monken left on good terms, pointing out the impressive production and records set under him.

 "When you are a player, you have to make the choice whether you want to make this game about Todd Monken or do you want to make it about going to play football," Bateman said. "I am pretty sure Todd Monken is not worried about Rashod Bateman or what he has done in Baltimore. He is worried about getting the Cleveland Browns right to beat us. So, I think for both sides, the respect is mutual."

 Monken feels grateful for how the Ravens handled his final month with the team, and the Ravens can be thankful to Monken for how he helped them land his successor with an influential phone call to Declan Doyle.  

 In January, Monken was allowed to work at the Ravens' facility after John Harbaugh was fired as head coach. He had his initial virtual meeting with the Browns while sitting in his Ravens office.

 

 "I don't think it was awkward for them," Monken said of the Ravens. "We'd been around it for three years. I mean, there's a lot of appreciation of me for the people in the building, and I would think there's appreciation for the job that I did every day there."

 When the Ravens showed interest in Declan Doyle to become their next offensive coordinator, one of the calls that Doyle made was to Monken. They knew each other because Monken was a graduate assistant at Notre Dame with Doyle's father, Chris.

 Monken's advice to Doyle: Take the Ravens' offensive coordinator job, because the players are there to win.

 "He certainly had a big influence," Doyle said. "If he had said, 'Hey, don't touch that place,' I would have placed a lot of value in that. But that was not the case."

 Monken knows a lot of the strengths and weaknesses of Baltimore's offensive players. The Ravens are familiar with Monken's schemes and tendencies.

 Ravens coach Jesse Minter doesn't think either side has an advantage, saying the situation is "overblown."

 "There are so many of those things where it's like, 'Well, they know that we know that they know,'" Minter said. "[I] don't put a lot of stock into it."

 Likewise, Monken wants to make sure the focus is on the teams and not him.

 "Ultimately, I have a job to do," Monken said. "And the job is, what can I do today to help our team get better and keep taking strides to play winning football. And that's really all I think about."

title: What Cowboys-Packers' Micah Parsons trade means a year later
summary: We examine the fallout and lingering impact on both franchises more than a year after the blockbuster deal.
full_text:
If Sunday's game between the Green Bay Packers and the Dallas Cowboys at Lambeau Field were a made-for-TV movie, it would open like this: The home team's starters would be introduced, and Micah Parsons would run out last to a raucous ovation while his former team stood and watched.

 Instead, Parsons will be without a uniform, will come out unannounced and his play will have zero impact on who wins the game. Nearly 14 months after Parsons was traded from the Cowboys to the Packers, and a little more than nine months removed from left ACL surgery, the All-Pro edge rusher has yet to be cleared to return from last year's season-ending injury.

 Given everything that has happened for the two teams since that Aug. 28, 2025, blockbuster deal , Parsons' presence still looms large over both franchises as they try to build championship contenders. Both teams are off to bumpy starts this season as Green Bay awaits Parsons' return to action and Dallas' defense continues to struggle.

 

 Parsons might still be the one player the Packers need to get back to a Super Bowl, but it didn't happen in Year 1. The Packers were 9-3-1 when Parsons blew out his knee at the Denver Broncos in Week 15, and they didn't win another game -- including an opening-round playoff loss. They're off to a 3-2 start this year while they wait for Parsons' return, which could still be weeks away .

 Meanwhile, the Cowboys had arguably the worst defense in the NFL last season, and at 2-3 this season, they're still trying to remake their defense into what owner and general manager Jerry Jones envisioned when he shipped Parsons to the Packers.

 Just like last season's 40-40 tie -- when Parsons had a sack and three tackles in his first matchup against the Cowboys -- Sunday's game ( 8:20 p.m. ET, NBC ) will not reveal a winner in the trade, but what does it mean for both franchises a year later?

 Cowboys quarterback  Dak Prescott said he will miss being able to play against his former teammate.

 "Wishing him all the best and getting healthy," Prescott said. "Caught up with him a lot this offseason and here in Dallas while he was rehabbing, so he knows I support him in that.

 "But at the end of the day, it's the Cowboys versus the Packers. It's not me versus Micah, or the Cowboys versus Micah. It's about us going in and getting to win."

 

 How the Parsons trade has affected the Cowboys 

 Since the trade, the Cowboys dealt for defensive tackle Quinnen Williams . After signing him to a three-year, $105 million extension in August, Jones said the Parsons trade could not have worked out better, but he stopped short of saying the Cowboys won the deal.

 In addition to defensive tackle Kenny Clark , the Cowboys received the Packers' first-round picks in 2026 and 2027.

 Last season, the Cowboys flipped the better of the 2027 first-rounders to the New York Jets for Williams and their 2026 second-round pick. With the No. 26 pick in this year's draft, the Cowboys added pass rusher Malachi Lawrence , who has only one sack, one tackle for loss and seven quarterback pressures but is expected to see more playing time Sunday.

 Jones went so far as to compare the Parsons trade to the 1989 trade of running back Herschel Walker to the Minnesota Vikings that helped the Cowboys win three Super Bowls in a four-year span in the 1990s.

 "You could say those picks got us key players, but the main thing that the Herschel Walker trade did, it caused me to be more aggressive and caused us to, if you will, take more risk because we had more picks," Jones said in August. "It's like going to Las Vegas with some extra money in your pocket.

 "In a way this actually created a mental part to us and to my role in it, to step out and make the moves and take, if you will, risks that are involved to be where we are today with a complete makeover of the defense."

 

 But the makeover, to be kind, remains a work in progress.

 Last season, the Cowboys allowed a franchise-record 511 points and were 30th in yards allowed per game. After the season, defensive coordinator Matt Eberflus was fired, and only one defensive coach remains from last year's staff (assistant linebackers coach J.J. Clark).

 Defensive coordinator Christian Parker came from the Philadelphia Eagles , where he was the passing game coordinator and defensive backs coach in 2024 and 2025. He brought a new scheme that has had some strong moments -- among them two fourth-and-1 stops of Baltimore Ravens running back Derrick Henry in Week 3 and improved third-down work at times -- but has not been consistent.

 Through five games, the Cowboys have allowed 395.4 yards per game, which ranks 31st in the league. Four of their five opponents have had a season high in yardage. They are allowing 168.4 rushing yards per game (32nd) and 27.2 points per game (26th). Dating back to last season, the Cowboys have allowed 20 or more points in each of their past 12 games, matching a team record.

 This week, Dallas added longtime NFL coach Mike Pettine , a former Packers defensive coordinator, as a senior defensive assistant to help Parker.

 "We have to play better all across the boards," coach Brian Schottenheimer said. "I think [Parsons is] a terrific player. I'm looking forward to seeing him, but I like the picks that we got from Micah. I think we've done some really great things getting those picks. 

 "And I hope that when it's all said and done, it goes to show that that made a big difference because I do feel that way when you look at the guys who we were able to add to our roster."

 Yet that difference hasn't been reflected in takeaways or sacks. 

 During Parsons' tenure in Dallas after being drafted No. 12 in 2021, the Cowboys averaged 1.72 takeaways per game. Since the trade, they have averaged .64. With Parsons on the roster, the Cowboys had three or more sacks 33 times (48.5%), but in the 22 games since the trade, the Cowboys have reached that mark seven times (31.8%). With Parsons in Dallas, the Cowboys were held to one sack or fewer 29.4% of the time. Without him, that figure is 52.3%.

 

 How the Parsons trade has affected the Packers 

 In Green Bay, the jolt that Parsons' arrival gave to the locker room was unlike anything many of the players had ever felt.

 "S---, his presence," Packers All-Pro safety Xavier McKinney said at the time. "Just being Micah Parsons. When you get a guy like that, of that talent, you can put him out there and tell him to just stand there. And before the play is snapped, they're going to be looking for him because if you're not prepared for him, it's not going to be good for you."

 Or as Packers coach Matt LaFleur said: "He definitely has an aura about him."

 Parsons delivered on the promise initially. He recorded 12.5 sacks before his left knee buckled in the 14th game of the season. Despite missing the last three games, he still led the NFL with 64 quarterback pressures, according to ESPN Analytics. The problem was, the Packers didn't win another game, including the deflating playoff loss to the Chicago Bears in the wild-card round, when they allowed 25 fourth-quarter points.

 

 The trade meant the Packers went into this past offseason without a first-round pick. But general manager Brian Gutekunst believed he had a roster that wasn't in need of many players, as evidenced by him trading away more picks and drafting six players -- his smallest class since taking over in 2018. He used his first three picks on defensive players -- cornerback Brandon Cisse (Round 2), defensive tackle Chris McClellan (Round 3) and edge rusher Dani Dennis-Sutton (Round 4). All three have been significant contributors so far.

 The Packers also lost defensive coordinator Jeff Hafley, who became the Miami Dolphins ' head coach in January. He was replaced by former Arizona Cardinals coach Jonathan Gannon, who has kept his plans for how he intends to use Parsons mostly under wraps.

 Gannon, however, said Parsons has made an impact despite not…

title: Why is Chargers RB Omarion Hampton's snap count decreasing?
summary: Coach Jim Harbaugh and OC Mike McDaniel on why RB Omarion Hampton is being used differently.
full_text:
For all intents and purposes, when the Los Angeles Chargers selected running back Omarion Hampton with the No. 22 pick in the 2025 NFL draft, it seemed a perfect fit.

 Hampton provided the physical, bruising style of running so often associated with coach Jim Harbaugh's teams. He was the type of three- or even four-down back that the front office envisioned pairing with quarterback Justin Herbert .

 But less than two seasons in, it's been more flashes than a surefire bet.

 

 A fractured left ankle early in the season and a right ankle injury late hampered his rookie campaign, but Hampton produced when on the field with 545 yards and a team-high four touchdowns. With offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel hired in January, Hampton's role seemingly neared a breakout in a new wide-zone-heavy run scheme.

 The former Miami Dolphins coach compared Hampton to Hall of Fame running back Terrell Davis. And after a week of training camp, McDaniel highlighted Hampton as a player with as much growth as, if not more than, any player.

 The proof hasn't been in the pudding so far.

 This season, Hampton's snap count has decreased since having 40 in Week 2 against the Las Vegas Raiders . Hampton also had a career-high 23 carries in that game. Since then, his numbers have dropped, going to 20 snaps against the Denver Broncos in Week 5 -- the fewest offensive snaps among the running back room of Kimani Vidal (26) and Keaton Mitchell (21).

 However, that isn't hindering Harbaugh's confidence in Hampton. Harbaugh said that Hampton is "playing extremely well in all phases." But, if that is true, then why the decrease in usage?

 "Yeah, hard to predict how many [snaps] a player is going to get but yeah, every time Omarion is in the game, I'm fired up," Harbaugh said Wednesday. "Kimani played really really good football too. And Keaton as well. There's three outstanding backs, but love them, love them all."

 Following a Week 4 loss to the Seattle Seahawks , Harbaugh didn't explain why the running back share changed in Week 3.

 

 Hampton had a costly fumble against the Raiders, his second of the season. Then in Week 3, he dropped to 27 snaps against the  Buffalo Bills . Then, he played 22 snaps versus Seattle. Harbaugh said the rotation is what they thought was best for the team and wanted to utilize the skills of three running backs who are "all playing good."

 From a statistical standpoint, Hampton's numbers aren't far off through five games this season compared to last. He currently has a team-high 73 carries for 271 yards as opposed to 66 carries for 314 yards last year. His runs have been deemed a "rush success" 37% of the time so far, according to NFL Next Gen Stats. That figure was at 42% in 2025.

 McDaniel finally broke the usage change down the week after Seattle. He said that depending on how the game plays out, he has had plenty of times when three running backs are involved on game day. According to him, the running back room is a "strength" and there's an advantage to having defenses prepare to tackle three different players with "various skill sets."

 "I'm assessing each week what our players are good at because I'm getting new information, and it's new in a season. So, trying to find the right balance, trying to give guys opportunities," McDaniel said. "It's very fluid, but it's not an attack on any one individual. It's my job to do better, score more points and utilize all the assets we have. And there's only one ball."

 

 Hampton is still listed as the starter in the depth chart. However, McDaniel felt he was "underutilizing a strength" -- in the RB room as a whole -- which might explain the carry distribution changing as this season has progressed.

 The issue with the distribution is that the Chargers spent a high pick on Hampton. Vidal was a 2024 sixth-rounder, and Mitchell arrived as a free agent in March. The investment in Hampton is more costly if it fails.

 "I can't make the statement more emphatic. It's not because I've lost any faith in [Omarion] at all. I thought he was a very hard tackle and made plays with his opportunities, and that's what I was looking to do in the game," McDaniel said after Week 4. "I didn't go into the game thinking of a touch ratio. It just was the way it played out based on what was happening in the game."

 Three days later, Hampton played the fewest snaps of his career. Meanwhile, Vidal and Mitchell's roles have been on the uptick. McDaniel said Thursday that "there's a lot of things from a matchmaking and game-planning perspective about what you're doing as an offense," before pointing out that Hampton had the most carries (14) of anyone on the team.

 So far, the running back room -- which McDaniel saw as a strength going into the season -- has been safe from the injuries that have decimated the offense. That leads to McDaniel diversifying the back involvement rather than running the game plan "through guys that got here in the last couple weeks."

 "The running back room is a very important piece of our team, and because it's a really strong, really good room by all NFL standards. For instance, I think there was a couple third downs that Keaton picked up for us that were crucial, and Kimani had a great touchdown run on the play after a turnover," McDaniel said Thursday. "So we'll continue to utilize those guys for their playmaking ability, particularly when you see lineup changes like we did [against Denver]."

 Each of them have had their productive stretches, offering a different look for defenses. Vidal specifically has seen his offensive snap count rise from four in Week 1 to 26 in Week 5, when he rumbled for a 42-yard touchdown run that changed the game's momentum. Mitchell has steadily played at least 15 snaps each game.

 

 Those three are "a little different" but each does a great job, Herbert said. But as for Hampton, he said he has seen him grow into someone the team can trust to put the ball in his hands.

 "He's just such a physical runner. A guy that's able to break so many tackles and he's great in pass protection too," Herbert said. "So, a guy that you just get the ball whether he's running over a guy or running around him with his speed, he's a great guy to get the ball to."

 Hampton was once viewed as the future of the Chargers' back field alongside Herbert and a dominant rushing attack. One new offensive coordinator later, his role is decreasing -- just like the Chargers' playoff hopes.

title: Rams can't seem to fix their special teams
summary: Special teams have played a significant role in five of the Rams' nine losses since the start of last season, including the playoffs.
full_text:
LOS ANGELES -- The Rams entered this season as Super Bowl favorites, but their special teams unit has been a big part of what has kept Los Angeles' "superteam" from having success.

 As Rams head coach Sean McVay tries to fix the issues for the unit in-season, he said he has leaned on a lesson from former Rams defensive coordinator Wade Phillips.

 "If it's important enough to you, you'll get it done." 

 The Rams enter Week 6 with a minus-15.3% special teams DVOA, which would be the worst in history over a full season.

 One of the first attempts to fix the unit came Oct. 2 when the Rams cut returner Xavier Smith . The second came Tuesday, when the Rams released kicker Harrison Mevis .

 The previous day, Mevis missed a 50-yard field goal attempt in the first quarter of the Rams' loss to the Buffalo Bills and had a potential winning field goal blocked in overtime. The kicks were the fourth and fifth failed kicks by Mevis this season, giving him a 56% field goal rate (5-of-9). That is the lowest field goal percentage in the NFL.

 The Rams replaced Mevis with Blake Grupe , whom they signed off of the New York Jets ' practice squad.

 "Ultimately, we need better production, and that's what we're hoping to get [from] Blake," McVay said.

 

 Grupe split his 2025 season with the New Orleans Saints and the Indianapolis Colts . Grupe, who spent the first 45 games of his career with the Saints, was cut after going 18-of-26 on field goals with New Orleans in 2025.

 He spent the final five games with the Colts, where he made all 11 of his field goal attempts and all 10 extra points.

 Grupe called that time in Indianapolis "a big stint in my career," saying he was able to show what he could do.

 "I hit the ground running," Grupe said. "We had a rainy game in Jacksonville, so it definitely wasn't an easy first one, but we got out there, we got to work, got the ball rolling. 
 
"Those five weeks in Indy were seriously big for me, big for my career."

 The kicking woes are not an issue isolated to this season. The Rams have a 77.2 field goal percentage over the past four seasons, the second worst in NFL over that span, according to ESPN Research.

 "There's a lot that goes into special teams," Grupe said. "Guys got to cover. We got to put the ball where it's supposed to be. You've got to have elite specialists play to be elite on special teams. So I feel like I can do that.

 "There's a lot of things that we can do on kickoff and bring some consistency in the field goal game."

 Special teams have played a significant role in five of the Rams' nine losses since the start of last season, including the playoffs. After the Rams allowed a 58-yard punt return touchdown that sparked a 16-point comeback by the Seattle Seahawks in Week 16, McVay fired special teams coordinator Chase Blackburn.

 "There are so many different things that you're trying to be able to fix, and then sometimes other problems open up," McVay said. "I felt like that field goal operation was trending in the right direction after all the work. I think we did some good things. I liked the way that we were protecting. Obviously, we can't give up the 'swim sea' area against a player like [Bills outside linebacker Greg] Rousseau in that moment [Monday] night.

 "You just have to lean in, and you have to be able to identify what are the problems? Let's provide some tangible solutions, and let's ultimately be able to bring it to life for the players." 

 And although the Rams are 2-3 through their first five games of the season, four of their games (and all three of their losses) came to 2025 playoff teams.

 Now, they face a stretch that should be easier: In the Rams' next five games, they play the 1-4 Arizona Cardinals  twice, the 3-2 Las Vegas Raiders , 0-5 Los Angeles Chargers and the 1-3-1 Washington Commanders . According to ESPN Analytics, their Week 6 through 10 schedule is the easiest five-game span of any team this season.

 "This isn't the first time that we've had adversity and the first time that we've had some different things that I have to do a better job of," McVay said of the special teams unit. "We'll lean in. We'll go back to work. We'll use these as growth opportunities."

title: Where is the Tennessee Titans' pass rush?
summary: The Titans invested more in the defensive front than any other area when Robert Saleh took over. So far, there hasn't been a significant ROI.
full_text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. -- The Tennessee Titans invested more in their defensive front than any other area when Robert Saleh took over as the coach this past offseason. General manager Mike Borgonzi immediately went to work getting Saleh the players they felt were necessary to develop the effective four-man pass rush that is essential to Saleh's defense. Tennessee committed $71 million in free agency contracts for this year to defensive linemen John Franklin-Myers , Solomon Thomas , Jordan Elliott , Jacob Martin and Malik Herring . The Titans also added to the front by trading defensive tackle T'Vondre Sweat for edge rusher Jermaine Johnson II and by drafting defensive end  Keldric Faulk  with the 31st pick.

   

 So far, there hasn't been a significant return on the investment.

 The Titans' 10-sack total has them tied with the Baltimore Ravens , New Orleans Saints  and Indianapolis Colts for the 25th most in the league through five games. Sitting in the bottom quarter of the league is nowhere near where Tennessee intended to be after all the moves to improve the defensive front.

 "I'm challenging them every day with regards to the fact that we need more," Saleh said Wednesday. "The heartbeat of the defense is the front, at least for the systems that we've ever had." 

 Saleh's preference is to use a four-man pass rush to attack quarterbacks. Rather than generating pressure by blitzing and pulling defenders out of coverage, Saleh's system seeks to control the line of scrimmage by using a high-frequency defensive line rotation. Typically, a defensive lineman will play roughly 60% of the snaps in a game. That rule hasn't applied to longtime Titan and All-Pro pass rusher Jeffery Simmons , who signed a three-year, $105.8 million contract extension with the Titans last June.

 

 If the Titans' pass rush was a music group, Simmons would be the lead singer. He is performing up to the standards set by the coaching staff. The rest of the group is not.

 Tennessee needs someone else to emerge and fill out the band. Opposing offenses are double-teaming Simmons at an 81.1% rate, 11th highest among qualified interior linemen this season, according to ESPN Analytics/NFL Next Gen Stats. That leaves one-on-one opportunities for the rest of the group to exploit, which is not happening.

 "We have to be 100% better," Johnson said. "If they're going to dedicate two or three guys to Jeff, we have to come alive. There's no way around it. We are not doing enough to help Jeff, the defense and the team. That's something I take a lot of pride in. In cases where we are getting one-on-ones, and they slide to Jeff, we have to take advantage of that."

 "The expectation is when you get a one-on-one, the expectation is you win," Saleh said. "With four hands being on Jeff pretty much every snap, we need more from the rest for sure."

 Martin's 2.5 sacks ties him with Simmons for the team lead, and his six quarterback hits are the most on the team. A case can be made for Martin emerging as another option. For the most part, production everywhere else has been lacking. Faulk, a 2026 first-round pick, has one sack on the season and has played only 31.5% of the snaps. There were high hopes for 2025 second-round pick Oluwafemi Oladejo 's continued transition from linebacker to pass rusher in Saleh's scheme that emphasizes getting upfield and attacking. But Oladejo has no sacks and only one pressure this season.

 

 After signing his big contract, Simmons reported to training camp in what he called the best shape of his life with an eye on playing as many snaps as possible. Simmons has played 85.2% of the defensive snaps, including 57 out of 58 snaps in a 10-tackle, one-sack performance during a 12-7 loss to the New York Giants in Week 3. Saleh struggled to recall that level of dominance from any defensive lineman he has coached before.

 According to NFL Tru Media, Simmons has 19 pressures this season, tied for the third most among defensive tackles, including six quick pressures (under 2.5 seconds), tied for the fifth most among defensive tackles. Since the start of the 2025 season, Simmons has 29 quick pressures, the most among defensive tackles over that span.

 Pairing Simmons with Franklin-Myers was supposed to create a formidable duo up front. Franklin-Myers, who posted 7.5 sacks with the Denver Broncos last season, has 1.5 sacks through five games, one of which occurred last week when Houston Texans quarterback C.J. Stroud ran out of bounds behind the line of scrimmage while he was in pursuit.

 Franklin-Myers has also been nursing a back injury, so the Titans haven't been able to fully deploy him in stunt and twist tandems with Simmons. But he's not using the injury as an excuse.

 "It don't matter how I feel because nobody cares," Franklin-Myers told ESPN. "I know for the team to go as we want it to go, it starts with me, it starts with Jeff, it starts with Jermaine. It's on us to make plays."

 Overall, the pass rush is not only failing to get home enough, but it's also failing to impact the quarterback and help force turnovers.

 The Titans' defense is dead last in the league with 0.4 turnovers per game. Not all of it is on the defensive front, but dating back to training camp, Saleh made it clear that unit would be the catalyst for the defense. The front four hasn't caused many turnovers apart from the pressure and hit Simmons had on Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts that forced a bad throw, which was intercepted by nickel corner Marcus Harris . 

 Opposing quarterbacks of the Titans, on average, have 2.99 seconds before the pass, third most in the NFL behind the Bengals (3.06) and Vikings (3.10). That's just not going to cut it, especially with a secondary that lacks marquee players. Saleh has tried to insert Harris as a blitzer off the edge, which has helped, but there is still no consistent pass rush. 

 
How will it get better?

 Titans defensive line coach Aaron Whitecotton says it comes down to better communication and cohesiveness.

 "We have a group that hasn't rushed together, so we've got to continue communicating," Whitecotton said. "You can't stand there and say, 'Hey, I'm going here. You go there.' We got to be able to look at one another and know what we're about to do. We got to be able to be on the same page."

 The next opportunity will come Sunday in an AFC South clash with the Colts (1:00 p.m. ET, Fox). The Colts' offensive line has allowed nine sacks this season, tying them with the Cincinnati Bengals for the fifth fewest in the league. The pass rush will need to be a factor for the Titans to break their 11-game losing streak against their division.
